In chapter 9 we described vibration with one degree of freedom by a viscous damper, and in chapter 10 we carried this over to several degrees of freedom and chose the damping so that the modes still decoupled. We used all of it with one silent assumption: the damper exists and has a known constant. This chapter tests that assumption. It also builds on chapter 3, which promised that a material does not return all its work, and on the chapters on finite elements (7, 12).

The word damping (dušenje) means everything that takes energy from a vibration, so that the amplitude fades with time. The word model means a simplified description that we can put into a calculation: a rule for how the force we feel as damping depends on displacement and velocity. Damping models are therefore different rules for the same experience, that a vibration dies out. The real causes differ, such as friction in a clamp and the inside of steel, but we can calculate with only one rule at a time.

Why does it matter? A cantilever carrying a mass of 50 kg, struck once, loses some energy in every period, yet no damper hangs under it. A machine on rubber mounts passes a smaller force into the ground when the mounts are soft, and damping in the mounts can make this worse. A two-storey frame with one damper under the first floor has a vibration that classical damping cannot describe. In each of these cases the choice of model changes the number the designer gets.

The chapter promises to test the damping model every time, not merely assume it. First we find a measure that lets us compare all the causes, namely the energy a vibration loses in one period. Then we show when another cause may be replaced by a viscous damper and when not, and how damping that arises in the material behaves under vibration at one frequency. Next we describe a material that responds slowly to a load, first with models made of springs and dampers, then with the history of the load. Finally we put this into finite elements, write the vibration in a form that also gives damping that the classical model cannot describe, and look at the damping of a beam and of a string.

20.1 Where the energy of a vibration goes and how we measure it

Cantilever A does come to rest after a blow, and in chapter 9 we described this with a viscous damper, chosen so that \(\zeta = 0{,}01\). No real damper hangs on it. So what does take the energy, and how do we compare causes as different as friction in the clamp, the air around the mass and the inside of the steel? This section looks for one common measure, with which we shall judge every model in the following sections.

Let us draw cantilever A (example 9.7). The bar is clamped into the wall, which is tied to the ground. At its end is the mass \(m\), which after a blow moves up and down with velocity \(\dot q\). Three things can take energy. The first is the joint at the wall: two plates and two bolts hold the bar, and at every swing it slips a little against the plates. The force of dry friction has constant size and points against the slip (section 9.13 of chapter 9, theorem 9.109), so during slip it takes energy. We draw the force \(f_{\mathrm{t}}\) as a double arrow in the gap between plate and bar, because the slip changes direction as the bar swings. The second is the air: the mass pushes the air in front of it, and by the law of action and reaction (Newton's third law) the air pushes the mass back with an equal force. When the mass moves up, the air acts on its top face downwards, so the force \(f_{\mathrm{z}}\) is drawn downwards and ends on that face. The third is the material of the bar. The bar bends as it swings, every piece of steel is stretched and compressed, and this loss is there without joints and without air. TIMO (PDF p. 297) says that there are systems in which the damping of vibration depends mainly on the internal friction (notranje trenje) of the material.

Which of the three prevails in A, these words do not tell. We only know that all three have the same consequence: in every period the vibration loses some energy. That consequence can be measured whatever the cause, and it will be our common measure. First, though, let us see what happens in the material, where no layer slides.

20.1.1 Loss in the material: heat between grains

What loses energy in a piece of steel that we stretch and release? TIMO (PDF pp. 295, 296) describes an experiment with a crystal that is stretched with a pulling force while its temperature is observed.

On the axes we measure the elongation \(q\) horizontally and the pulling force \(P\) vertically. When we pull very slowly, the crystal keeps the temperature of its surroundings all the time, and the force grows along the dashed line \(0\) to \(2\), whose slope is proportional to the modulus of elasticity at constant temperature (the isothermal modulus \(E_{\mathrm{iz}}\), definition 3.1). When we pull quickly, no heat escapes and the crystal cools. The quick pull is the segment \(0\) to \(1\), with a larger slope, the adiabatic modulus \(E_{\mathrm{ad}} > E_{\mathrm{iz}}\) (adiabatic means without exchange of heat). At \(1\) we stop and hold the force constant. The cooled bar slowly warms to the temperature of its surroundings and therefore stretches a little more, which is the horizontal line \(1\) to \(2\). Now we release the load suddenly. The bar contracts along the line \(2\) to \(3\), parallel to \(0\) to \(1\), because this contraction again has no exchange of heat. It warms up in doing so, so after the release it cools to the temperature of its surroundings and contracts a further segment \(3\) to \(0\). The cycle returns to its start and is a parallelogram. At the corner \(3\) the force is zero but the elongation still positive, so the parallelogram leans to the right.

Why is the area of the parallelogram a loss of energy? The work we do on the bar at elongation \(q\) and force \(P\) is the time integral of \(P\,\dot q\), and this is the area under the graph of \(P\) against \(q\) (fundamental theorem of calculus, theorem 3.40). On loading the graph lies above the graph on unloading, so the difference of the two areas is the area of the parallelogram. We prove this in detail in the next section (lemma 20.2). The bar acts with force \(-P\) on whatever pulls it (Newton's third law), in vibration on the mass. So in these axes the loop of the force on the mass is turned over compared with figure 20.3, but the area is the same. This energy does not go into the bar as elastic energy, since after the cycle the bar is back in the same state. It ends as heat that the bar gives to its surroundings. TIMO (PDF p. 296) writes that the difference between the adiabatic and the isothermal modulus is usually small, so the loss of energy per cycle is very small too, but in vibration many cycles follow one another, and such losses are what is called internal friction and damp the motion. In reality heat is exchanged all the time, and instead of the parallelogram we get a rounded loop.

Steel is not a single crystal but many grains with differently oriented crystal lattices. TIMO (PDF pp. 296, 297) says that the cooling during stretching depends on the orientation of the crystal, so temperatures differ from grain to grain. The figure shows two grains with temperatures \(T_1\) and \(T_2\). The grain with the lower temperature \(T_2\) is shaded more strongly, the grain \(T_1\) is cooled less. Heat flows from the warmer to the colder grain across their common boundary, the arrow, and the temperatures even out. This is an additional flow of heat, which a single crystal would not have, and it increases the loss of energy.

How can the loss be increased? By TIMO (PDF p. 297) the heat generated in a grain is proportional to its volume and the exchange of heat to its surface, so the evening out is easier and the loss larger when the grains are made smaller. Let us count on a cube of side \(2d\) and on the same cube cut into eight cubes of side \(d\), drawn in the plane as a square and four squares. The volume is \(8d^3\) in both cases. The surface of the whole cube is \(6\,(2d)^2 = 24\,d^2\), the surface of the eight cubes \(8 \cdot 6d^2 = 48\,d^2\). The surface across which heat flows is thus twice as large when the grains are twice as small. In the plane of the figure the perimeter \(8d\) grows to \(16d\) in the same way. That is why, in systems whose damping depends mainly on the internal friction of the material, we increase the damping with a material of small grains (TIMO, PDF p. 297).

From history

Losses of energy in metals were measured before their cause was known. TIMO (PDF p. 297, footnote 1) reports that the damping capacity (zmožnost dušenja) of various materials was measured by Rowett (1913), and later by Otto Föppl and his collaborators at the Wöhler Institute in Brunswick (1926 to 1929). A measurement tells how much energy a material loses, not where. The importance of the thermoelastic cause of internal friction was shown by the investigations of C. Zener and his associates (1937 to 1941), that is, the flow of heat of figure 20.2. Zener collected the results in the book "Elasticity and Anelasticity of Metals" (1948).

Let us return to the grains and the loop in the material of figure 20.2. All three causes of figure 20.1 have the same consequence: the force that the member exerts on the mass is not a function of the displacement alone, but differs on loading and on unloading. We now write this down exactly.

20.1.2 Work in a period is the area of the loop

What should we measure? The loss of energy in one period of the motion, because this is a number that can be read off a graph of force against displacement whatever the cause. Take one degree of freedom with mass \(m\), coordinate \(q\) and a member that acts on the mass with force \(f\) in the direction of \(q\) (a spring, a damper, a joint or the material, or all at once). Chapter 9 did this for the damper.

Definition 20.1 Energy lost per period (izguba energije v periodi)

Let \(q(t)\) be a continuously differentiable motion with period \(T > 0\), that is \(q(t + T) = q(t)\), and \(f(t)\) a piecewise continuous force (definition 6.8), with which the member acts on the mass in the direction of \(q\), and which also has period \(T\). The energy lost per period (izguba energije v periodi) is the number

\[W_{\mathrm{izg}} = -\int_0^T f(t)\,\dot q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t , \tag{20.1}\]

that is, minus the work of the force \(f\) in one period (definition 8.54, the power is \(f\,\dot q\)). The unit is the joule.

Source: Loss per period as the work of the damping force: CK section 4.7 (PDF p. 126), equations (4.70) and (4.72). The definition with a sign that makes the loss of a damper positive is ours.

Why this name? When the mass is in the same state after a period, it has the same velocity, so the total work of all forces on it in the period is zero. From \(m\,\ddot q = f + Q\), where \(Q\) is the external force, we get after multiplying by \(\dot q\) and integrating over the period \(\big[\tfrac12 m\,\dot q^2\big]_0^T = 0 = \int_0^T f\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t + \int_0^T Q\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t\) (fundamental theorem, theorem 3.40). The external force thus supplies exactly \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) in a period. This is the energy that a force must keep supplying for the motion to stay periodic, as at resonance in chapter 9 (theorem 9.61).

Now let us draw \(f\) against \(q\) over one period. For the damper this is the ellipse of figure 9.27. We ask the same question of every member we know.

We draw the axes: the displacement \(q\) horizontally and the force \(f\) vertically, in each of the four panels. First the spring. Its force is \(-kq\) and it is a single line, since on rising and on falling at the same \(q\) it acts the same. The loop has no area, so a spring loses no energy at any amplitude. In (b) we add a viscous damper: the total force \(-kq - c\,\dot q\) runs along an ellipse, tilted by the spring (the dashed line \(-kq\) is its axis), and the shaded area is \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\). The ellipse is run through counter-clockwise. In (c) is dry friction: on rising the force is \(-F_{\mathrm{t}}\), on falling \(+F_{\mathrm{t}}\), so the loop is a rectangle with sides \(2X\) and \(2F_{\mathrm{t}}\). In (d) is the driving force \(Q_0\cos\Omega t\) at resonance against the displacement \(X\sin\Omega t\). This too is an ellipse, but it is run through clockwise, while the damping force runs the other way. Why does the direction matter? Because the area with its sign is the work, as the lemma that follows proves.

We prove the statement for every motion in which the displacement rises once and falls once in a period. Harmonic motion is such. For others, for instance with two peaks in a period, the curve of force against displacement can make several loops, definition 20.1 still holds, only reading off a single area is lost.

Lemma 20.2 Work in a period and the area of the loop (delo v periodi in ploščina zanke)

Let \(q\) be a continuously differentiable function with period \(T\) that strictly increases on \([0, t_1]\) from \(-X\) to \(X\) and strictly decreases on \([t_1, T]\) from \(X\) to \(-X\), with \(X > 0\). Let \(f\) be piecewise continuous and let there be continuous functions \(F_\uparrow\), \(F_\downarrow\) on \([-X, X]\) with \(f(t) = F_\uparrow(q(t))\) for \(0 \le t < t_1\) and \(f(t) = F_\downarrow(q(t))\) for \(t_1 < t < T\). Then:

  1. \(\displaystyle\int_0^T f\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = \int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{X}\big(F_\uparrow(q) - F_\downarrow(q)\big)\,\mathrm{d}q\).
  2. If \(F_\downarrow \ge F_\uparrow\) on \([-X, X]\), then \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is the area between the graphs of \(F_\downarrow\) and \(F_\uparrow\), that is the area of the loop that the point \((q(t), f(t))\) goes round counter-clockwise. If \(F_\downarrow \le F_\uparrow\), then \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is minus the area of the loop that the point goes round clockwise, and the member supplies energy.
  3. If we add the same continuous function \(G(q)\) to both branches, the integral in item 1 does not change. In particular, a force \(f = G(q)\) that depends on the displacement alone (a spring) has \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 0\).
Proof

We must show three items. The first we get by recognizing on each branch the integral as a difference of values of an antiderivative, the second from the meaning of the difference of graphs, the third from item 1.

  1. Let \(\Phi_\uparrow(y) = \int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{y} F_\uparrow(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\). By the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.40, item 2) \(\Phi_\uparrow\) is differentiable with derivative \(F_\uparrow\), because \(F_\uparrow\) is continuous.
  2. On the open interval \((0, t_1)\) the values \(q(t)\) lie in the open interval \((-X, X)\), where \(\Phi_\uparrow\) has the continuous derivative \(F_\uparrow\). By the chain rule (lemma 8.29, item 3) the function \(t \mapsto \Phi_\uparrow(q(t))\) is therefore differentiable on \((0, t_1)\) with derivative \(F_\uparrow(q(t))\,\dot q(t)\). The function is continuous on \([0, t_1]\), being a composition of continuous functions, and its derivative extends continuously to \([0, t_1]\), being a product of continuous functions.
  3. By the fundamental theorem (item 1) \(\int_0^{t_1} F_\uparrow(q)\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = \Phi_\uparrow(q(t_1)) - \Phi_\uparrow(q(0)) = \Phi_\uparrow(X) - \Phi_\uparrow(-X) = \int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{X} F_\uparrow(q)\,\mathrm{d}q\), because \(\Phi_\uparrow(-X) = 0\).
  4. On the falling branch, with \(\Phi_\downarrow(y) = \int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{y} F_\downarrow\), we get in the same way \(\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{T} F_\downarrow(q)\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = \Phi_\downarrow(q(T)) - \Phi_\downarrow(q(t_1)) = \Phi_\downarrow(-X) - \Phi_\downarrow(X) = -\int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{X} F_\downarrow\,\mathrm{d}q\).
  5. The points \(t_1\) and \(T\) do not change the integral (definition 6.9), so the sum of steps 3 and 4 is item 1.
  6. For item 2, \(F_\downarrow - F_\uparrow \ge 0\) is the height of the region between the graphs at \(q\), so \(\int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{X}(F_\downarrow - F_\uparrow)\,\mathrm{d}q\) is its area. From item 1 and definition 20.1, \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = -\int_0^T f\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t\) is this area. As \(q\) increases the point \((q, f)\) runs along the lower graph \(F_\uparrow\) from left to right, and as \(q\) decreases along the upper graph \(F_\downarrow\) from right to left, that is counter-clockwise. For \(F_\downarrow \le F_\uparrow\) the graphs are swapped and the direction reversed.
  7. For item 3, after adding \(G\) both branches are raised by the same number at every \(q\), and the difference \(F_\uparrow - F_\downarrow\) is the same. For \(F_\uparrow = F_\downarrow = G\) the difference is zero.

Source: Work of the damping force as the area of a loop: CK section 4.7 (PDF p. 127, figure 4.17). The proof is not from the sources.

Let us see what the proof says, and test it on what we know. For the ellipse of chapter 9 take \(q = -X\cos\Omega t\), which increases from \(-X\) to \(X\) on \([0, T/2]\). The damper force \(-c\,\dot q = -c\,\Omega X\sin\Omega t\) equals \(F_\uparrow(q) = -c\,\Omega\sqrt{X^2 - q^2}\), because \(\sin\Omega t \ge 0\) on this branch, and on the falling branch \(F_\downarrow(q) = +c\,\Omega\sqrt{X^2 - q^2}\). The difference is \(F_\downarrow - F_\uparrow = 2c\,\Omega\sqrt{X^2 - q^2}\), which by the lemma has area \(2c\,\Omega\cdot\tfrac12\pi X^2 = \pi\,c\,\Omega X^2\), since \(\int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{X}\sqrt{X^2 - q^2}\,\mathrm{d}q\) is the area of a half disc of radius \(X\) (the area of a disc is \(\pi X^2\)). This is exactly the loss of theorem 9.61.

The first loop of figure 20.3, the spring alone, is the case that the lemma tells apart from the damper, although \(-kq\) is also a force in the direction of \(q\). For \(-kq\) we have \(F_\uparrow = F_\downarrow = -kq\), area zero and \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 0\) by item 3. Let us check by calculation too. For A, \(\int_0^T(-kq)\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = -\tfrac12 k\,[q^2]_0^T = 0\) (fundamental theorem, since \(q(T) = q(0)\)), and NumPy with \(200\,001\) points returns \(0{,}0\) J. The spring thus takes nothing away, whatever the amplitude. That is why the loop of the total force \(-kq - c\,\dot q\) in (b) has the same area as the loop of the damping force alone, the ellipse, as item 3 says: the spring only tilts the ellipse and does not change its area.

The opposite case is the driving force in (d). At resonance \(q = X\sin\Omega t\) and \(Q = Q_0\cos\Omega t\), a loop run clockwise, \(F_\downarrow \le F_\uparrow\). By item 2, \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is minus the area, that is \(-\pi\,Q_0 X = -1{,}0018\) J. A member that goes round its loop in this way is not a damper but a source of energy. At resonance the driving force has exactly the same ellipse as the damping force, only in the opposite direction, which is the balance \(Q_0 = c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\) of chapter 9. The sign of \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) separates a damper from a source.

A case where the hypothesis of the lemma is missing is a motion with two peaks in a period. There \(F_\uparrow\) is not determined by \(q\) alone, since at the same \(q\) the force can differ on the two rises. The work \(\int_0^T f\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t\) is still computed from definition 20.1 (equation (20.1)), but it gives only the total number and not the area of one loop. So we need the lemma only where we want to read the number off a picture.

20.1.3 Loss factor

How do we compare the loss between systems that have different stiffnesses and amplitudes? By dividing by the energy stored in the system. At the largest displacement \(X\) the mass has zero velocity, all the energy is in the spring and equals \(U = \tfrac12 kX^2\), the stored energy (shranjena energija). CK (PDF p. 127) shows this energy in figure 4.17 as the triangle under the line of the spring. Why the factor \(2\pi\)? Because \(2\pi\) is the number of radians of phase in one period, \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}/2\pi\) is the loss per radian, and for a viscous damper at resonance the ratio \(2\pi U/W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) gives the number \(1/(2\zeta)\) (corollary 9.63), which we already know.

Definition 20.3 Loss factor (faktor izgub)

Let the motion be periodic with amplitude \(X > 0\), let the loss per period have the value \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) (definition 20.1), and let \(k > 0\) be the stiffness of the spring that holds the mass. The loss factor (faktor izgub) is the dimensionless number

\[\gamma = \frac{W_{\mathrm{izg}}}{2\pi\,U} , \qquad U = \tfrac12 k X^2 . \tag{20.2}\]

It can depend on the mechanism, on the amplitude \(X\) and on the frequency \(\Omega\) of the motion, while the mass does not appear in the definition.

Source: CK (4.79) (PDF p. 129) introduces \(\gamma\) as the structural damping factor and compares it with the number \(2\zeta r\) of viscous damping (PDF p. 129, (4.82), (4.83)), but does not relate it to the loss of energy. Here we derive it from the energy, and the ratio \(2\pi U/W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is that of chapter 9 (corollary 9.63).

The name says what share of the stored energy is lost: \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 2\pi\gamma\,U\). The letter \(\gamma\) has several meanings in the book, so we separate them. In chapter 1 \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is the engineering shear strain, and \(\gamma\) is a closed curve in section 1.18 (definition 1.136), but here \(\gamma\) is always the loss factor. The modal coordinate of chapter 10 is \(\eta\), so we do not use that letter for the loss factor.

Lemma 20.4 Loss factor of a viscous damper (faktor izgub viskoznega dušilnika)

Let a system with mass \(m\), stiffness \(k\) and viscous damper \(c\) (definition 9.1) move steadily as \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\), let \(r = \Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and let \(\zeta\) be the damping ratio (definition 9.5). Then

\[\gamma = \frac{c\,\Omega}{k} = 2\zeta\,r . \tag{20.3}\]

At resonance (\(r = 1\)) we have \(\gamma = 2\zeta = 1/D(1)\) with the dynamic factor \(D\) (definition 9.53), so \(2\pi U/W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 1/\gamma\) (corollary 9.63).

Proof

We must show equation (20.3) and its special case.

  1. By theorem 9.61 the loss per period is \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \pi\,c\,\Omega X^2\), because the mean power lost is \(\tfrac12 c\,\Omega^2X^2\) and \(T = 2\pi/\Omega\).
  2. By definition 20.3, \(\gamma = \pi\,c\,\Omega X^2/(2\pi\cdot\tfrac12 kX^2) = c\,\Omega/k\).
  3. From \(c = 2\zeta m\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(k = m\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) (definition 9.5) we get \(c\,\Omega/k = 2\zeta\,\Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 2\zeta\,r\).
  4. At \(r = 1\), \(\gamma = 2\zeta\), and \(D(1) = 1/(2\zeta)\) by corollary 9.63.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. CK (4.77), (4.78) (PDF p. 128) for \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) is the same calculation.

Let us try it on A. For viscous \(\zeta = 0{,}01\) and resonance, \(X = 15{,}944\) mm, \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 1{,}0018\) J and \(U = \tfrac12\cdot 62\,720\cdot 0{,}015944^2 = 7{,}9719\) J. So \(\gamma = 1{,}0018/(2\pi\cdot 7{,}9719) = 0{,}0200 = 2\zeta\), as the lemma says. The loss per period is \(2\pi\gamma = 12{,}6\ \%\) of the stored energy. Since \(\gamma = c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}/k = c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X/(kX)\), \(1/\gamma = 50\) is also the ratio of the largest spring force \(kX = 1000\) N to the largest damper force \(c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X = 20\) N. So for A the ellipse in (b) in fact leaves the spring line by only \(\pm 20\) N, while the spring line reaches \(\pm 1000\) N. The loop is thin and shows that the damping is small (on this rests the replacement by an equivalent viscous damper, treated in the next section).

Example 20.5 Loss factor of viscous damping and of friction on cantilever A (faktor izgub viskoznega dušenja in trenja pri konzoli A)

Cantilever A (\(k = 62\,720\) N/m, \(m = 50\) kg, \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 35{,}4175\) 1/s) vibrates at resonance with amplitude \(X\).

  1. Viscous, \(\zeta = 0{,}01\): \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2 = 1{,}0018\) J at \(X = 15{,}944\) mm. The loss factor is \(\gamma = 0{,}0200\). At \(r = 0{,}5\) we get \(\gamma = 0{,}0100\), at \(r = 2\) we get \(0{,}0400\), at any amplitude the same (by lemma 20.4 it depends on \(r\) alone).
  2. Friction \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N: on rising \(F_\uparrow = -F_{\mathrm{t}}\), on falling \(F_\downarrow = +F_{\mathrm{t}}\), so by lemma 20.2 \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \int_{-\mathrm{X}}^{X}\big(F_\downarrow - F_\uparrow\big)\,\mathrm{d}q = 2F_{\mathrm{t}}\cdot 2X = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\). At \(X = 15{,}944\) mm this is \(0{,}1276\) J, and \(\gamma = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X/(\pi k X^2) = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}/(\pi k X) = 0{,}00255\). That is \(12{,}7\ \%\) of the loss of the viscous damping.
  3. The same friction at smaller amplitudes: \(X = 5\) mm gives \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 0{,}0400\) J, \(U = 0{,}784\) J, \(\gamma = 0{,}00812\). \(X = 1\) mm gives \(0{,}00800\) J, \(0{,}03136\) J, \(\gamma = 0{,}0406\).

The third item shows the difference. For the viscous damper \(\gamma\) does not depend on the amplitude, for friction it is proportional to \(1/X\): the smaller the vibration, the larger the share of energy lost. So for friction there is no single number \(\gamma\), only a number at a given amplitude. The two mechanisms also differ in what they depend on: for the viscous one the loss per period is proportional to \(\Omega X^2\), for friction to \(X\) and independent of the frequency. What this means for the equation of motion and when we may replace the loop by an ellipse is told by the next section (section 20.2).

For steel we do not state a number for the loss factor here, because TIMO does not give one on these pages (PDF pp. 296, 297). We shall use the loss factor to judge all the models of this chapter: the viscous one (section 20.2), the hysteretic one (section 20.3) and the viscoelastic models of the material (section 20.4).

20.2 Equivalent viscous damping

At resonance, cantilever \(A\) of section 9.1 with viscous damping \(\zeta = 0{,}01\) has amplitude \(X = 15{,}944\) mm and loses \(1{,}0018\) J in every period (theorem 9.61). In example 9.110 we added dry friction of force \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N. What is the amplitude at resonance now? The equation of motion

\[m\,\ddot q + c\,\dot q + k\,q + F_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q) = Q_0\cos\Omega t\]

is not linear, so the methods of chapter 9 do not solve it: they relied on the sum of two solutions being a solution again, and on the complex form of the harmonic response (theorem 9.52). Here we look for another way. In steady vibration the exciting force supplies as much energy as the damping removes (theorem 9.61), so we do not need the shape of the damping force, only how much energy it removes in a period. If we know that number we can take it as the measure and replace the damper by a viscous one that removes the same amount.

The model is system \(A\) of section 9.1: a mass \(m = 50\) kg on a spring \(k = 62\,720\) N/m, the coordinate \(q\) is the displacement of the mass. Besides the spring force and the exciting force \(Q = Q_0\cos\Omega t\), the mass is acted on by a damping force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}(t)\) (N), produced by any mechanism: a viscous damper (\(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -c\,\dot q\), definition 9.1), friction, or something else. The letter \(c\) in this section always means the coefficient of a dashpot as in chapter 9, and never the wave speed of chapter 13. The assumption, which we name because it cannot be justified in advance, is that the motion is (approximately) harmonic, \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) with amplitude \(X > 0\), circular frequency \(\Omega > 0\) and period \(T_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi/\Omega\). Section 20.2.2 below says how close this is to the truth, with numbers.

How much energy does the mechanism remove? We multiply the equation of motion \(m\,\ddot q + k\,q = Q + f_{\mathrm{D}}\) by the velocity, as in lemma 9.59. There the equation held \(-c\,\dot q\), here the right side holds a general force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\), and we get \(\mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}/\mathrm{d}t = Q\,\dot q + f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q\) for the stored energy \(\mathcal{E} = \tfrac12 m\,\dot q^2 + \tfrac12 k\,q^2\). The term \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q\) is the power of the damping force (definition 8.54), its integral over a period is the work. The energy lost in a period is therefore

\[W_{\mathrm{izg}} = -\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}} f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{20.4}\]

The sign is chosen so that \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} > 0\) for every real damping that slows the motion. What does this integral mean on a plot of the force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\) against the displacement \(q\)? By lemma 20.2 (section 20.1), \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is the area of the loop that the point \((q, f_{\mathrm{D}})\) traces in a period. We draw the loop (figure 20.4).

On the horizontal axis we plot the displacement \(q\), on the vertical axis the damping force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\), and with the marks \(\pm X\) we mark the extreme positions between which the mass moves. In dry friction the force has the constant magnitude \(F_{\mathrm{t}}\) and always points against the velocity. When the mass moves to the right (\(\dot q > 0\)), \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -F_{\mathrm{t}}\), so this is the lower side of the rectangle from \(-X\) to \(X\). At the right end the velocity reverses and the force jumps to \(+F_{\mathrm{t}}\) while the mass moves to the left, this is the upper side. The point travels around the rectangle counterclockwise, like around the ellipse of the viscous damper in figure 9.27. The area of the rectangle is the width \(2X\) times the height \(2F_{\mathrm{t}}\),

\[W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 2X\cdot 2F_{\mathrm{t}} = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}\,X ,\]

since in every period the mass covers the distance \(4X\) (\(2X\) to the right and \(2X\) back) against a force of constant magnitude \(F_{\mathrm{t}}\). At \(X = 13{,}914\) mm this is \(0{,}1113\) J.

For a viscous damper with coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) and the same motion, the loop is the ellipse with the same horizontal semi-axis \(X\), since the displacement is the same, and vertical semi-axis \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\), since \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\dot q\) and \(\dot q\) has amplitude \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\) (at resonance \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\)). Its area is \(\pi\,X\cdot c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\) (the area of an ellipse with semi-axes \(a\) and \(b\) is \(\pi a b\), as used in figure 9.27). We choose \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) so that the areas agree: \(\pi\,c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2 = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\) gives \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi = 2{,}5465\) N. The vertical semi-axis of the ellipse is therefore \(2{,}5465\) N and exceeds \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N: the ellipse sticks out of the rectangle at \(q = 0\) and does not reach it at the corners, and the two loops enclose the same area. The direction of travel on the ellipse is the same as on the rectangle.

This is the rule that we introduce as a definition. The name has a reason: the damper is "equivalent" by what it removes (\(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) in a period), and "viscous" because its force is proportional to the velocity, so the equation of motion stays linear. For a viscous damper the loss is \(\pi\,c\,\Omega X^2\) by theorem 9.61, so we get \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) by setting this loss equal to the real one.

Definition 20.6 Equivalent viscous damping (enakovredno viskozno dušenje)

Let \(q(t) = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) be a motion with amplitude \(X > 0\) and circular frequency \(\Omega > 0\), \(T_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi/\Omega\), and let \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\) be a piecewise continuous function of time with period \(T_{\mathrm{p}}\) (the damping force in this motion). Let the energy lost in a period \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) be equation (20.4). The equivalent viscous damping coefficient is the number

\[c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{W_{\mathrm{izg}}}{\pi\,\Omega\,X^2} \quad (\mathrm{N\,s/m}) \tag{20.5}\]

and the equivalent damping ratio is \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = c_{\mathrm{eq}}/(2\sqrt{km})\) (definition 9.5). A viscous damper with coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) in the same motion loses exactly \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) in a period.

Source: CK section 4.7 (PDF p. 125 to 128): equation (4.75) (PDF p. 127) writes \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = -\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{D}}/(\pi\,\Omega\,U^2)\), where \(\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{D}} = -W_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is the work of the damping force in a cycle and \(U\) is our \(X\). The equivalent damping ratio is in equations (4.76) to (4.78) (PDF p. 128). Our notation uses the letter \(q\) and \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} > 0\) as in definition 20.1.

The number \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) is not a property of the mechanism but of the mechanism in a given motion: it depends on \(X\) and in general on \(\Omega\). For an actual viscous damper (\(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -c\,\dot q\)) theorem 9.61 gives \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = c\) for every \(X\) and \(\Omega\), since then \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \pi\,c\,\Omega X^2\). Is equating the energies the only sensible choice, or could we take something else, say the same peak force? The answer is in the next theorem. We draw the friction force over a period (figure 20.5).

We label the horizontal axis with \(\theta = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\), an angle that grows by \(2\pi\) in a period, and the displacement is \(q = X\sin\theta\) while its velocity is proportional to \(\cos\theta\). The dry friction force is piecewise constant: \(-F_{\mathrm{t}}\) while \(\cos\theta > 0\) (from \(0\) to \(\pi/2\) and from \(3\pi/2\) to \(2\pi\)), and \(+F_{\mathrm{t}}\) in between, when the velocity is negative. The viscous force \(-c\,\dot q = -c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\cos\theta\) is a cosine of amplitude \(c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\), the blue curve for the chosen \(c = c_{\mathrm{eq}}\). Which multiple of the velocity fits friction best? We measure the difference of the two forces, the remainder \(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c\,\dot q\), by the integral of its square over a period, \(\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c\,\dot q)^2\,\mathrm{d}t\), which is \(T_{\mathrm{p}}\) times the mean square. We take the square because it does not depend on the sign of the deviation and squares are easy to work with (the proof below is a single completed square). The theorem says that the best \(c\) is exactly \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\).

Theorem 20.7 The energy rule is the best viscous fit (pravilo energije je najboljši viskozni približek)

Let \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) with \(X > 0\), \(\Omega > 0\), \(T_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi/\Omega\) and let \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\) be a piecewise continuous function with period \(T_{\mathrm{p}}\). For a real number \(c\) let

\[R(c) = \int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}\bigl(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c\,\dot q\bigr)^2\,\mathrm{d}t .\]

Then:

  1. \(R(c) = R(c_{\mathrm{eq}}) + \pi\,\Omega X^2\,(c - c_{\mathrm{eq}})^2\) with \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) from definition 20.6. The function \(R\) therefore has exactly one minimum, at \(c = c_{\mathrm{eq}}\).
  2. The remainder \(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\dot q\) is orthogonal to the velocity: \(\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}\bigl(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\dot q\bigr)\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\). So the remainder does no work in a period.
Proof

We must show that \(R\) is a quadratic function with leading coefficient \(\pi\,\Omega X^2\) and vertex at \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\).

  1. We expand the square: \(R(c) = \int f_{\mathrm{D}}^2\,\mathrm{d}t + 2c\int f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t + c^2\int \dot q^2\,\mathrm{d}t\), all integrals over \([0, T_{\mathrm{p}}]\). The integrals exist because the integrands are piecewise continuous.
  2. From \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) we get \(\dot q = -\Omega X\sin(\Omega t - \varphi)\) (theorem 8.12), and by lemma 9.60 (item 2 with \(a = -\varphi\)) \(\int\dot q^2\,\mathrm{d}t = \Omega^2X^2\,T_{\mathrm{p}}/2 = \pi\,\Omega X^2\).
  3. By equation (20.4), \(\int f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = -W_{\mathrm{izg}}\), and by equation (20.5) \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\pi\,\Omega X^2\). With \(A = \pi\,\Omega X^2 > 0\) we therefore have \(R(c) = \int f_{\mathrm{D}}^2\,\mathrm{d}t - 2c\,c_{\mathrm{eq}}A + c^2A\).
  4. We complete the square: \(c^2A - 2c\,c_{\mathrm{eq}}A = A\,(c - c_{\mathrm{eq}})^2 - A\,c_{\mathrm{eq}}^2\), so \(R(c) = A\,(c - c_{\mathrm{eq}})^2 + \bigl(\int f_{\mathrm{D}}^2\,\mathrm{d}t - A\,c_{\mathrm{eq}}^2\bigr)\). The binomial in the bracket does not contain \(c\) and equals \(R(c_{\mathrm{eq}})\) (insert \(c = c_{\mathrm{eq}}\)). Since \(A > 0\) and \((c - c_{\mathrm{eq}})^2 \ge 0\) with equality exactly at \(c = c_{\mathrm{eq}}\), this is item 1.
  5. Item 2: \(\int(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c_{\mathrm{eq}}\dot q)\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = -W_{\mathrm{izg}} + c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\pi\,\Omega X^2 = 0\) by steps 2 and 3.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. CK (4.75) (PDF p. 127) gives the energy rule, not the property of the best fit.

The proof showed that the two rules are one and the same: whoever equates the energy lost in a period also finds the viscous force that is closest to the real one in the mean square. The reason is item 2: the remainder is orthogonal to the velocity, its work is zero, so the real force and the substitute do the same work in a period. We read figure 20.5 like this: the blue curve is the projection of the orange one onto the direction of the velocity (like the shadow of a vector on a line, hence the name "projection"), and the grey curve is what remains of the projection. For friction the square root of the mean square of the remainder is \(\sqrt{1 - 8/\pi^2} = 0{,}4352\) times the square root of the mean square of the friction force itself, that is \(43{,}5\ \%\). The number comes from item 2: since the remainder is orthogonal to the velocity, the mean square of the force splits into the mean square of the remainder and the mean square of the blue curve, as in Pythagoras' theorem. The friction force has mean square \(F_{\mathrm{t}}^2\), the blue cosine curve of amplitude \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi\) has \((4F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi)^2/2 = 8F_{\mathrm{t}}^2/\pi^2\) (lemma 9.60), so \(F_{\mathrm{t}}^2(1 - 8/\pi^2)\) is left for the remainder. As a force the remainder is therefore large, but in a harmonic motion it does not affect the energy in a period, and in describing the motion we neglect it. Section 20.2.2 shows what we neglect and how little it contributes.

The theorem holds for every mechanism. We test it on two that we already know: dry friction, and the quadratic drag of air or a liquid.

Corollary 20.8 Equivalent damping of dry friction (enakovredno dušenje suhega trenja)

For \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -F_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q)\) and \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) we have \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}\,X\) and

\[c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{4F_{\mathrm{t}}}{\pi\,\Omega\,X} , \qquad \zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{2F_{\mathrm{t}}}{\pi\,k\,X}\,\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{n}}}{\Omega} . \tag{20.6}\]
Proof

We must show the energy loss and from it \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\).

  1. Piece by piece, \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q = -F_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q)\,\dot q = -F_{\mathrm{t}}\,|\dot q|\), so \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = F_{\mathrm{t}}\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}|\dot q|\,\mathrm{d}t\) by equation (20.4).
  2. \(|\dot q| = \Omega X\,|\sin(\Omega t - \varphi)|\) has period \(T_{\mathrm{p}}\), so we may take the integral over \([0, T_{\mathrm{p}}]\) over \([\varphi/\Omega, \varphi/\Omega + T_{\mathrm{p}}]\) instead (lemma 9.86, item 3), where \(\Omega t - \varphi\) runs from \(0\) to \(2\pi\). The sine is nonnegative on the first half of this interval and nonpositive on the second, each half lasts \(T_{\mathrm{p}}/2\), and the integral of the magnitude of the sine over a half is \(2/\Omega\) (fundamental theorem 3.40, since \(\bigl(-\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)/\Omega\bigr)' = \sin(\Omega t - \varphi)\)). Hence \(\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}|\dot q|\,\mathrm{d}t = \Omega X\cdot 2\cdot 2/\Omega = 4X\), which is exactly the path of the mass in a period, from \(-X\) to \(X\) and back.
  3. \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\), and by equation (20.5) \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X/(\pi\,\Omega X^2) = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}/(\pi\,\Omega X)\).
  4. \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = c_{\mathrm{eq}}/(2m\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}})\) (since \(\sqrt{km} = m\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\)) and \(m\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = k\) give \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}/(2\pi\,m\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\Omega X) = (2F_{\mathrm{t}}/(\pi\,k\,X))(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}/\Omega)\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. The loss \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\) is the geometric work of friction on the path \(4X\), CK (3.45) to (3.50) (PDF p. 89) gives the equation of motion with friction.

For \(A\) at resonance and \(X = 13{,}914\) mm, \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = 4\cdot 2/(\pi\cdot 35{,}4175\cdot 0{,}013914) = 5{,}167\) N s/m, that is \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = 0{,}00146\). The viscous damping of system \(A\) is \(c = 35{,}418\) N s/m (\(\zeta = 0{,}01\)), so friction adds only about a seventh (\(14{,}6\ \%\) of the coefficient). We note that the \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) of friction falls with frequency and with amplitude. The loss \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\) does not depend on the frequency at all and grows only in proportion to \(X\), while the loss \(\pi\,c\,\Omega X^2\) of a viscous damper grows with \(\Omega\) and with \(X^2\), so at a larger \(\Omega\) or \(X\) the coefficient that gives the same loss must be smaller.

Corollary 20.9 Equivalent damping of quadratic drag (enakovredno dušenje kvadratnega upora)

For \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -a\,|\dot q|\,\dot q\) with \(a > 0\) (N s²/m²) and \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) we have \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \tfrac{8}{3}\,a\,\Omega^2X^3\) and

\[c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{8}{3\pi}\,a\,\Omega\,X . \tag{20.7}\]
Proof

We must show the energy loss and from it \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\).

  1. From \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\,\dot q = -a\,|\dot q|^3\), equation (20.4) gives \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = a\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}|\dot q|^3\,\mathrm{d}t = a\,\Omega^3X^3\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}|\sin(\Omega t - \varphi)|^3\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  2. With \(\theta = \Omega t - \varphi\) the integral over a period is \((1/\Omega)\int_0^{2\pi}|\sin\theta|^3\,\mathrm{d}\theta = (2/\Omega)\int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta\) (the interval \([-\varphi, 2\pi - \varphi]\) is shifted to \([0, 2\pi]\) by lemma 9.86, item 3), since \(|\sin|\) is periodic with period \(\pi\) (lemma 8.10).
  3. Because \(\sin^3\theta = \sin\theta\,(1 - \cos^2\theta)\) we have \(\bigl(-\cos\theta + \tfrac13\cos^3\theta\bigr)' = \sin\theta - \cos^2\theta\sin\theta = \sin^3\theta\). By the fundamental theorem 3.40, \(\int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \bigl(1 - \tfrac13\bigr) - \bigl(-1 + \tfrac13\bigr) = \tfrac43\).
  4. So the integral over a period is \((2/\Omega)\cdot\tfrac43 = 8/(3\Omega)\) and \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \tfrac83\,a\,\Omega^2X^3\).
  5. By equation (20.5), \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \tfrac83\,a\,\Omega^2X^3/(\pi\,\Omega X^2) = \tfrac{8}{3\pi}\,a\,\Omega\,X\).

Source: CK example 4.4 (PDF p. 127 to 128) treats the same drag and obtains \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = 8\,a\,\Omega\,U/(3\pi)\) (p. 128, the numerator 8 stands in the text of the page). Steps 1 to 5 are ours.

A check with SymPy and NumPy: for \(a = 1\) N s²/m², \(X = 10\) mm and \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) the numerical projection of theorem 20.7 gives \(0{,}300633\) N s/m, and formula (20.7) gives \(8\cdot 35{,}4175\cdot 0{,}01/(3\pi) = 0{,}300633\) N s/m as well. For friction the same check gives \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = 5{,}1674\) N s/m from least squares and \(5{,}1674\) from formula (20.6). For quadratic drag \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) grows with the amplitude, for friction it falls: the first removes proportionally more energy at large displacements, the second at small ones.

A real joint usually has several mechanisms at once: a viscous damper, friction in the connections, air drag. Must we compute each one separately, or can we add them into one number?

Corollary 20.10 Sum of mechanisms (vsota mehanizmov)

Let \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = f_1 + f_2 + \dots + f_{\mathrm{N}}\) be a sum of piecewise continuous functions with period \(T_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\). If \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the equivalent coefficient of the force \(f_{\mathrm{j}}\) in this motion, then

\[W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^N W_{\mathrm{j}} , \qquad c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^N c_{\mathrm{j}} , \qquad \zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^N \zeta_{\mathrm{j}} . \tag{20.8}\]
Proof

We must show that the energy is linear in \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\).

  1. By equation (20.4), \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = -\int(f_1 + \dots + f_{\mathrm{N}})\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = \sum_{\mathrm{j}}\bigl(-\int f_{\mathrm{j}}\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t\bigr) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} W_{\mathrm{j}}\) by linearity of the integral (lemma 3.39).
  2. Division by \(\pi\,\Omega X^2\) by equation (20.5) gives \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{j}}\), and division by \(2\sqrt{km}\) gives \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}}\zeta_{\mathrm{j}}\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. CK (§4.7, PDF p. 125 to 128) treats each mechanism separately.

The corollary holds for the same motion: we add the \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\) at the same \(X\) and \(\Omega\). The sum is the number \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) that we use in the formulas of chapter 9. For \(A\) the viscous part is \(\zeta = 0{,}01\) and the friction adds \(0{,}00146\) at \(X = 13{,}914\) mm, so \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = 0{,}01146\). At another amplitude the addition would be different, so the correct order is: first solve for \(X\) from the energy balance, then compute \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) from it. The theorem below does this.

20.2.1 Resonance with friction

We return to the opening question. At resonance, \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), a viscous system has the phase lag \(\varphi = 90^\circ\) by theorem 9.52 (\(\cos\varphi = 0\) because \(k - m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = 0\)), and so does the system with equivalent viscous damping, so \(q = X\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) and the force \(Q_0\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) is in phase with the velocity \(\dot q = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\). The exciting force therefore always points in the same direction as the velocity and supplies the largest possible energy in a period. How much is this, and when do friction and viscosity use it up?

Theorem 20.11 Resonance with dry friction (resonanca s trenjem)

Let a system with mass \(m > 0\) and spring \(k > 0\) (\(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m}\)) have a viscous coefficient \(c \ge 0\), friction \(F_{\mathrm{t}} > 0\) and a force \(Q_0\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) (\(Q_0 > 0\)). Let \(T = 2\pi/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). Then:

  1. Every solution \(q\) with period \(T\) and a continuous velocity satisfies
    \[\int_0^T Q_0\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t)\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = \int_0^T\bigl(c\,\dot q^2 + F_{\mathrm{t}}\,|\dot q|\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t .\]
  2. For the trial motion \(q = X\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) with \(X > 0\) (a harmonic approximation that does not solve the equation of motion exactly) the two sides of this equation evaluate to \(\pi\,Q_0\,X = \pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2 + 4F_{\mathrm{t}}\,X\). For \(c > 0\) this equality holds exactly for
    \[X = \frac{\pi\,Q_0 - 4F_{\mathrm{t}}}{\pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}} , \tag{20.9}\]
    which requires \(4F_{\mathrm{t}} < \pi\,Q_0\).
  3. For \(c = 0\) and \(4F_{\mathrm{t}} \ne \pi\,Q_0\) the equality of item 2 holds for no \(X > 0\): no trial motion \(q = X\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) satisfies the energy balance.
Proof

We must show first the energy balance over a period, then evaluate it for \(q = X\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\).

  1. We multiply the equation \(m\,\ddot q + c\,\dot q + k\,q + F_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q) = Q_0\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) by the velocity. As in lemma 9.59, \(\mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}/\mathrm{d}t = Q_0\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t)\,\dot q - c\,\dot q^2 - F_{\mathrm{t}}\,|\dot q|\), since \(\mathrm{sgn}(\dot q)\,\dot q = |\dot q|\).
  2. Because \(q\) is periodic with period \(T\), so is \(\dot q\), and hence \(\mathcal{E}(T) = \mathcal{E}(0)\). By the fundamental theorem 3.40, \(0 = \int_0^T \mathrm{d}\mathcal{E}/\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}t\), and this is item 1.
  3. With \(q = X\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) we have \(\dot q = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\). By lemma 9.60 (item 2 with \(a = 0\)), \(\int_0^T Q_0\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t)\,\dot q\,\mathrm{d}t = Q_0\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\,T/2 = \pi\,Q_0X\) and \(\int_0^T c\,\dot q^2\,\mathrm{d}t = \pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2\). By step 2 of corollary 20.8, \(\int_0^T F_{\mathrm{t}}|\dot q|\,\mathrm{d}t = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\).
  4. Division by \(X > 0\) gives \(\pi\,Q_0 = \pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X + 4F_{\mathrm{t}}\), so equation (20.9). Positivity of \(X\) requires \(\pi\,Q_0 > 4F_{\mathrm{t}}\) when \(c > 0\).
  5. For \(c = 0\) the equation becomes \(\pi\,Q_0X = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\), that is \(\pi\,Q_0 = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}\) after division by \(X \ne 0\). If this condition is violated, the equation has no solution \(X > 0\), which is item 3.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. CK treats resonance only with viscous damping (see theorem 9.54). The comparison with RK4 time stepping is in num-02.py.

For \(A\), \(\pi Q_0 = 62{,}832\) N and \(4F_{\mathrm{t}} = 8\) N, so \(X = (62{,}832 - 8)/(\pi\cdot 35{,}418\cdot 35{,}4175) = 13{,}914\) mm. Viscous damping alone, \(4F_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\), gives \(20/(35{,}418\cdot 35{,}4175) = 15{,}944\) mm as in chapter 9. Friction \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N, a tenth of the exciting force \(Q_0 = 20\) N, reduces the amplitude by \(12{,}7\ \%\). In terms of energy: in a period the force supplies \(\pi Q_0 X = \pi\cdot 20\cdot 0{,}013914 = 0{,}8742\) J, of which viscosity takes \(\pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2 = 0{,}7629\) J and friction \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X = 0{,}1113\) J, together \(0{,}8742\) J, equal to the energy supplied. We get the same with the replacement: the total coefficient is \(c + c_{\mathrm{eq}} = 35{,}418 + 5{,}167 = 40{,}585\) N s/m and the resonance formula of chapter 9, \(X = Q_0/(c_{\mathrm{total}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}})\), gives \(20/(40{,}585\cdot 35{,}4175) = 13{,}914\) mm.

The trial motion is not an exact solution: with it \(m\ddot q + k q = 0\), and the equation of motion would require \(F_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t) = (Q_0 - c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X)\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\), which fails for \(F_{\mathrm{t}} > 0\) because the sign function is not a multiple of the cosine. The theorem therefore does not say whether the motion really settles at \(X = 13{,}914\) mm. We check this by time stepping (fourth-order Runge-Kutta, 200 steps per period, smoothed sign function, 400 periods, computed in num-02.py): the peak in period 400 is \(13{,}9138\) mm, the fundamental component \(13{,}9138\) mm and the energy formula \(13{,}9138\) mm, all agreeing to four decimals. Figure 20.6 shows how the amplitude settles.

On the horizontal axis we plot the number of periods \(n\), on the vertical axis the peak displacement \(X\). The system starts from rest, at \(n = 0\) we have \(X = 0\). Without damping, the dashed line, the peak grows by \(\pi Q_0/k = 1{,}0018\) mm per period, because the force supplies \(\pi Q_0 X\) in every period and \(\mathcal{E} = \tfrac12 kX^2\) (we derive the increment \(\pi Q_0/k\) two paragraphs below, with \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\)). The grey curve, given by viscosity alone, is stopped by the damper at \(15{,}944\) mm, when the loss \(\pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2\) reaches the energy supplied. The blue curve is damping with friction: it settles lower, at \(13{,}914\) mm, and has \(6{,}376\) mm after \(n = 10\) periods, \(9{,}893\) mm after \(20\), \(12{,}769\) mm after \(40\) and \(13{,}821\) mm after \(80\).

Why is there no settling with friction alone? This is the near miss of the theorem, item 3.

Take friction without viscosity (\(c = 0\)). At resonance with \(Q_0 = 20\) N and \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N the energy supplied is \(\pi Q_0X = 62{,}83\,X\) (J, \(X\) in m) and the loss of friction is \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X = 8\,X\). The difference \((\pi Q_0 - 4F_{\mathrm{t}})\,X = 54{,}83\,X\) is positive for every \(X\): friction never catches up with the force. The loss and the energy supplied are both proportional to \(X\), so their ratio does not depend on the amplitude and there is no \(X\) at which they would be equal. For a viscous damper or for quadratic drag the loss grows with a higher power of \(X\) (\(X^2\) or \(X^3\)), so the line of the energy supplied and the curve of the loss intersect at a finite \(X\).

How much does the amplitude grow in each period? The energy at a turning point is \(\tfrac12 k X^2\), and in a period it grows by approximately \((\pi Q_0 - 4F_{\mathrm{t}})\,\bar X\) with \(\bar X\) the mean peak in that period (we compute the energy supplied and the friction loss as if the motion in that period were harmonic with amplitude \(\bar X\)). From \(\tfrac12 k(X_{\mathrm{n}+1}^2 - X_{\mathrm{n}}^2) = \tfrac12 k\,(X_{\mathrm{n}+1} - X_{\mathrm{n}})(X_{\mathrm{n}+1} + X_{\mathrm{n}}) = k\,\bar X\,(X_{\mathrm{n}+1} - X_{\mathrm{n}})\) with \(\bar X = (X_{\mathrm{n}} + X_{\mathrm{n}+1})/2\) we get \(X_{\mathrm{n}+1} - X_{\mathrm{n}} \approx (\pi Q_0 - 4F_{\mathrm{t}})/k = 0{,}8742\) mm: the growth is a straight line, not an exponential curve. Time stepping confirms: after \(5\), \(10\) and \(20\) periods the peak is \(4{,}159\), \(8{,}530\) and \(17{,}272\) mm, with a mean increment from the fifth period on of \(0{,}8742\) mm per period (figure 20.6, the orange line). Without friction the increment would be \(1{,}0018\) mm. Friction \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N reduces the increment to \(0{,}8726\) of its former value but does not stop the growth. For \(F_{\mathrm{t}} > \pi Q_0/4 = 15{,}708\) N the loss would exceed the energy supplied at every amplitude and a harmonic motion could not last. What happens instead (the mass stops and starts again) the harmonic model does not say.

20.2.2 When the replacement is allowed

Replacing a damper by an equivalent viscous one rests on the assumption that the motion is harmonic. Theorem 20.7 tells us what we neglect: the remainder \(f_{\mathrm{D}} + c_{\mathrm{eq}}\dot q\) of figure 20.5 has a root mean square of \(43{,}5\ \%\) of the root mean square of the friction force, and it consists of higher harmonic components. How large a deviation do they cause? The dry friction force \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -F_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{sgn}(\cos\theta)\) has, by lemma 9.87 (orthogonality of the trigonometric system), an expansion in \(\cos n\theta\). The coefficient is \(a_{\mathrm{n}} = (1/\pi)\int_0^{2\pi}f_{\mathrm{D}}\cos n\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = -(F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi)\int_0^{2\pi}\mathrm{sgn}(\cos\theta)\cos n\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta\). By the symmetries \(\theta \to -\theta\) and \(\theta \to \pi - \theta\) the integral is \(4\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos n\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = 4\sin(n\pi/2)/n\) for odd \(n\), so \(a_1 = -4F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi\) (this is exactly the blue \(-c_{\mathrm{eq}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X\cos\theta\)) and \(a_3 = +4F_{\mathrm{t}}/(3\pi) = 0{,}8488\) N. The third-harmonic force with amplitude \(0{,}8488\) N drives the system at frequency \(3\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), where by theorem 9.52 the amplitude of the response is \(0{,}8488\,|H(3\omega_{\mathrm{n}})|\) with \(|H| = 1/\sqrt{(k - 9m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2)^2 + (3c\omega_{\mathrm{n}})^2}\). For \(A\), \(k - 9m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = -8k = -501\,760\) N/m and \(3c\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 3763\) N/m, so \(|H| = 1{,}993\cdot 10^{-6}\) m/N and the response is \(1{,}69\cdot 10^{-3}\) mm, that is \(1{,}2\cdot 10^{-4}\) of the amplitude \(X = 13{,}914\) mm. This deviation is almost exactly \(-1{,}69\cdot 10^{-3}\cos 3\theta\) mm (the phase shift is only \(3c\omega_{\mathrm{n}}/(8k) = 0{,}0075\) rad), and at the peak of the fundamental component, at \(\theta = \pi/2\), \(\cos 3\theta = 0\). The peak and the fundamental component therefore differ in time stepping by less than \(10^{-4}\) mm, and formula (20.9) gives the true amplitude to four decimals. The smallness has a reason: at resonance the system is not in resonance with the third harmonic, its response is \(1/8\) of the static one (\(8k\) in the denominator), and the friction force is already a small part of the excitation (\(4F_{\mathrm{t}}/\pi = 2{,}5465\) N against \(Q_0 = 20\) N).

The replacement is therefore valid when three conditions hold:

  1. The motion is close to harmonic: the higher components of the damping force are small and the corresponding response smaller still. For \(A\) at resonance with friction \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 0{,}1\,Q_0\) this share is \(1{,}2\cdot 10^{-4}\). With larger friction or a weaker excitation, where the mass stops in between (sticks), the motion is no longer close to harmonic and the replacement fails.
  2. The damping is light, the ratio \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) is small (at resonance \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = 0{,}0115\) for \(A\)). The resonance peak is then narrow, the half-power band is \(2\zeta\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) wide (theorem 9.62), and the system already filters the harmonic components outside this band.
  3. The replacement holds for one amplitude and one frequency: \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) is a number at \(X\) and \(\Omega\), and if \(X\) changes, \(c_{\mathrm{eq}}\) changes too. Free vibration shows this last point.

Free vibration with friction has a known answer: by theorem 9.109 the amplitude falls linearly, by \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}/k = 0{,}12755\) mm per full vibration, and in example 9.110 the mass starting at \(5\) mm stops after \(39\) vibrations. What would we get if we computed \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) from the first vibration and used it as a fixed number? By equation (20.6) \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = 2u_{\mathrm{D}}/(\pi X)\) with \(u_{\mathrm{D}} = F_{\mathrm{t}}/k = 0{,}03189\) mm, at \(X = 5\) mm this is \(0{,}00406\). With it the decay would be exponential with a peak ratio \(\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}} = 0{,}9748\) per vibration and after \(39\) vibrations the peak would still be \(5\cdot 0{,}3697 = 1{,}85\) mm (theorem 9.107), whereas the real motion stops, its peak at \(39\) vibrations is \(5 - 39\cdot 0{,}12755 = 0{,}025\) mm. The reason: \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} \propto 1/X\) and so it grows as the amplitude falls. At \(X = 1\) mm it is \(0{,}0203\), at \(0{,}5\) mm \(0{,}0406\) and at \(0{,}1531\) mm \(0{,}1326\). The decrement that we measure between the last two peaks (\(0{,}2806\) and \(0{,}1531\) mm) gave \(\zeta = 0{,}0960\) in example 9.110, and this is close to the equivalent ratio at the middle of these two peaks, \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}(0{,}217\ \mathrm{mm}) = 0{,}094\) (figure 9.57). The number \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) of friction is therefore a reading at a single amplitude.

Summary: the damping force of any mechanism is replaced by a viscous one that removes the same energy in a period (definition 20.6). This is at the same time the best viscous fit in the mean square (theorem 20.7). So for resonance with friction (theorem 20.11) we obtained an amplitude that friction reduces by \(12{,}7\ \%\) without solving a nonlinear equation. The replacement holds for one amplitude and one frequency: for friction \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}}\) falls as the amplitude or the frequency grows. Hysteretic damping, whose loss is by construction \(\pi\gamma kX^2\) and independent of frequency, is treated in section 20.3.

20.3 Hysteretic damping

In section 20.1 we measured the loss in one period by the area of the loop of the damping force against displacement (figure 9.27), and in section 20.2 we replaced every mechanism by a viscous damper that loses the same energy. The viscous damper has a property that often fails in built structures: its loss in a period, \(\pi\,c\,\Omega X^2\), grows in proportion to the frequency \(\Omega\) (theorem 9.61). GR (§3.2.2, PDF p. 181, footnote 3) mentions structures with joints, where the mechanical joints cause dry friction and damping forces that do not grow linearly with frequency in harmonic motion. For such friction the reason is simple: the force is constant, \(F_{\mathrm{t}}\), and the path covered in a period is \(4X\) (twice \(2X\), there and back), so the work is \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\) however fast the motion goes. For cantilever \(A\) with \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N and \(X = 13{,}914\) mm this is \(0{,}1113\) J at every frequency (computation in num-03.py). We ask whether there is a linear model of damping whose loss in a period does not depend on frequency.

From history

CK (§4.8, PDF p. 129) calls such damping structural and writes that it is often used in structural dynamics, for example in studies of aircraft vibration and flutter, and that Theodorsen and Garrick used it in an early study of flutter. CK introduces it with the notation of the complex frequency response of his section 4.3 and says that this notation is especially suitable for this damping.

Let us return to the question that opened the section. We draw the loop that the point \((q, f_{\mathrm{D}})\) runs through in a period, as before, for cantilever \(A\) at amplitude \(X = 15{,}944\) mm (figure 20.7). We hold the amplitude constant so that only the loops are compared, although the driving force would have to be adjusted at every frequency.

First the axes: displacement \(q\) horizontally, force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\) vertically, on the horizontal axis the limit displacements \(-X\) and \(X\). The viscous damper at resonance, \(r = 1\), gives an ellipse of height \(c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X = 20\) N and area \(\pi\,c\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}} X^2 = 1{,}00\) J, which is the energy lost in a period (theorem 9.61). If we halve the frequency, the amplitude stays the same and the velocity is half, so the damper force is half and the ellipse is lower, \(10\) N, and its area is \(0{,}50\) J. If we double the frequency, the ellipse is \(40\) N high and its area is \(2{,}00\) J. The point \((q, f_{\mathrm{D}})\) runs along them counterclockwise. The area grows with frequency because the force of a viscous damper is proportional to velocity, and its amplitude \(c\,\Omega X\) is therefore proportional to \(\Omega\).

We look for a different mechanism. On the right are the axes and a loop of the same height at every frequency. The height of the loop is the amplitude of the damping force. Since we want a linear model, let it be proportional to the displacement amplitude \(X\), that is \(\gamma k X\). The number \(\gamma\) has no unit, and the stiffness \(k\) makes the result a force. For \(A\) we take \(\gamma = 0{,}02\), which gives \(\gamma k X = 20\) N, the same as for the viscous damper at resonance. The loop is an ellipse with semi-axes \(X\) and \(\gamma k X\), its area is \(\pi\,X\cdot\gamma k X = \pi\gamma k X^2 = 1{,}00\) J at every frequency, and it is run counterclockwise as well. We call the loop hysteretic because the forces at the same displacement on the way there and on the way back differ: the force \(f_{\mathrm{D}}\) lags behind the displacement by a quarter period (the Greek word hysterein means to lag behind). CK (PDF p. 127, figure 4.17) calls the loop of the total force of a spring and a viscous damper a "hysteresis loop" and says that it is characteristic of forces that dissipate energy. So the left loops are hysteretic too, but their height depends on velocity. The name hysteretic damping stayed for the model in which it does not depend on velocity (GR, PDF p. 180: the damping force is independent of frequency, proportional to amplitude and in phase with velocity, where GR counts the force acting on the damper, that is \(-f_{\mathrm{D}}\)).

What damper gives this loop (right in figure 20.7)? A viscous damper with coefficient \(c\) has at amplitude \(X\) the loop height \(c\,\Omega X\). Let this be \(\gamma k X\), so \(c = \gamma k/\Omega\). The coefficient is different at every frequency, as the left loops in figure 20.7 are different at every frequency, so the model holds only for steady motion with a single frequency. We write this down.

Definition 20.12 Hysteretic damping (histerezno dušenje)

Let \(m > 0\) and \(k > 0\) be real numbers and \(\gamma \ge 0\) a number without unit (the loss factor, as lemma 20.13 shows). Hysteretic damping with loss factor \(\gamma\) is a rule for the system \(m\ddot q + k q = Q\), valid only for steady harmonic motion with angular frequency \(\Omega > 0\): besides the spring, a force acts on the mass

\[f_{\mathrm{D}} = -c_{\mathrm{h}}(\Omega)\,\dot q , \qquad c_{\mathrm{h}}(\Omega) = \frac{\gamma k}{\Omega} ,\]

that is, a viscous damper (definition 9.1) with a coefficient for which the amplitude of the damping force \(c_{\mathrm{h}}\,\Omega X = \gamma k X\) is proportional to the displacement amplitude \(X\) and independent of \(\Omega\). The equation of motion at frequency \(\Omega\) is

\[m\ddot q + \frac{\gamma k}{\Omega}\,\dot q + k q = Q_0\cos\Omega t . \tag{20.10}\]

The complex number \(\hat k = k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\) is the complex stiffness: it is complex because besides the real part \(k\) it has the imaginary part \(\gamma k\), which represents damping. The model is also called structural damping.

Source: CK §4.8 (PDF p. 129): equation (4.79) with \(\gamma\) as the "structural damping factor" and the complex stiffness \(k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\). GR §3.2.2 (PDF pp. 180-181): "hysteretic damping", equation (3.31), damping force independent of frequency, proportional to amplitude and in phase with velocity, "also sometimes called structural damping". The notation with the coefficient \(\gamma k/\Omega\) is ours, the sources give it in complex notation. The letter \(\gamma\) here is the loss factor of section 20.1, not the shear angle.

What does this damper lose, the one that gives the right loop? The first thing we show is that \(\gamma\) really is the loss factor of section 20.1.

Lemma 20.13 Loss per period under hysteretic damping (izguba v periodi pri histereznem dušenju)

Let \(m, k > 0\), \(\gamma > 0\) and \(\Omega > 0\), and let \(q = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) be a steady motion of the system with hysteretic damping (definition 20.12) with amplitude \(X\). Then:

  1. In the period \(T_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi/\Omega\) the damping force loses the energy \(W_{\mathrm{izg}} = \pi\,\gamma\,k\,X^2\), whatever \(\Omega\) and \(\varphi\) are.
  2. In a period the point \((q, f_{\mathrm{D}})\) runs around an ellipse with semi-axes \(X\) and \(\gamma k X\), and its area is \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}\).
  3. Let \(U = \tfrac12 k X^2\) be the largest energy of the spring. Then \(W_{\mathrm{izg}}/(2\pi U) = \gamma\), which is the loss factor of definition 20.3.
Proof

We must show the loss, the shape of the loop and the ratio. At a chosen frequency the system is a viscous damper with \(c = c_{\mathrm{h}}(\Omega)\), so we use the theorems for the viscous damper.

  1. The coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{h}} = \gamma k/\Omega\) is real and positive, the imaginary part of the denominator \(k - m\Omega^2 + \mathrm{i}\,c_{\mathrm{h}}\Omega = k - m\Omega^2 + \mathrm{i}\gamma k\) is \(\gamma k > 0\), so it is different from zero. The assumptions of theorem 9.61 hold.
  2. By theorem 9.61 the loss in a period is \(\pi\,c_{\mathrm{h}}\,\Omega X^2 = \pi\,\dfrac{\gamma k}{\Omega}\,\Omega X^2 = \pi\gamma k X^2\). The frequency cancels, \(\varphi\) does not occur in the expression. This is point 1.
  3. The damping force is \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -c_{\mathrm{h}}\dot q = c_{\mathrm{h}}\Omega X\sin(\Omega t - \varphi) = \gamma k X\sin(\Omega t - \varphi)\) (theorem 8.12). From \(\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1\) (lemma 8.10, point 1) we get \((q/X)^2 + (f_{\mathrm{D}}/(\gamma k X))^2 = 1\), which is an ellipse with semi-axes \(X\) and \(\gamma k X\). Its area is \(\pi X\cdot\gamma k X = \pi\gamma k X^2\), as in the text before figure 9.27. This is point 2.
  4. Dividing point 1 by \(2\pi U = \pi k X^2\) gives \(\gamma\). This is point 3.

Source: The proof is not from a source. CK (4.75) and figure 4.17 (PDF p. 127) connect the loss in a period with the area of the loop, CK (4.83) (PDF p. 129) sets \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = \gamma/2\).

The lemma says that damping with loss factor \(\gamma\), as the right loop in figure 20.7 shows, is described equally well at every frequency by the number \(\gamma\), and that this is exactly the number that section 20.1 computes from the loop. The same holds in the complex-stiffness notation: when we write steady motion as \(z = Z\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), we have \(\dot z = \mathrm{i}\Omega z\), so the term \(\dfrac{\gamma k}{\Omega}\dot z\) equals \(\mathrm{i}\gamma k\,z\) and together with the spring gives \(k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)z\). How large the displacement is and when it lags behind the force is told by the next theorem.

Theorem 20.14 Response of a system with hysteretic damping (odziv sistema s histereznim dušenjem)

Let \(m, k > 0\), \(\gamma > 0\), \(Q_0\) a real number, \(\Omega > 0\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m}\) and \(r = \Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). For equation (20.10):

  1. The number \(k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma) - m\Omega^2\) is different from zero. The steady state is \(q_{\mathrm{p}} = \mathrm{Re}\big(Q_0\,\hat H\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big) = X\cos(\Omega t - \varphi)\) with frequency response
    \[\hat H(\Omega) = \frac{1}{k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma) - m\Omega^2} , \tag{20.11}\]
    and the function \(z = Q_0\hat H\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) solves the complex equation
    \[m\ddot z + k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\,z = Q_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} . \tag{20.12}\]
  2. The amplitude is \(X = \dfrac{Q_0}{k}\,D_{\mathrm{h}}(r)\) with
    \[D_{\mathrm{h}}(r) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1 - r^2)^2 + \gamma^2}} . \tag{20.13}\]
    The phase lag \(\varphi\in(0, \pi)\) is determined by \(\tan\varphi = \gamma/(1 - r^2)\) for \(r \ne 1\) and is \(\pi/2\) at \(r = 1\). As \(r \to 0\), \(\varphi\) tends to \(\arctan\gamma > 0\).
  3. For every \(r \ge 0\), \(D_{\mathrm{h}}(r) \le 1/\gamma\), with equality exactly at \(r = 1\).
  4. At \(r = 1\), \(D_{\mathrm{h}}(1) = 1/\gamma = D(1)\) and \(\varphi = \pi/2\) for a viscous system with \(\zeta = \gamma/2\) (definition 9.53). For \(r \ne 1\) the denominators differ: for the viscous one the damping term is \((2\zeta r)^2\), for the hysteretic one \(\gamma^2 = (2\zeta)^2\).
Proof

We must show that for equation (20.10) theorem 9.52 holds with \(c = c_{\mathrm{h}}(\Omega)\), and then read off the amplitude, the lag and the largest value.

  1. The coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{h}} = \gamma k/\Omega \ge 0\) is real and \(c_{\mathrm{h}}\Omega = \gamma k\). The characteristic polynomial \(P(s) = ms^2 + c_{\mathrm{h}} s + k\) has \(P(\mathrm{i}\Omega) = k - m\Omega^2 + \mathrm{i}\,\gamma k = k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma) - m\Omega^2\), its imaginary part \(\gamma k\) is positive, so \(P(\mathrm{i}\Omega) \ne 0\). The assumptions of theorem 9.52 hold, and it gives \(q_{\mathrm{p}} = \mathrm{Re}(Q_0 H\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) with \(H = 1/P(\mathrm{i}\Omega) = \hat H\).
  2. For \(z = Q_0\hat H\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), by theorem 9.29 \(\ddot z = -\Omega^2 z\), so \(m\ddot z + k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)z = \big(k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma) - m\Omega^2\big)Q_0\hat H\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} = Q_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), because \(P(\mathrm{i}\Omega)\hat H = 1\). This proves point 1.
  3. From \(m\Omega^2 = k r^2\) we get \(|P(\mathrm{i}\Omega)|^2 = (k - m\Omega^2)^2 + \gamma^2k^2 = k^2\big((1 - r^2)^2 + \gamma^2\big)\). By theorem 9.52, \(X = Q_0/|P|\), which is \((Q_0/k)D_{\mathrm{h}}\).
  4. By the same theorem \(\cos\varphi = (k - m\Omega^2)/|P|\) and \(\sin\varphi = c_{\mathrm{h}}\Omega/|P| = \gamma k/|P| > 0\), so \(\varphi \in (0, \pi)\). Division gives \(\tan\varphi = \gamma k/(k - m\Omega^2) = \gamma/(1 - r^2)\) for \(r \ne 1\). At \(r = 1\), \(\cos\varphi = 0\) and \(\sin\varphi > 0\), so \(\varphi = \pi/2\). As \(r \to 0\), \(\cos\varphi \to 1/\sqrt{1 + \gamma^2}\) and \(\sin\varphi \to \gamma/\sqrt{1 + \gamma^2}\), so \(\tan\varphi \to \gamma\). This proves point 2.
  5. The expression \((1 - r^2)^2 + \gamma^2\) is the sum of a square and \(\gamma^2\), so it is \(\ge \gamma^2\) with equality exactly at \(1 - r^2 = 0\), that is at \(r = 1\) for \(r \ge 0\). The function \(x \mapsto x^{-1/2}\) is strictly decreasing on \(x > 0\), so \(D_{\mathrm{h}} \le 1/\gamma\) with equality exactly at \(r = 1\). This is point 3.
  6. For \(\zeta = \gamma/2\), \(D(1) = 1/(2\zeta) = 1/\gamma\) by definition 9.53, and \(\varphi = \pi/2\) by theorem 9.54 (point 3). The denominators of equations (9.47) and (20.13) are \((1 - r^2)^2 + (2\zeta r)^2\) and \((1 - r^2)^2 + (2\zeta)^2\), which agree exactly at \(r = 1\) (or \(\zeta = 0\)). This is point 4.

Source: CK (4.81)-(4.85) and (4.83) (PDF p. 129): \(\bar H_0 = 1/((1 - r^2) + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\), amplitude \(1/[(1 - r^2)^2 + \gamma^2]^{1/2}\), \(\tan\alpha = \gamma/(1 - r^2)\), \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = \gamma/2\) (CK sets \(\bar U/U_0 = -\mathrm{i}/\gamma\) at \(r = 1\), PDF p. 130). The proof by steps from theorem 9.52 is ours.

Let us look at cantilever \(A\) with hysteretic damping \(\gamma = 2\zeta = 0{,}02\), which has the loop of figure 20.7.

Example 20.15 Cantilever A with hysteretic damping (konzola A s histereznim dušenjem)

Cantilever \(A\) of chapter 9 has \(m = 50\) kg, \(k = 62\,720\) N/m, \(Q_0 = 20\) N. For \(\gamma = 0{,}02\), by equation (20.13) at resonance \(D_{\mathrm{h}}(1) = 1/\gamma = 50\) and \(X = Q_0/(\gamma k) = 15{,}944\) mm, the same as for viscous damping with \(\zeta = 0{,}01\). The amplitude of the damping force is \(\gamma k X = 20\) N and the loss in a period is \(\pi\gamma k X^2 = 1{,}0018\) J (lemma 20.13), which are the height and the area of the loop on the right of figure 20.7. Elsewhere the models differ little (num-03.out):

\(r\) \(D\) viscous, \(\zeta = 0{,}01\) \(D_{\mathrm{h}}\), \(\gamma = 0{,}02\) difference
\(0{,}5\) \(1{,}3332\) \(1{,}3329\) \(0{,}03\ \%\)
\(0{,}9\) \(5{,}2397\) \(5{,}2342\) \(0{,}10\ \%\)
\(1\) \(50{,}0000\) \(50{,}0000\) \(0\)
\(1{,}1\) \(4{,}7360\) \(4{,}7405\) \(0{,}09\ \%\)
\(2\) \(0{,}3333\) \(0{,}3333\) \(0{,}01\ \%\)

The curves \(D\) and \(D_{\mathrm{h}}\) would almost coincide in figure 9.20. For \(r\) from \(0{,}9\) to \(1{,}1\) the largest difference is \(0{,}5\ \%\). The reason: at \(r = 0{,}9\), \((1 - r^2)^2 = 0{,}0361\), while the damping terms are only \((2\zeta r)^2 = 0{,}000324\) and \(\gamma^2 = 0{,}0004\), which is \(0{,}9\ \%\) and \(1{,}1\ \%\) of the first, and their difference \(0{,}000076\) is \(0{,}2\ \%\) of the denominator. The viscous peak is at \(r = \sqrt{1 - 2\zeta^2} = 0{,}9999\) with height \(50{,}0025\), the hysteretic exactly at \(r = 1\) with height \(50{,}0000\) (theorem 20.14, point 3, and theorem 9.54).

The curves \(D\) and \(D_{\mathrm{h}}\) agree so well because the damping is small: for \(\zeta = 0{,}01\), \(2\zeta = 0{,}02 \ll 1\). The substitution \(\zeta = \gamma/2\) is therefore an approximation for light damping. The damping term in the denominator matters only near resonance, where \((1 - r^2)^2\) is small (CK, PDF p. 129: for small damping, damping is effective primarily near resonance). There \(r\) is close to \(1\) and \(2\zeta r\) differs from \(2\zeta\) only by the factor \(r\). Far from resonance both damping terms are small compared with \((1 - r^2)^2\), as at \(r = 0{,}9\) above. What happens when the damping or \(r\) is large is shown by machine \(B\).

Machine \(B\) of chapter 9 stands on pads that transmit force to the ground (figure 9.30). A pad is a spring and a damper, so the force it transmits to the ground is \(f_{\mathrm{t}} = k q + c\,\dot q\) (definition 9.65). For a hysteretically damped pad the damper is the one of definition 20.12.

Corollary 20.16 Transmissibility with hysteretic damping (prenosnost s histereznim dušenjem)

Let \(\mathrm{TR}_{\mathrm{h}} = F_{\mathrm{t}}/Q_0\) be the transmissibility (definition 9.65) of a system with hysteretic damping at frequency \(\Omega\), under the conditions of theorem 20.14 and with \(Q_0 > 0\). Then

\[\mathrm{TR}_{\mathrm{h}} = \frac{\sqrt{1 + \gamma^2}}{\sqrt{(1 - r^2)^2 + \gamma^2}} = \sqrt{1 + \gamma^2}\,D_{\mathrm{h}}(r) , \tag{20.14}\]

\(\mathrm{TR}_{\mathrm{h}} = 1\) at \(r = \sqrt2\) for every \(\gamma\), \(\mathrm{TR}_{\mathrm{h}} < 1\) exactly for \(r > \sqrt2\), for \(r > \sqrt2\) \(\mathrm{TR}_{\mathrm{h}}\) strictly increases with increasing \(\gamma\), for \(0 < r < \sqrt2\) it strictly decreases.

Proof

We must show the form (20.14), and take the rest over from theorem 9.66.

  1. At frequency \(\Omega\) the system is viscous with \(c = c_{\mathrm{h}}\), its damping ratio is \(\zeta_{\mathrm{h}} = c_{\mathrm{h}}/(2\sqrt{km}) = \gamma k/(2\Omega\sqrt{km})\). From \(\Omega = r\sqrt{k/m}\), \(\zeta_{\mathrm{h}} = \gamma/(2r)\), so \(2\zeta_{\mathrm{h}} r = \gamma\).
  2. Theorem 9.66 gives \(\mathrm{TR} = \sqrt{1 + (2\zeta_{\mathrm{h}} r)^2}\,D(r)\) with \(D = 1/\sqrt{(1 - r^2)^2 + (2\zeta_{\mathrm{h}} r)^2}\). With \(2\zeta_{\mathrm{h}} r = \gamma\) this is (20.14).
  3. Theorem 9.66 also says: \(\mathrm{TR} = 1\) at \(r = \sqrt2\) for every damping ratio, \(\mathrm{TR} < 1\) exactly for \(r > \sqrt2\), for \(r > \sqrt2\) it grows with the damping ratio and for \(0 < r < \sqrt2\) it falls. At a given \(r\), \(\zeta_{\mathrm{h}} = \gamma/(2r)\) is a strictly increasing function of \(\gamma\), so the same holds for \(\gamma\).

Source: CK (4.44) (PDF p. 115) for the viscous transmissibility. The proof that the same holds for hysteretic damping is ours, SymPy checked \(\mathrm{TR}_{\mathrm{h}}^2 - 1 = r^2(2 - r^2)/\big((1 - r^2)^2 + \gamma^2\big)\).

For machine \(B\) at \(r = 5\) and \(r = 1\) we compare the viscous damper and hysteretic damping with \(\gamma = 2\zeta\) (figure 20.8).

We draw first the axes: frequency ratio \(r\) horizontally and transmissibility vertically, logarithmic, so that we see the values \(2{,}7\) and \(0{,}03\) at once. Without damping the transmissibility at \(r = 1\) grows beyond all bounds and above resonance falls as \(1/(r^2 - 1)\). The horizontal line is \(\mathrm{TR} = 1\) and all curves cross it at the point \(r = \sqrt2\), as corollary 20.16 says, and theorem 9.66 for viscous damping. Let us add viscous damping with \(\zeta = 0{,}2\) and hysteretic with \(\gamma = 0{,}4\). At \(r = 1\) both have \(\mathrm{TR} = 2{,}693\), because there \(2\zeta r = \gamma\) (theorem 20.14, point 4). At \(r = 5\) the machine on the pads has natural frequency \(5\) Hz and the excitation frequency is \(25\) Hz, as in example 9.67, and here the curves part.

Example 20.17 Machine B on hysteretically damped mounts (stroj B na histerezno dušenih podložkah)

Machine \(B\) of figure 20.8: \(M = 250\) kg, pads with \(f_{\mathrm{n}} = 5\) Hz, \(Q_0 = 493{,}48\) N, \(r = 5\) (example 9.67). The force into the ground is \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = Q_0\,\mathrm{TR}\), by theorem 9.66 for viscous damping and by corollary 20.16 for hysteretic (computation in num-03.py):

model \(\mathrm{TR}\) at \(r = 1\) \(\mathrm{TR}\) at \(r = 5\) \(F_{\mathrm{t}}\) at \(r = 5\) in N
no damping \(\infty\) \(0{,}04167\) \(20{,}56\)
viscous, \(\zeta = 0{,}05\) \(10{,}050\) \(0{,}04657\) \(22{,}98\)
hysteretic, \(\gamma = 0{,}1\) \(10{,}050\) \(0{,}04187\) \(20{,}66\)
viscous, \(\zeta = 0{,}2\) \(2{,}693\) \(0{,}09285\) \(45{,}82\)
hysteretic, \(\gamma = 0{,}4\) \(2{,}693\) \(0{,}04487\) \(22{,}14\)

At \(r = 1\) the models are equal, as figure 20.8 shows. At \(r = 5\) viscous damping with \(\zeta = 0{,}2\) increases the force into the ground \(2{,}23\) times, hysteretic with the same \(\gamma = 2\zeta\) only \(1{,}077\) times.
