The reason is the term \(2\zeta r\) of corollary 20.16 and theorem 9.66: for the viscous damper its contribution to the root in the numerator is \((2\zeta r)^2 = 4\), because the damper force \(c\,\Omega X\) grows with frequency and at \(r = 5\) is five times larger than at \(r = 1\). For the hysteretic one this contribution is \(\gamma^2 = 0{,}16\) at every \(r\), because the damping force \(\gamma k X\) does not depend on frequency. The factors are \(\sqrt{1 + 4} = 2{,}236\) and \(\sqrt{1 + 0{,}16} = 1{,}077\). The denominator hardly changes, \((1 - r^2)^2 = 576\) grows to \(580\) and \(576{,}16\), so the ratios of the forces are \(2{,}228\) and \(1{,}077\).

The conclusion on isolation from chapter 9 (figure 9.30), that damping far above resonance hurts, holds here too: by corollary 20.16 hysteretic damping increases the transmissibility at every \(r > \sqrt2\). How much it hurts depends on the model. Whether the viscous or the hysteretic model is closer to the truth for a given pad is decided by a measurement: if the loss of the pad in a period does not change with frequency, the hysteretic model is more suitable, if it grows in proportion to frequency, the viscous one. How the loss factor of a real material depends on frequency is shown by section 20.6: it is constant only approximately and only over a limited range of frequencies.

The computation so far held only for steady harmonic motion, into which the vibration passes after the transient (figure 9.23). Let us try to use the same notation for free vibration, when there is no force and no steady state. In complex notation the equation of free vibration is \(m\ddot z + k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)z = 0\), which is equation (20.12) without the right-hand side. Why is the model not meant for time? The term \(\mathrm{i}\gamma k z\) meant \((\gamma k/\Omega)\,\dot z\), where \(\Omega\) is the frequency with which the motion goes. In free vibration there is no force with frequency \(\Omega\) and the motion is not steady harmonic, so definition 20.12 does not apply to it and does not determine the coefficient \(\gamma k/\Omega\). Let us see what the equation itself does.

Lemma 20.18 Complex stiffness in the time domain (kompleksna togost v časovnem zapisu)

Let \(m, k > 0\), \(\gamma > 0\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m}\). Let

\[a = \sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{1 + \gamma^2} + 1}{2}} , \qquad b = \sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{1 + \gamma^2} - 1}{2}} , \qquad \alpha = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} b , \quad \beta = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} a\]

and let \(z\) be a complex function with \(m\ddot z + k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)z = 0\). Then:

  1. The characteristic polynomial of the equation has the zeros \(s_1 = -\alpha + \mathrm{i}\beta\) and \(s_2 = -s_1 = \alpha - \mathrm{i}\beta\), and \(\alpha > 0\).
  2. The unique solution with \(z(0) = 1\), \(\dot z(0) = 0\) is \(z = \tfrac12\big(\mathrm{e}^{s_1t} + \mathrm{e}^{s_2t}\big)\) and its real part is \(\tfrac12\big(\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t} + \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha t}\big)\cos\beta t\).
  3. At the instants \(t_{\mathrm{j}} = 2\pi j/\beta\), \(\mathrm{Re}\,z(t_{\mathrm{j}}) \ge \tfrac12\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t_{\mathrm{j}}}\), so \(\mathrm{Re}\,z(t_{\mathrm{j}})\) grows beyond all bounds as \(j \to \infty\).
Proof

We must show the zeros of the polynomial, the solution with the given initial values and its growth.

  1. For \(z = \mathrm{e}^{st}\), by theorem 9.29 \(\ddot z = s^2 z\), and after dividing by \(m\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{st}\) and with \(k = m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) the characteristic polynomial is \(s^2 + \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\).
  2. By lemma 9.26 with \(d = 1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma\) (\(p = 1\), \(q = \gamma > 0\), \(|d| = \sqrt{1 + \gamma^2}\)), \(w = a + \mathrm{i}b\) is a number with \(w^2 = 1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma\), and \(-w\) is the only other one. Since \((\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} w)^2 = -\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 w^2 = -\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\), the zeros of the polynomial are \(\pm\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} w\). For \(+\), \(\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}(a + \mathrm{i}b) = -\omega_{\mathrm{n}} b + \mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}} a = s_1\), for \(-\) it is \(s_2 = -s_1\).
  3. For \(\gamma > 0\), \(\sqrt{1 + \gamma^2} > 1\), so \(b > 0\) and \(\alpha > 0\). This proves point 1.
  4. Each of the functions \(\mathrm{e}^{s_1t}\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{s_2t}\) solves the equation (step 1), so their half-sum does too. We have \(z(0) = \tfrac12(1 + 1) = 1\) and \(\dot z(0) = \tfrac12(s_1 + s_2) = 0\). By theorem 9.36, which holds for complex coefficients, this is the only solution.
  5. By definition 9.28, \(\mathrm{e}^{s_1t} = \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha t}(\cos\beta t + \mathrm{i}\sin\beta t)\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{s_2t} = \mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}(\cos\beta t - \mathrm{i}\sin\beta t)\). The real part of the half-sum is \(\tfrac12(\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha t} + \mathrm{e}^{\alpha t})\cos\beta t\). This is point 2.
  6. At \(t_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(\beta t_{\mathrm{j}} = 2\pi j\) and \(\cos\beta t_{\mathrm{j}} = 1\) (lemma 8.10, point 4), so \(\mathrm{Re}\,z(t_{\mathrm{j}}) = \tfrac12(\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t_{\mathrm{j}}} + \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha t_{\mathrm{j}}}) \ge \tfrac12\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t_{\mathrm{j}}}\). Since \(\alpha > 0\) and \(t_{\mathrm{j}} \to \infty\), the exponential function grows beyond all bounds (lemma 9.15). This is point 3.

Source: The proof is not from a source. GR (§3.2.2, PDF p. 181, footnote 3) says that the hysteretic model violates the principle of causality and is therefore not transferable to the time domain, and that damping forces exist even under static excitation. This is only stated there, not proved here.

Let us look at numbers for the pads of machine \(B\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 2\pi\cdot 5 = 31{,}416\) 1/s. For \(\gamma = 0{,}04\), \(w = 1{,}000200 + 0{,}019996\,\mathrm{i}\), \(s_1 = -0{,}6282 + 31{,}4222\,\mathrm{i}\) 1/s and \(s_2 = +0{,}6282 - 31{,}4222\,\mathrm{i}\) 1/s. The amplitude of the second solution increases \(e\) times every \(1/\alpha = 1{,}592\) s. For \(\gamma = 0{,}4\), \(s_1 = -6{,}1656 + 32{,}0152\,\mathrm{i}\), growth \(e\) times every \(0{,}162\) s (figure 20.9).

In the figure are the axes: time in seconds horizontally and \(\mathrm{Re}\,z\) vertically. The orange curve is the real part of the solution: it oscillates with period \(2\pi/\beta = 0{,}196\) s, and its height grows. The solution of the lemma is a sum of two parts. The first, \(\tfrac12\mathrm{e}^{s_1t}\), decays as in a damped oscillator: its rate \(\alpha = 6{,}1656\) 1/s is close to \(\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = (\gamma/2)\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 6{,}2832\) 1/s (\(0{,}981\) times, and \(0{,}9998\) times for \(\gamma = 0{,}04\)). The second, \(\tfrac12\mathrm{e}^{s_2t}\), grows, and the envelope of the sum is \(\tfrac12(\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t} + \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha t})\). Already after \(0{,}5\) s, which is about two and a half oscillations (\(0{,}5/0{,}196 = 2{,}55\)), the envelope is \(10{,}9\) times the initial displacement. A motion that grows would mean that the damper supplies energy, but by theorem 9.43 for \(\zeta > 0\) free motion always decays.

Why does a zero with growth appear? A polynomial with real coefficients has for every zero \(s\) also \(\bar s\) as a zero, because \(P(\bar s) = \overline{P(s)}\). In this equation the coefficient \(\mathrm{i}\gamma k\) is complex and this rule does not hold. The polynomial \(P(s) = s^2 + \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\) contains only \(s^2\), so \(P(-s) = P(s)\) and with \(s_1\) also \(-s_1 = \alpha - \mathrm{i}\beta\) is a zero, the mirror image with respect to the origin. The conjugate \(\bar s_1 = -\alpha - \mathrm{i}\beta\), however, is not a zero: from \(\bar s_1^2 = \overline{s_1^2} = -\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2(1 - \mathrm{i}\gamma)\) we get \(P(\bar s_1) = 2\mathrm{i}\gamma\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 \ne 0\). So a growing part belongs to the decaying one.

The model of hysteretic damping is therefore used only as defined: for steady harmonic motion at one frequency, in the frequency domain. If we need the response in time, we replace it by a viscous damper with coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{eq}} = \gamma k/\Omega_0\) at the frequency \(\Omega_0\) that interests us (section 20.2, at \(\Omega_0 = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) this is \(\zeta_{\mathrm{eq}} = \gamma/2\) of theorem 20.14), or we use a material model that has causality built in: the viscoelastic model of section 20.4. There are two idealizations. The first is harmonic motion with one frequency. The second is a constant \(\gamma\): for friction in a joint the loss in a period \(4F_{\mathrm{t}}X\) is proportional to \(X\), not to \(X^2\), so \(\gamma\) is the same only at one amplitude, \(\gamma = 4F_{\mathrm{t}}/(\pi k X)\). For \(A\) with \(F_{\mathrm{t}} = 2\) N this is \(0{,}00292\) at \(X = 13{,}914\) mm and \(0{,}00146\) at \(27{,}828\) mm, so half at double the amplitude. Hysteretic damping is therefore suitable when the motion is near one amplitude and one frequency, for example the vibration of a structure at resonance, but not for start-up or decay. GR (PDF p. 181, footnote 3) says that the model is quantitatively usable in a limited range of frequencies for many kinds of real structures, among them built structures with joints with dry friction.

20.4 Viscoelastic models

We stretch a steel bar by one thousandth of its length and hold it. The force that pulls it stays practically the same. A nylon bar behaves differently: if we stretch it and hold it at that length, the force slowly falls, and if we hang a constant weight on it, it keeps getting longer long after we hung the weight. For steel we neglected this in chapter 3 and wrote \(\sigma = E\varepsilon\) (definition 3.1). For nylon that does not work. We called such materials viscoelastic (viskoelastični) and promised to treat them in this chapter. How do we write a law in which the stress depends not only on the strain at this moment, and what follows from it for damping?

We test the material in two ways, which BOWER gives (§3.6.1.1, PDF p. 132). In the first we quickly stretch the bar at time \(t = 0\) to the strain \(\varepsilon_0\) and hold it. The stress we need for this falls. This phenomenon is called relaxation (relaksacija), which means loosening: the stress loosens although we do not change the strain. In the second we load the bar at time \(t = 0\) with the stress \(\sigma_0\) and hold it. The strain keeps increasing. This phenomenon is called creep (lezenje), because the strain slowly creeps on. From these two tests BOWER defines the relaxation modulus and the creep compliance, and we will turn them into definitions.

We compute under three assumptions. The strains are small, BOWER (PDF p. 130) gives less than \(0{,}5\ \%\), so as in chapter 3 we may compute stress and strain on the original cross-section and length. The temperature is constant, because the response of polymers depends strongly on it (BOWER, PDF p. 131-132). The load is uniaxial, as in the tensile test. What happens in the material? For metals we looked at this in section 20.1: heat flows between parts of a crystal and between grains, so the path of loading differs from the path of unloading. For polymers BOWER distinguishes two kinds (PDF p. 133). Heavily cross-linked polymers show retarded elastic behaviour (zakasnjeno elastično obnašanje): under constant stress the strain settles at a final value and returns after unloading. Uncross-linked polymers show steady-state creep (lezenje s stalno hitrostjo): under constant stress the strain does not settle. We will meet both kinds in the models.

From history

In 1849 the Russian government founded the Central Laboratory of Weights and Measures and installed A. T. Kupffer (1799-1865) as its director (TIMO, PDF p. 193). Kupffer studied the properties of metals because they can affect standards of measurement (TIMO, PDF p. 193). In torsional vibration he investigated damping and showed that only a part of it comes from air resistance and the rest from the viscosity of the material (TIMO, PDF p. 194). In steel bars he found that the deflection does not vanish at once after unloading but keeps decreasing for several days, which TIMO calls elastic afterstrain (elastična naknadna deformacija). This effect also gives rise to damping of vibrations (TIMO, PDF p. 194). Kupffer also showed that the damping due to the afterstrain grows with temperature, and for his work on the influence of temperature he won a prize of the Royal Society of Göttingen in 1855 (TIMO, PDF p. 194).

The story is here for two reasons. Separating air damping from damping in the material is the question of section 20.1. The slow return of the strain over several days is creep, which the Kelvin-Voigt element and the standard linear solid in this section describe.

Back to the bar that we stretch and hold, and to the question of how to write a law in which the stress does not depend only on the strain at this moment. The model needs two properties at once: it must respond at once, like a spring, and yet stress and strain must loosen with time, as with a dashpot. We know both elements. The spring is a linear elastic material, \(\sigma = E\varepsilon\) (definition 3.3). The dashpot we know from chapter 9: the force with which it resists stretching is proportional to the rate of stretching (definition 9.1). We draw them on the bar and assemble them like a circuit.

We begin with the bar: each model is a bar pulled by forces at its ends. We pull it with the stress \(\sigma\), so with the force \(\sigma A\) on the cross-section \(A\). The force is drawn on the axis of the bar and starts at the point that we pull. Next we draw the spring with modulus \(E\) as a coiled wire, because it stretches under a force, and by Hooke's law its stress is proportional to the strain, \(\sigma = E\varepsilon\). Then the dashpot: a piston in a cylinder of oil, which flows past the piston and resists its motion, so the stress is proportional to the rate of strain. A dashpot with coefficient \(c\) from chapter 9 resists stretching with the force \(c\,\dot\ell\) if the distance between the ends changes at the rate \(\dot\ell\). On a bar of length \(L\) and cross-section \(A\) the force is \(F = \sigma A\) and the elongation \(\Delta\ell = \varepsilon L\), so \(\sigma = (c L/A)\,\dot\varepsilon\). We call the number \(\eta = cL/A\) the viscosity (viskoznost) of the dashpot, its unit is Pa s, because \(\sigma\) is in Pa and \(\dot\varepsilon\) in 1/s. CM (PDF p. 426) uses the same letter. In chapter 10 \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the modal coordinate, but there are no modal coordinates here, so the two meanings do not meet. Likewise \(\tau\) is the shear stress elsewhere in the book, in this chapter there is no shear stress and we measure time with \(\tau\).

We connect two elements in two ways. In series the spring and the dashpot lie one after the other on the axis, the same force flows through both and they have the same stress \(\sigma\), while their elongations \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\varepsilon_2\) add up to the total strain \(\varepsilon\). In parallel they lie beside each other on the axis between two rigid plates that the force pulls. The elongation is the same for both, \(\varepsilon\), and the stresses add. The third model combines both connections: the spring \(E_\infty\) is parallel to a branch in which the spring \(E_1\) and the dashpot \(\eta\) are in series.

Definition 20.19 Linear viscoelastic material (linearni viskoelastični material)

Let a bar be under uniaxial stress \(\sigma(t)\) with small strain \(\varepsilon(t)\) at constant temperature, as in chapter 3. A spring element (elastični člen) with modulus \(E > 0\) has \(\sigma = E\varepsilon\). A dashpot element (viskozni člen) with viscosity \(\eta > 0\) has \(\sigma = \eta\,\dot\varepsilon\), its strain is a continuous function of time also at a jump of the stress, because at a jump of its strain the dashpot would need an infinite stress. In series the elements have the same stress and their strains add. In parallel they have the same strain and their stresses add. A material is a linear viscoelastic material if \(\sigma(t)\) and \(\varepsilon(t)\) are related by the equation \(\sum_{\mathrm{m}=0}^{M} p_{\mathrm{m}}\,\sigma^{(m)} = \sum_{\mathrm{n}=0}^{N} q_{\mathrm{n}}\,\varepsilon^{(n)}\) with constant coefficients \(p_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(q_{\mathrm{n}}\), where \(\sigma^{(m)}\) is the \(m\)-th time derivative of the stress and \(\varepsilon^{(n)}\) the \(n\)-th derivative of the strain. This is the equation of every model made of springs and dashpots. For \(M = N = 1\) the material is a first-order linear viscoelastic material (linearni viskoelastični material prvega reda) and the equation is

\[p_0\,\sigma + p_1\,\dot\sigma = q_0\,\varepsilon + q_1\,\dot\varepsilon \tag{20.15}\]

with constant coefficients \(p_0, p_1, q_0, q_1\). At a jump of \(\sigma\) or \(\varepsilon\) the equation (20.15) holds at every point where \(\sigma\) and \(\varepsilon\) are differentiable, and at the jump the relations of the elements above hold.

Source: CM (9.1.1)-(9.1.2) (PDF p. 419), the general form, CM §9.2 (PDF p. 425-433), equation (9.2.12) for the case \(M = N = 1\), and BOWER §3.6.3 (PDF p. 137-138). The statement at a jump is from this section. Higher orders (four-element models, CM §9.2.5, PDF p. 433-435) are not treated here.

The three models of the figure are special cases: for the Maxwell element \(q_0 = 0\), for the Kelvin-Voigt element \(p_1 = 0\), for the standard linear solid all four coefficients are non-zero. We derive each from its elements in the theorem on its response.

This is a simplification and it has to be said. The spring and dashpot together have a single time, the ratio \(\eta/E\), whereas a real polymer, by BOWER (PDF p. 139), has a response that three elements do not hit over a long time. CM (PDF p. 419) writes that such models give a qualitative picture and not a satisfactory quantitative description of any real material. For a better description we take several Maxwell elements at once (Prony series, BOWER §3.6.4, PDF p. 139), which is the subject of section 20.5.

Now we turn the tests into numbers. In relaxation the strain jumps at \(t = 0\) to \(\varepsilon_0\), before that the bar was at rest.

Definition 20.20 Relaxation modulus (relaksacijski modul)

Let a bar of linear viscoelastic material be at rest until time \(t = 0\) and let \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0\) for all \(t \ge 0\). Let the stress be bounded on every interval \((0, T]\). The relaxation modulus (relaksacijski modul) is the function \(E_{\mathrm{rel}} : (0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}\),

\[E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t) = \frac{\sigma(t)}{\varepsilon_0} , \tag{20.16}\]

in Pa. If they exist, \(E_0 = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(0+)\) is the instantaneous modulus (trenutni modul) and \(E_\infty = \lim_{\mathrm{t}\to\infty} E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\) the long-time modulus (dolgotrajni modul). For a linear material \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\) does not depend on \(\varepsilon_0\), which we will see for each model.

Source: CM §9.2.1 (PDF p. 425), where the relaxation modulus is written \(Y(t)\), and BOWER §3.6.1.1 (PDF p. 132), where \(G(t) = \tau(t)/2\Delta\varepsilon\) for shear. It is written \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\) here so that it stays connected with the modulus \(E\) of chapter 3.

In creep the stress jumps at \(t = 0\) to \(\sigma_0\).

Definition 20.21 Creep compliance (podajnost lezenja)

Let a bar of linear viscoelastic material be at rest until time \(t = 0\) and let \(\sigma(t) = \sigma_0\) for all \(t \ge 0\). The creep compliance (podajnost lezenja) is the function \(J_{\mathrm{lez}} : (0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}\),

\[J_{\mathrm{lez}}(t) = \frac{\varepsilon(t)}{\sigma_0} , \tag{20.17}\]

in 1/Pa. The value \(J_{\mathrm{lez}}(0+)\) is the instantaneous compliance and \(\lim_{\mathrm{t}\to\infty} J_{\mathrm{lez}}(t)\) the long-time compliance, if they exist.

Source: CM §9.2.1 (PDF p. 425), where the compliance is written \(J(t)\), and BOWER §3.6.1.1 (PDF p. 132). The letter \(J\) is also the Jacobian matrix of the chapters on deformation, hence the index.

The word compliance says how much the material gives way per unit stress, and it is the reciprocal of stiffness. For a spring \(J_{\mathrm{lez}} = 1/E\) and \(E_{\mathrm{rel}} = E\) are constants. For a viscoelastic material they are functions of time.

For each model we will ask two questions. First: does the strain settle under constant stress, as it must in a solid that keeps its shape? Second: does the material respond to a jump of strain with a finite stress, like a spring? We begin with the model that fails the first. A dashpot in series with a spring is the Maxwell element, which the figure shows in the top row.

Definition 20.22 Maxwell element (Maxwellov člen)

The Maxwell element is the series connection of a spring element with modulus \(E > 0\) and a dashpot element with viscosity \(\eta > 0\). The number \(\tau = \eta/E\) is the relaxation time (relaksacijski čas) and has the unit second.

Source: CM §9.2.2 (PDF p. 426), BOWER §3.6.3 (PDF p. 137-138).

The number \(\tau\) is called the relaxation time by what it means in the test: the theorem below shows that at a jump of strain the stress falls to \(1/\mathrm{e}\) of its initial value in the time \(\tau\).

Theorem 20.23 Response of a Maxwell element (odziv Maxwellovega člena)

Let a Maxwell element have \(E\), \(\eta\) and \(\tau = \eta/E\).

  1. Stress and strain satisfy \(\sigma + \tau\dot\sigma = \eta\,\dot\varepsilon\).
  2. At a jump of the strain to \(\varepsilon_0\) at \(t = 0\), \(\sigma(t) = E\varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\) for \(t > 0\), so \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t) = E\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\), \(E_0 = E\) and \(E_\infty = 0\).
  3. At a jump of the stress to \(\sigma_0\) at \(t = 0\), \(\varepsilon(t) = \sigma_0\,(1/E + t/\eta)\) for \(t \ge 0\), so \(J_{\mathrm{lez}}(t) = 1/E + t/\eta\), which grows beyond every bound as \(t \to \infty\).
  4. If the stress \(\sigma_0\) is removed after a time \(T > 0\), the strain first jumps back by \(\sigma_0/E\) and then stays at the value \(\sigma_0 T/\eta\), which is not zero.
Proof

We must show four claims. In all of them we use both elements and the connection of definition 20.19, in point 2 also lemma 9.34.

  1. Let \(\varepsilon_1\) be the strain of the spring and \(\varepsilon_2\) the strain of the dashpot, \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2\), the stress \(\sigma\) is the same (series). The elements give \(\varepsilon_1 = \sigma/E\) and \(\dot\varepsilon_2 = \sigma/\eta\).
  2. We differentiate the first equation, \(\dot\varepsilon_1 = \dot\sigma/E\). The sum is \(\dot\varepsilon = \dot\sigma/E + \sigma/\eta\). We multiply by \(\eta\) and use \(\eta/E = \tau\): \(\eta\,\dot\varepsilon = \tau\dot\sigma + \sigma\). This is point 1.
  3. Relaxation: the stress is bounded, so \(\varepsilon_2(t) = \int_0^t \sigma(u)/\eta\,\mathrm{d}u\) is continuous and \(\varepsilon_2(0) = 0\) (fundamental theorem, theorem 3.40). So the spring takes the whole jump, \(\varepsilon_1(0+) = \varepsilon_0\) and \(\sigma(0+) = E\varepsilon_0\).
  4. For \(t > 0\), \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\) is constant, \(\dot\varepsilon = 0\), and point 1 gives \(\tau\dot\sigma + \sigma = 0\), that is \(\dot\sigma - (-1/\tau)\,\sigma = 0\). By lemma 9.34 with \(s = -1/\tau\), \(f = 0\) and \(y_0 = E\varepsilon_0\) this equation has exactly one solution, \(\sigma(t) = E\varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\). This is point 2.
  5. Creep: for \(t \ge 0\), \(\sigma = \sigma_0\), so \(\varepsilon_1 = \sigma_0/E\) is constant. The dashpot gives \(\dot\varepsilon_2 = \sigma_0/\eta\) with \(\varepsilon_2(0) = 0\) as in step 3. By the fundamental theorem \(\varepsilon_2(t) = \sigma_0 t/\eta\) and \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 = \sigma_0(1/E + t/\eta)\). This is point 3.
  6. Unloading: for \(t > T\), \(\sigma = 0\), so \(\dot\varepsilon_2 = 0\) and \(\varepsilon_2\) stays at the value \(\sigma_0 T/\eta\) that it had at \(T\) (continuous as in step 3). The spring has \(\varepsilon_1 = 0\) and has jumped back by \(\sigma_0/E\). The final strain is \(\sigma_0 T/\eta\). This is point 4.

Source: CM (9.2.12)-(9.2.19) (PDF p. 426-428) and BOWER §3.6.3 (PDF p. 137-138). The proof is with lemma 9.34, CM uses the Laplace transform.

Let us see this in numbers. We take a Maxwell element with \(E = 1\) and \(\tau = 1\), dimensionless, a chosen model and not a material. At \(t/\tau = 0{,}5;\ 1;\ 2;\ 5\) we have \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}/E = 0{,}6065;\ 0{,}3679;\ 0{,}1353;\ 0{,}0067\) and it goes to zero, while the compliance \(E J_{\mathrm{lez}}\) is \(1{,}5;\ 2;\ 3;\ 6\). If we load the element with \(\sigma_0 = 1\) until \(T = 2\tau\) and unload it, the strain \(2\) remains: of the \(3\) that it had reached, the spring returned \(1\).

The figure shows what the theorem says. We draw the left graph: the stress at a jump of strain by \(1\) in units of \(E\). First the Maxwell element. It starts at \(1\), because the spring takes the whole jump, and falls towards zero, because the dashpot slowly lengthens and the spring unloads. Then the right graph, the strain at a jump of stress. The Maxwell curve goes up as a straight line without bound, so under constant stress the Maxwell element never finds equilibrium. The first question fails for a solid: the element behaves like a liquid that flows under constant stress (CM, PDF p. 419, which calls the Maxwell model the model of a viscoelastic fluid). After unloading the strain remains, the opposite of a steel bar, which returns. For polymers in which the permanent strain dominates this is fitting: BOWER (PDF p. 138) says that the Maxwell model gives steady-state creep and represents an uncross-linked polymer.

In parallel it is the other way round. In the Kelvin-Voigt element of the middle row the spring has the same strain as the dashpot, so the dashpot holds the spring back.

Definition 20.24 Kelvin-Voigt element (Kelvin-Voigtov člen)

The Kelvin-Voigt element is the parallel connection of a spring element with modulus \(E > 0\) and a dashpot element with viscosity \(\eta > 0\). Stress and strain satisfy \(\sigma = E\varepsilon + \eta\,\dot\varepsilon\). The number \(\tau_\varepsilon = \eta/E\) is the retardation time (čas zakasnitve) and has the unit second.

Source: CM §9.2.3 (PDF p. 429, equation (9.2.22)), BOWER §3.6.3 (PDF p. 137-138).

The equation in the definition is the sum of the stress of the spring \(E\varepsilon\) and the stress of the dashpot \(\eta\dot\varepsilon\), which have the same strain. The time \(\tau_\varepsilon\) is called the retardation time because the strain follows the stress with a delay: at a jump of stress it does not jump, it approaches the new value in a time of this size, as shown below.

Theorem 20.25 Response of a Kelvin-Voigt element (odziv Kelvin-Voigtovega člena)

Let a Kelvin-Voigt element have \(E\), \(\eta\) and \(\tau_\varepsilon = \eta/E\).

  1. At a jump of the stress to \(\sigma_0\) at \(t = 0\), \(\varepsilon(t) = (\sigma_0/E)\,(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_\varepsilon})\) for \(t \ge 0\), so \(J_{\mathrm{lez}}(t) = (1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_\varepsilon})/E\). It is bounded by \(1/E\) and approaches it as \(t \to \infty\).
  2. If the stress is removed after a time \(T\), \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon(T)\,\mathrm{e}^{-(t - T)/\tau_\varepsilon}\) for \(t \ge T\). The strain decreases towards zero: after every time \(\tau_\varepsilon\) it is \(\mathrm{e}\) times smaller.
  3. Let the strain grow uniformly in a time \(h > 0\) from \(0\) to \(\varepsilon_0\), \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0 t/h\) for \(0 \le t \le h\). Then \(\sigma(t) = \varepsilon_0\,(E t + \eta)/h\) on this interval and the mean value of the stress is \(\eta\varepsilon_0/h + E\varepsilon_0/2\). For \(h \to 0\) it exceeds every bound.
Proof

We must show three claims. The first two we solve with lemma 9.34, the third with the fundamental theorem.

  1. At constant stress \(\sigma_0\) for \(t \ge 0\) the equation of the element gives \(\eta\,\dot\varepsilon + E\varepsilon = \sigma_0\), that is \(\dot\varepsilon - (-1/\tau_\varepsilon)\,\varepsilon = \sigma_0/\eta\).
  2. The strain is continuous at \(t = 0\), because otherwise the force of the dashpot \(\eta\dot\varepsilon\) would be infinite: \(\dot\varepsilon = (\sigma_0 - E\varepsilon)/\eta\) must be bounded. So \(\varepsilon(0) = 0\).
  3. By lemma 9.34 with \(s = -1/\tau_\varepsilon\), \(f = \sigma_0/\eta\) and \(y_0 = 0\), \(\varepsilon(t) = \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_\varepsilon}\int_0^t \mathrm{e}^{u/\tau_\varepsilon}\,\sigma_0/\eta\,\mathrm{d}u\). The function \(\tau_\varepsilon\,\mathrm{e}^{u/\tau_\varepsilon}\) has the derivative \(\mathrm{e}^{u/\tau_\varepsilon}\), so by the fundamental theorem the integral equals \((\sigma_0/\eta)\,\tau_\varepsilon\,(\mathrm{e}^{t/\tau_\varepsilon} - 1) = (\sigma_0/E)(\mathrm{e}^{t/\tau_\varepsilon} - 1)\), since \(\tau_\varepsilon/\eta = 1/E\). Hence point 1. Since \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_\varepsilon} \to 0\), \(\varepsilon \to \sigma_0/E\).
  4. For \(t \ge T\), \(\sigma = 0\) and the equation is \(\dot\varepsilon - (-1/\tau_\varepsilon)\,\varepsilon = 0\) with start at time \(T\) and \(y_0 = \varepsilon(T)\). Lemma 9.34, applied with the start at \(T\) instead of \(0\), gives point 2.
  5. Point 3: on \(0 < t < h\), \(\dot\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0/h\) is constant, and \(\sigma = E\varepsilon + \eta\dot\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0(Et + \eta)/h\). The mean value is \(\frac1h\int_0^h \sigma\,\mathrm{d}t = \varepsilon_0(Eh/2 + \eta)/h\) (fundamental theorem), which is \(\eta\varepsilon_0/h + E\varepsilon_0/2\). The first term grows beyond every bound as \(h \to 0\).

Source: CM (9.2.22)-(9.2.26) (PDF p. 429-430), CM (9.2.54) (PDF p. 434), where the Dirac delta shows that the model has no impact response, and BOWER (PDF p. 138), which says that the Kelvin-Voigt model has no well-defined relaxation modulus. Points 2 and 3 are written in this section, not from the source.

Let us look at the numbers for \(E = 1\) and \(\tau_\varepsilon = 1\): \(E J_{\mathrm{lez}} = 0{,}3935;\ 0{,}6321;\ 0{,}8647;\ 0{,}9933\) at \(t/\tau_\varepsilon = 0{,}5;\ 1;\ 2;\ 5\). This is the curve on the right graph, which rises and settles. After the time \(\tau_\varepsilon\) it reaches the fraction \(1 - 1/\mathrm{e} = 0{,}6321\) of the final value, which explains the name. The first question is passed here: the strain settles at \(\sigma_0/E\) and returns after unloading, which BOWER (PDF p. 138) calls the retarded elastic behaviour of a cross-linked polymer, similar to the afterstrain that Kupffer described, except that the model returns it in the time \(\tau_\varepsilon\). The second question fails. If we increase the strain from \(0\) to \(\varepsilon_0\) in the time \(h = 0{,}01\,\tau_\varepsilon\), the mean stress by point 3 is more than \(\eta\varepsilon_0/h = 100\,E\varepsilon_0\), and a smaller \(h\) gives an even larger one. The Kelvin-Voigt element does not bear a jump of strain: it would need an infinite stress, which the arrow at the axis of the left graph shows. So the relaxation modulus (definition 20.20) is not defined, as BOWER also says.

The first model was left without boundedness, the second without an instantaneous response. Each has what the other lacks, so we combine them. The third model, the bottom row, has the spring \(E_\infty\) in parallel with a Maxwell branch.

Definition 20.26 Standard linear solid (standardni trdnik)

The standard linear solid is the parallel connection of a spring element with modulus \(E_\infty > 0\) and a Maxwell element with modulus \(E_1 > 0\) and viscosity \(\eta > 0\). We write \(E_0 = E_\infty + E_1\), \(\tau = \eta/E_1\) (the relaxation time of the branch) and \(\tau_\varepsilon = \tau E_0/E_\infty\) (the retardation time).

Source: CM §9.2.4 (PDF p. 431-433), Fig. 9.2.9(b), which calls it the three-element model, and Example 9.2.1 (PDF p. 435), the standard linear solid. BOWER §3.6.3 (PDF p. 138) calls it the three-parameter model.

The theorem below explains the names \(\tau\) and \(\tau_\varepsilon\): \(\tau\) determines how fast the stress loosens at a jump of strain, \(\tau_\varepsilon\) how fast the strain settles at a jump of stress. The ratio \(\tau_\varepsilon/\tau = E_0/E_\infty > 1\) says that they differ.

Theorem 20.27 Response of the standard linear solid (odziv standardnega trdnika)

Let a standard linear solid have \(E_\infty\), \(E_1\), \(\eta\) and \(E_0\), \(\tau\), \(\tau_\varepsilon\) from definition 20.26.

  1. Stress and strain satisfy \(\sigma + \tau\dot\sigma = E_\infty\varepsilon + \tau E_0\,\dot\varepsilon\).
  2. The relaxation modulus is \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t) = E_\infty + (E_0 - E_\infty)\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\), so it goes from \(E_0\) at \(t = 0+\) to \(E_\infty > 0\).
  3. The creep compliance is \(J_{\mathrm{lez}}(t) = 1/E_\infty - (1/E_\infty - 1/E_0)\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_\varepsilon}\), so it goes from \(1/E_0\) to \(1/E_\infty\).
  4. If the stress \(\sigma_0\) is removed after a time \(T\), the strain first jumps back by \(\sigma_0/E_0\) and then decreases towards zero: after every time \(\tau_\varepsilon\) it is \(\mathrm{e}\) times smaller.
Proof

We must show four claims. The branches are parallel and have the same strain \(\varepsilon\), the stress is the sum \(\sigma = \sigma_\infty + \sigma_{\mathrm{M}}\) with \(\sigma_\infty = E_\infty\varepsilon\) and the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{M}}\) of the Maxwell branch.

  1. By theorem 20.23, point 1, with \(E_1\) in place of \(E\) and \(\eta = \tau E_1\), the Maxwell branch satisfies \(\sigma_{\mathrm{M}} + \tau\dot\sigma_{\mathrm{M}} = \tau E_1\,\dot\varepsilon\).
  2. Point 1 of the theorem: \(\sigma + \tau\dot\sigma = E_\infty\varepsilon + \tau E_\infty\dot\varepsilon + (\sigma_{\mathrm{M}} + \tau\dot\sigma_{\mathrm{M}}) = E_\infty\varepsilon + \tau E_\infty\dot\varepsilon + \tau E_1\dot\varepsilon = E_\infty\varepsilon + \tau E_0\dot\varepsilon\).
  3. Relaxation: by theorem 20.23, point 2 (with \(E_1\)), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{M}} = E_1\varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\) for \(t > 0\), and \(\sigma_\infty = E_\infty\varepsilon_0\). The sum is \(\sigma = \varepsilon_0(E_\infty + E_1\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau})\) with \(E_1 = E_0 - E_\infty\). This is point 2.
  4. Creep: for \(t \ge 0\), \(\sigma = \sigma_0\). The dashpot does not move at \(t = 0\) (its strain \(\varepsilon_2\) is continuous and \(\varepsilon_2(0) = 0\)), so the strain of the spring of the Maxwell branch is \(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon\) and \(\sigma_0 = E_\infty\varepsilon(0+) + E_1\varepsilon(0+) = E_0\,\varepsilon(0+)\).
  5. For \(t > 0\), \(\dot\sigma = 0\) and point 1 gives \(\tau E_0\,\dot\varepsilon + E_\infty\varepsilon = \sigma_0\), that is \(\dot\varepsilon - (-1/\tau_\varepsilon)\,\varepsilon = \sigma_0/(\tau E_0)\) with \(\tau_\varepsilon = \tau E_0/E_\infty\). Lemma 9.34 with \(y_0 = \sigma_0/E_0\) gives \(\varepsilon = \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_\varepsilon}\big(\sigma_0/E_0 + \tfrac{\sigma_0}{\tau E_0}\,\tau_\varepsilon(\mathrm{e}^{t/\tau_\varepsilon} - 1)\big)\) (the integral as in theorem 20.25). Since \(\tau_\varepsilon/(\tau E_0) = 1/E_\infty\), \(\varepsilon = \sigma_0\big(1/E_\infty - (1/E_\infty - 1/E_0)\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_\varepsilon}\big)\). This is point 3.
  6. Unloading at \(T\): the dashpot does not move, so \(\sigma = E_\infty\varepsilon + E_1(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_2)\) is linear in \(\varepsilon\) with the same \(\varepsilon_2\). The drop of \(\sigma\) from \(\sigma_0\) to \(0\) is thus \(-\sigma_0 = E_0\,\Delta\varepsilon\) and \(\Delta\varepsilon = -\sigma_0/E_0\). For \(t > T\), \(\sigma = 0\) and point 1 gives \(\dot\varepsilon - (-1/\tau_\varepsilon)\,\varepsilon = 0\), and by lemma 9.34 \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon(T+)\,\mathrm{e}^{-(t - T)/\tau_\varepsilon}\). This is point 4.

Source: CM §9.2.4 and Example 9.2.1 (PDF p. 431-433, 435), BOWER §3.6.3 (PDF p. 138). The split into a spring and a Maxwell branch is written in this section, not from the source.

We take \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\), so \(E_1 = E_\infty\) and \(\tau_\varepsilon = 2\tau\). This is a chosen model and not a material, the numbers are dimensionless. For \(t/\tau = 0{,}5;\ 1;\ 2;\ 5\) the values are in the table.

\(t/\tau\) \(0{,}5\) \(1\) \(2\) \(5\)
\(E_{\mathrm{rel}}/E_\infty\) \(1{,}6065\) \(1{,}3679\) \(1{,}1353\) \(1{,}0067\)
\(E_\infty J_{\mathrm{lez}}\) \(0{,}6106\) \(0{,}6967\) \(0{,}8161\) \(0{,}9590\)

The curve of the standard linear solid falls from \(2\) to \(1\) on the left graph and rises from \(0{,}5\) to \(1\) on the right. The first question is passed, because the strain settles at \(\sigma_0/E_\infty\). The second is passed, because the bar responds to a jump of stress at once with \(\varepsilon(0+) = \sigma_0/E_0\), and at a jump of strain it gets the finite stress \(E_0\varepsilon_0\). This is the smallest model that passes both tests. We checked the values with an independent computation: numerical integration (RK4, step \(0{,}001\,\tau\)) of the equation for the strain of the dashpot, \(\dot\varepsilon_2 = (\varepsilon - \varepsilon_2)/\tau\), gives the same four values in both rows, and SymPy shows that both functions satisfy the equation of point 1.

Two mistakes are easy to make with this model. The first is to take the same time for relaxation and for creep. If in the compliance we take \(\tau\) in place of \(\tau_\varepsilon\), at \(t = \tau\) the value is \(E_\infty J_{\mathrm{lez}} = 0{,}8161\) instead of \(0{,}6967\), so creep would look twice as fast. The true reason that \(\tau_\varepsilon > \tau\) is seen on the dashpot. Its strain \(\varepsilon_2\) catches up with the strain \(\varepsilon\) at the rate \(\dot\varepsilon_2 = (\varepsilon - \varepsilon_2)/\tau\) (step 1 of theorem 20.23 with \(E_1\)). At a jump of strain \(\varepsilon\) is fixed and the difference \(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_2\) falls at the rate \(1/\tau\). At a jump of stress \(\varepsilon\) moves with the dashpot: from \(\sigma_0 = E_\infty\varepsilon + E_1(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_2)\) we get \(\varepsilon - \varepsilon_2 = (\sigma_0 - E_\infty\varepsilon_2)/E_0\), so the difference falls \(E_\infty/E_0\) times slower, at the rate \(1/\tau_\varepsilon\). The second mistake is to think that \(J_{\mathrm{lez}}(t) = 1/E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\). At \(t = 0+\) and as \(t \to \infty\) it holds, \(E_0 J_{\mathrm{lez}}(0+) = 1\) and \(E_\infty J_{\mathrm{lez}}(\infty) = 1\). In between the product \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\,J_{\mathrm{lez}}\) at \(t/\tau = 1;\ 2;\ 5\) equals \(0{,}9530;\ 0{,}9265;\ 0{,}9654\) and is not \(1\). The true relation is a relation between the Laplace transforms (CM (9.2.9), PDF p. 425), which we do not prove here and only cite.

What have we got? Three models, each derived from a spring and a dashpot, have shown that stress and strain in a viscoelastic material move with a delay and that this is what we need for losses. The Maxwell element fails the first question, the Kelvin-Voigt element the second, the standard linear solid passes both. The next section (20.5) writes the stress for any history of strain as a sum of loosenings, and section 20.6 shows how much energy the standard linear solid loses per cycle.

20.5 Hereditary integral

In section 20.4 we obtained for springs and dashpots the relaxation modulus (relaksacijski modul) \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\) (definition 20.20): the stress that a bar shows at time \(t\) after we suddenly stretched it at time zero by a unit strain and held it so. The standard linear solid gave \(E_{\mathrm{rel}} = E_\infty + (E_0 - E_\infty)\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\) (theorem 20.27). But a machine has no step. A bar in a bearing, in a spring washer or in a rubber element experiences a strain that changes in any way: a ramp, a cycle, a vibration. The question of this section is therefore: if we know the whole history of the strain \(\varepsilon(s)\) for \(0 \le s \le t\), what is the stress \(\sigma(t)\)? The answer will not depend on which springs and dashpots the model is built from, only on \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\).

Let us give a reason for the name. The formula that we will obtain is hereditary (dedni): CM calls it so (hereditary integral), because the strain or stress at some time depends not only on that moment but on everything that happened before, in contrast to an elastic material, where they depend only on the moment (CM, PDF p. 438). The Slovenian word comes from the verb "dedovati" (to inherit): the stress now inherits all earlier strains. We use the full name only at the theorem.

The model that we use. The body is a straight bar under uniaxial stress: one stress \(\sigma\) and one strain \(\varepsilon\) appear, each a number at every time (as in section 20.4). We prescribe the strain, for example by moving the jaw of a testing machine, and compute the stress. Up to time zero the bar is at rest: \(\varepsilon = 0\) and no internal change has yet happened. We name the idealizations. First, small strains, as in section 3.1.4 (point 1): for them stress and strain are proportional, so stresses add. How small they must be is told by experiment (a doubled history must give a doubled stress), and we do not quote numbers for polymers from memory: all numbers of this section are dimensionless numbers of the chosen model, not material data (the standard linear solid of the example in section 20.4 with \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\), so \(E_1 = E_\infty\), which we call model D). Second, constant temperature, because BOWER derives the law for constant temperature up to time \(t\) (BOWER, PDF p. 137). Third, at time zero we start from rest, as we did for the Duhamel integral (theorem 9.79).

20.5.1 Idea: the history as steps

Before we prove anything, let us think as if drawing on a board. We replace a strain history that is not a step by steps, because for these we know the response. For the history we take the function \(\varepsilon(s) = \varepsilon_0\,(1 + 0{,}5\sin(2s/\tau))\) for times from \(0\) to \(3\tau\), where \(\tau\) is the relaxation time of model D. The letter \(\tau\) here is a time, not a shear stress (there is no shear stress in the chapter).

On the top axis we draw time \(s\) and the strain \(\varepsilon/\varepsilon_0\), then the given history, which starts at \(\varepsilon(0) = \varepsilon_0\). Until time zero the bar was at rest, so the history starts with a jump from \(0\) to \(\varepsilon_0\). We replace the history by steps: at times \(s_{\mathrm{i}}\) the strain jumps to the value that the history has at that point and stays constant until the next time. The step heights are the differences \(\Delta_0 = \varepsilon(0)\) and \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} = \varepsilon(s_{\mathrm{i}}) - \varepsilon(s_{\mathrm{i}-1})\) for \(i \ge 1\). The negative \(\Delta_2\) means unloading, the strain between \(\tau\) and \(2\tau\) falls. The bottom axis shows the same time \(t\), and above it we draw the stress.

How does the bar respond to one step? By definition 20.20 a bar stretched at the instant \(s_{\mathrm{i}}\) by \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) behaves at time \(t \ge s_{\mathrm{i}}\) like a bar that has already been stretched for the time \(t - s_{\mathrm{i}}\): the stress is \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\). This reasoning uses two properties. The law is linear, so a doubled strain gives a doubled stress and the stresses of successive steps add (this is the Boltzmann superposition principle, CM, PDF pp. 436-438). The law has constant coefficients, so the response to a step at time \(s_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the same as the response at time zero, only shifted by \(s_{\mathrm{i}}\). In the figure the responses of the steps are thin blue lines: each starts at its own step, and the response to the negative step \(\Delta_2\) lies below the axis. The stress is the sum of the responses,

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{h}}(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{i} \,:\, \mathrm{s}_\mathrm{i} \le \mathrm{t}} E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} ,\]

so the figure shows the blackwhite line as the sum of the blue lines, and the jump of the blackwhite line at the start of each step is \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(0)\,\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} = E_0\,\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) (right after a step the bar responds with the instantaneous modulus \(E_0\) that section 20.4 defined). The first term, the jump at time zero, is \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon(0)\) and we must not forget it: at \(t = 3\tau\) it is \(1{,}0498\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\), while the other three steps together give only \(-0{,}1459\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\). The values of the four terms at \(t = 3\tau\) are \(1{,}0498\), \(0{,}5162\), \(-1{,}1395\) and \(0{,}4774\), the sum is \(0{,}9038\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\). The same sum is given by the law of the material that we write in section 20.5.2, if we compute it for the stepwise strain piece by piece (in every piece the strain is constant, so the computation is an exponential function, and at a jump \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) stays continuous, since the dashpot does not move in an instant): \(0{,}903841\) in both computations (num-05.out).

The true stress (dashed line) at \(t = 3\tau\) is \(0{,}9804\), so with three steps the error is \(0{,}0766\), that is \(7{,}8\) %. Narrower steps do better, with the same computation (NumPy, steps at times \(s_{\mathrm{i}} = 3\tau i/N\)):

\(N\) step width \(\sigma_{\mathrm{h}}(3\tau)/(E_\infty\varepsilon_0)\) error
3 \(1\,\tau\) 0,903841 \(-7{,}81\) %
12 \(0{,}25\,\tau\) 0,984577 \(+0{,}43\) %
24 \(0{,}125\,\tau\) 0,983711 \(+0{,}34\) %
48 \(0{,}0625\,\tau\) 0,982328 \(+0{,}20\) %
96 \(0{,}03125\,\tau\) 0,981425 \(+0{,}11\) %
192 \(0{,}015625\,\tau\) 0,980923 \(+0{,}054\) %

For \(N \ge 24\) the error roughly halves with every doubling of \(N\) (the ratios of successive errors are \(0{,}58\), \(0{,}53\) and \(0{,}52\)), so for narrow steps it is roughly proportional to the step width \(h\). What is the sum when we narrow the steps? The step height is the difference of the values of a differentiable function at the ends of a piece of width \(h\), and by the mean value theorem \(\Delta_{\mathrm{i}} = \dot\varepsilon(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,h\) for some point \(\xi_{\mathrm{i}}\) in the piece. The sum is therefore like a Riemann sum

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{h}}(t) = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon(0) + \sum_{\mathrm{i} \ge 1} E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s_{\mathrm{i}})\,\dot\varepsilon(\xi_{\mathrm{i}})\,h ,\]

which has for its limit \(h \to 0\) the integral \(\int_0^t E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) (the mark at the end of the integral only closes it, it is not a factor). This is an idea, not a proof: we do not know that the limit really is the stress of the model, and for a general linear material it is the Boltzmann principle, which we cite without proof (CM, equations (9.3.7)-(9.3.9), PDF p. 438, BOWER, PDF p. 137). A proof for the models that the section treats we get as with the Duhamel integral: we write the formula as a candidate and check that it solves the equations of the model.

20.5.2 Prony material

Which models have equations that we can check? The standard linear solid of section 20.4 is a spring \(E_\infty\) in parallel with one Maxwell element (definition 20.22). Why not more elements? BOWER says that simple models are too far from the measurements of a polymer over a longer time, and so he connects in parallel several Maxwell elements, each with its own time, and a spring in parallel with all of them (BOWER, PDF p. 139). The text layer of the book on this page says that the elements are connected "in series", but the formula for \(G(t)\) is the relaxation modulus of a parallel connection (a misprint of the book, PDF p. 139): at a common strain the stresses add, in a series connection the compliances would add. We take the parallel connection, which theorem 20.30 below confirms.

We write the law of one Maxwell element with the strain of the dashpot, so that the equation has no derivative of the strain \(\varepsilon\), since at a jump it does not exist. A Maxwell element is a spring of stiffness \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\) in series with a dashpot in which the stress is proportional to the rate of its strain, \(\sigma = \eta_{\mathrm{j}}\dot\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) with the coefficient \(\eta_{\mathrm{j}}\). Let \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\) be the strain of the dashpot, so that the strain of the spring is \(\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\). Both elements carry the same stress (series connection, the elements are massless): \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\,(\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}) = \eta_{\mathrm{j}}\dot\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\). With \(\tau_{\mathrm{j}} = \eta_{\mathrm{j}}/E_{\mathrm{j}}\) we get \(\dot\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} = (\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}})/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). At time zero the dashpot has not yet moved, \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(0) = 0\). We call the time \(\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) the relaxation time (relaksacijski čas) of element \(j\): it has the unit second and tells in what time, after a step, the strain of the spring \(\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) decreases by a factor \(\mathrm{e}\) (which lemma 20.29 proves).

Definition 20.28 Prony series and Prony material (Pronyjeva vrsta in Pronyjev material)

Let \(N \ge 1\) be an integer, \(E_\infty \ge 0\) and \(E_1, \dots, E_{\mathrm{N}} > 0\) moduli in pascals, and \(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_{\mathrm{N}} > 0\) times in seconds. The function \(E_{\mathrm{rel}} : [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}\),

\[E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t) = E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^N E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} , \tag{20.18}\]

is a Prony series (Pronyjeva vrsta). Let \(T > 0\) and \(\varepsilon : [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}\) a continuous function (the strain after time zero, the value \(\varepsilon(0)\) is the strain right after the start, before time zero the strain is zero). A Prony material (Pronyjev material) has the stress

\[\sigma(t) = E_\infty\,\varepsilon(t) + \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^N E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\big(\varepsilon(t) - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\big) , \tag{20.19}\]

where the internal variables (notranje spremenljivke) \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} : [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}\) are solutions of the equations

\[\dot\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} = \frac{\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}}{\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} , \qquad \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(0) = 0 \qquad (j = 1, \dots, N) . \tag{20.20}\]

Since \(\varepsilon\) is continuous, each equation has by lemma 9.34 (with \(s = -1/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(f = \varepsilon/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\)) exactly one solution, which is differentiable everywhere, so \(\sigma\) is thereby a uniquely determined continuous function.

Source: A series of exponential terms and a spring in parallel with the Maxwell elements are BOWER, PDF p. 139 ("Prony series", the text says "in series", see above). The notation with the strain of the dashpot as an internal variable is ours. We quote the name "Prony" as BOWER uses it, we have not read the reason for it.

For \(N = 1\) and \(E_1 = E_0 - E_\infty\) the Prony series has the same \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\) as the standard linear solid. We check that this function really is the response to a step.

Lemma 20.29 Relaxation modulus of a Prony material (relaksacijski modul Pronyjevega materiala)

Let a Prony material have the strain \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0\) for every \(t \in [0, T]\) (a step at time zero). Then \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t) = \varepsilon_0\,(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}})\) and \(\sigma(t) = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon_0\) with \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\) from equation (20.18). The function \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\) is positive and strictly decreasing, \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(0) = E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} E_{\mathrm{j}} =: E_0\) and \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t) \to E_\infty\) for \(t \to \infty\).

Proof

We must show that the announced \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) solves equation (20.20), then compute the sum (20.19).

  1. The function \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t) = \varepsilon_0\,(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}})\) has \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(0) = 0\) and \(\dot\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). On the other hand \((\varepsilon_0 - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}})/\tau_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). The function solves equation (20.20), and by uniqueness (lemma 9.34) it is \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  2. We insert into equation (20.19): \(\varepsilon_0 - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\), so \(\sigma = \varepsilon_0\,\big(E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\big) = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon_0\).
  3. All terms \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\) are positive and \(E_\infty \ge 0\), so \(E_{\mathrm{rel}} > 0\). The derivative \(\dot E_{\mathrm{rel}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (E_{\mathrm{j}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}})\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} < 0\), so it is strictly decreasing. At \(t = 0\) we have \(\mathrm{e}^0 = 1\). Since the exponential function with a negative argument decreases toward zero, the limit is \(E_\infty\).

Source: The formula is BOWER, PDF p. 139. CM, PDF p. 438, demands of the relaxation modulus non-negativity, monotone decrease and a finite limit, which we prove here for the series (20.18). The proof is ours.

The lemma tells two things that we use. First, \(E_0\) is the modulus right after a step, \(E_\infty\) the modulus after a long time. This suggests that a bar is stiffer when we load it faster, which is the promise of the section on linear elasticity for polymers such as nylon (BOWER, PDF pp. 96, 120). The example in section 20.5.6 shows it with a number. Second, \(\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) really is the time in which the stress of element \(j\), \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\varepsilon_0\), falls by a factor \(\mathrm{e}\), since \(\mathrm{e}^{-\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} = \mathrm{e}^{-1}\).

20.5.3 Hereditary integral

Now we have everything to prove the idea of figure 20.12. We insert the candidate that the idea announces into the equations (20.20) and check that it satisfies them. For this we need the derivative of an integral in which \(t\) appears both in the upper limit and in the integrand (lemma 9.77 from chapter 9), and the theorem on uniqueness of the solution of a first-order equation (lemma 9.34). The strain may be piecewise continuously differentiable (definition 6.11), which covers a ramp that stops after time \(t_{\mathrm{r}}\), and a jump in the rate.

Theorem 20.30 Hereditary integral (dedni integral)

Let the material be a Prony material (definition 20.28) with relaxation modulus \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\), \(T > 0\) and \(\varepsilon : [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}\) a continuous function that is piecewise continuously differentiable (definition 6.11), with a piecewise continuous derivative \(\dot\varepsilon\). Then the stress (20.19) for every \(t \in [0, T]\) is

\[\sigma(t) = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon(0) + \int_0^t E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s . \tag{20.21}\]
Proof

We must show that every term of the sum (20.19) has the form (20.21). The term with \(E_\infty\) is the fundamental theorem of calculus. For the term with index \(j\) we take the candidate \(R_{\mathrm{j}}\) that the idea announces, and show that it has the same equation and the same initial value as \(\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\).

  1. Let \(E_\infty \ge 0\). By lemma 6.12 (a continuous piecewise continuously differentiable function) \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon(0) + \int_0^t\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), so \(E_\infty\,\varepsilon(t) = E_\infty\,\varepsilon(0) + \int_0^t E_\infty\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  2. Let \(j\) be fixed and \(\tau = \tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). Let \(R(t) = \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\varepsilon(0) + G(t)\) with \(G(t) = \int_0^t \mathrm{e}^{-(t-s)/\tau}\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\). The kernel \(g(t, s) = \mathrm{e}^{-(t-s)/\tau}\) is continuous on the square \([0, T]^2\), differentiable in \(t\) with the derivative \(\partial g/\partial t = -g/\tau\), which is continuous, and \(g(t, t) = 1\).
  3. By lemma 9.77 \(G\) is continuous and at every point \(t\) that is not a division point of \(\dot\varepsilon\) differentiable with the derivative \(G'(t) = g(t, t)\,\dot\varepsilon(t) + \int_0^t (-g(t, s)/\tau)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = \dot\varepsilon(t) - G(t)/\tau\). The derivative of the first term of \(R\) is \(-\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\varepsilon(0)/\tau\). So \(R\) is continuous, \(R(0) = \varepsilon(0)\) and at these points \(\dot R = \dot\varepsilon - R/\tau\). The derivative is piecewise continuous.
  4. Let \(D = \varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\). The function \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}\) is continuously differentiable (lemma 9.34, \(f = \varepsilon/\tau\) continuous), so \(D\) is continuous and \(D(0) = \varepsilon(0) - 0\). At the same points as in step 3 we have \(\dot D = \dot\varepsilon - (\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}})/\tau = \dot\varepsilon - D/\tau\).
  5. Let \(W = D - R\). It is continuous, \(W(0) = 0\) and at every point outside finitely many division points \(\dot W = -W/\tau\), that is \(\dot W - sW = 0\) for \(s = -1/\tau\). By uniqueness in lemma 9.34 (\(f = 0\), \(y_0 = 0\)) \(W = 0\), so \(\varepsilon - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}} = R\).
  6. We multiply step 5 by \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\) and add over \(j\) together with step 1. By linearity of the integral (lemma 6.10, point 2) \(\sigma(t) = \big(E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\big)\,\varepsilon(0) + \int_0^t \big(E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-(t-s)/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\big)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), and this is equation (20.21).

Source: The formula is CM, equations (9.3.7)-(9.3.8), PDF p. 438, and BOWER, PDF p. 137, for an arbitrary linear material (Boltzmann superposition principle, not proved there and not here either). The proof for a Prony material by verification and first-order uniqueness is not from the source, it is the same as the path of the proof of theorem 9.79.

What did the theorem show and what not? It showed that for a Prony material the stress at time \(t\) is the integral of the strain rate \(\dot\varepsilon(s)\) multiplied by the weight \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\), and that the jump at the start contributes its own term. It did not show that the same holds for an arbitrary linear material (this is the Boltzmann principle, which we cite), nor for a history with jumps later than at time zero: then the expression gets a further term \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta_{\mathrm{i}}\) for every jump (as in figure 20.12, but we do not prove this here. CM, PDF p. 438, equation (9.3.6), writes the initial jump together with the integral as a Stieltjes integral, for the creep compliance). The weight \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\) tells with what modulus a change of strain at time \(s\) still contributes to the stress at time \(t\). Since \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\) decreases (lemma 20.29), older changes count less than newer ones.

We test the theorem on the same example as in figure 20.12, now for \(t = 3\tau\). We draw the axis \(s\) and on it the strain rate \(\dot\varepsilon(s)/\varepsilon_0 = \cos(2s/\tau)\), which is positive at the start, negative from \(0{,}79\,\tau\) to \(2{,}36\,\tau\) and again positive. Across it we draw the weight \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(3\tau - s)\): at \(s = 0\) it is \(1{,}0498\), because \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(3\tau) = E_\infty(1 + \mathrm{e}^{-3})\), and at \(s = t\), where the integral ends, it is \(2\), because \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(0) = E_0\). Below is the product of the two. Its signed area is \(\int_0^{3\tau}E_{\mathrm{rel}}(3\tau - s)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = -0{,}0694\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\): the positive parts (\(s < 0{,}79\,\tau\) and \(s > 2{,}36\,\tau\)) together do not offset the negative part, so the integral is negative. We add the jump \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon(0) = 1{,}0498\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\), and get \(\sigma(3\tau) = 0{,}9804\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\). The same follows from the law with the internal variable if we solve equation (20.20) with the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method (4000 steps): \(0{,}980390\), the difference from the integral is \(4 \cdot 10^{-14}\). The data are in num-05.out.

20.5.4 An example that fails the test: without the jump

We could regard the term \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon(0)\) in the theorem as unnecessary, since the integral holds all the strain rate. Let us test this. We try the simplest history, the step \(\varepsilon(s) = \varepsilon_0\) for all \(s \in [0, T]\), which is continuous and has \(\dot\varepsilon = 0\). The formula with only the integral would give \(\sigma(t) = \int_0^t E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\cdot 0\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\). A bar that we stretched at time zero and hold would have no stress. But lemma 20.29 says that the stress is \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon_0\), that is \(1{,}6065\), \(1{,}3679\) and \(1{,}1353\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\) at \(t = 0{,}5\tau\), \(\tau\) and \(2\tau\) (model D). The difference is all of the stress. The reason is that the whole jump from zero to \(\varepsilon_0\) at time zero is collected in the value \(\varepsilon(0)\): the history on \([0, T]\) is a constant and its derivative is zero everywhere, and the jump before the start the integral \(\int_0^t\dot\varepsilon\) does not see. Theorem 20.30 says this with the term \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon(0)\) and in the case \(\varepsilon \equiv \varepsilon_0\) the whole answer is this term. In figure 20.12 it is the same: the jump \(\Delta_0\) gives the first term of the sum, and without it the sum at \(3\tau\) would be \(-0{,}1459\) instead of \(0{,}9038\).

A second example that fails the test is the Kelvin-Voigt element: a spring and a dashpot in parallel have no relaxation modulus as a function. If we stretch it in an instant, the dashpot would have to cover the finite elongation in an instant, the rate would be infinite and so would the stress in the dashpot. This is why BOWER says that the Kelvin-Voigt model has no well-defined relaxation modulus (BOWER, PDF p. 138). Such an element is not a Prony material and theorem 20.30 does not hold for it. Its response to a stress history is computed by CM from the compliance (CM, example 9.3.1, PDF p. 439), the reverse question, which we do not treat here.

20.5.5 Memory in \(N\) numbers

Formula (20.21) demands the whole history: in the sum of steps we must store all steps and at every time step multiply them all by a new weight, so there is more work with every step. A Prony material, however, has a short memory: the strain history influences the stress only through \(N\) numbers \(\alpha_1(t), \dots, \alpha_{\mathrm{N}}(t)\). Let us show this on one time step.

Lemma 20.31 Update of the internal variables (posodobitev notranjih spremenljivk)

Let the material be a Prony material, \(0 \le t_{\mathrm{n}} < t_{\mathrm{n}+1} \le T\), \(h = t_{\mathrm{n}+1} - t_{\mathrm{n}}\), and let \(\varepsilon\) be linear on \([t_{\mathrm{n}}, t_{\mathrm{n}+1}]\), \(\varepsilon(t_{\mathrm{n}} + u) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} + r\,u\) with \(r = (\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}+1} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}})/h\). Then for every \(j\)

\[\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}+1}) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}+1} - r\,\tau_{\mathrm{j}} + \big(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}}) - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} + r\,\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\big)\,\mathrm{e}^{-h/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} , \tag{20.22}\]

and the stress at \(t_{\mathrm{n}+1}\) is equation (20.19) with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}+1}\) and the \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}+1})\) so obtained. The history before \(t_{\mathrm{n}}\) influences the stress at \(t_{\mathrm{n}+1}\) only through the \(N\) numbers \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}})\).

Proof

We must show that the expression in \(u\) solves equation (20.20) on the piece and has the right initial value, then use uniqueness.

  1. Let \(\tau = \tau_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(a = \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}})\) and \(y(u) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} + r\,u - r\,\tau + (a - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} + r\,\tau)\,\mathrm{e}^{-u/\tau}\) for \(u \in [0, h]\). Then \(y(0) = a\) and \(y'(u) = r - (a - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} + r\,\tau)\,\mathrm{e}^{-u/\tau}/\tau\).
  2. On the other hand \((\varepsilon(t_{\mathrm{n}} + u) - y(u))/\tau = \big(r\,\tau - (a - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} + r\,\tau)\,\mathrm{e}^{-u/\tau}\big)/\tau\), which is exactly the same as \(y'(u)\).
  3. The function \(u \mapsto \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}} + u)\) solves the same equation with the same initial value \(a\) (the coefficients do not depend on time, chain rule, as in step 10 of the proof of theorem 9.79). By uniqueness (lemma 9.34, with a shift of time) \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}}(t_{\mathrm{n}} + u) = y(u)\). At \(u = h\) this is equation (20.22).

Source: The proof is not from a source, it is derived from lemma 9.34.

A test. Let us take the history of figure 20.13, but now piece by piece linear between the values \(\varepsilon(s_{\mathrm{n}})\) at steps \(h = 0{,}5\tau\), from \(0\) to \(3\tau\). Six updates by equation (20.22) give \(\sigma(3\tau) = 0{,}9625824501\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\), and the hereditary integral of the same piecewise linear history gives \(0{,}9625824501\), the difference is in computer precision. Let us compare also with a simpler route. If we solve equation (20.20) with the explicit Euler method with the same step, \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} \leftarrow \alpha_{\mathrm{j}} + h\,(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{n}} - \alpha_{\mathrm{j}})/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\), we get \(1{,}0202\), \(6\) % too much. The reason is the memory factor: instead of \(\mathrm{e}^{-h/\tau} = 0{,}6065\) Euler takes \(1 - h/\tau = 0{,}5\) (for \(\tau = \tau_1\)), so the bar forgets too fast, because the step \(0{,}5\,\tau\) is not small against the relaxation time. Equation (20.22) has the exponent exactly. The comparison is not a proof, it only shows that a crude difference scheme must not be used when the step is comparable to the relaxation time.

20.5.6 Example: loading rate

The promise of the section on the linearly elastic material, that the behaviour of polymers depends on the loading rate, we now fulfil with a number. We stretch the bar uniformly to \(\varepsilon_0\) in the time \(t_{\mathrm{r}}\): \(\varepsilon(s) = \varepsilon_0 s/t_{\mathrm{r}}\) for \(s \le t_{\mathrm{r}}\), so \(\varepsilon(0) = 0\) and \(\dot\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0/t_{\mathrm{r}}\). There is no jump and theorem 20.30 gives

\[\sigma(t_{\mathrm{r}}) = \frac{\varepsilon_0}{t_{\mathrm{r}}}\int_0^{t_{\mathrm{r}}} E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t_{\mathrm{r}} - s)\,\mathrm{d}s = \varepsilon_0\Big(E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{t_{\mathrm{r}}}\big(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t_{\mathrm{r}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\big)\Big) ,\]

since \(\int_0^{t_{\mathrm{r}}}\mathrm{e}^{-(t_{\mathrm{r}}-s)/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\,\mathrm{d}s = \tau_{\mathrm{j}}(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t_{\mathrm{r}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}})\) (lemma 9.78, point 1). For \(t_{\mathrm{r}} \to 0\) we have \((\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/t_{\mathrm{r}})(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t_{\mathrm{r}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}) \to 1\) (the derivative of the function \(x \mapsto \mathrm{e}^{-x}\) at \(x = 0\) is \(-1\), so \((1 - \mathrm{e}^{-x})/x \to 1\) for \(x \to 0\), here with \(x = t_{\mathrm{r}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\)), the stress is \(E_0\,\varepsilon_0\) as for a step. For \(t_{\mathrm{r}} \to \infty\) we have \((\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/t_{\mathrm{r}})(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t_{\mathrm{r}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}) \le \tau_{\mathrm{j}}/t_{\mathrm{r}} \to 0\), and the stress is \(E_\infty\,\varepsilon_0\).

In the figure there is the axis \(t_{\mathrm{r}}/\tau\) in logarithmic form, the limits \(E_0\) and \(E_\infty\) as dashed lines and the curve between them. For model D the stress at the end for three ramps is \(1{,}9516\), \(1{,}6321\) and \(1{,}1000\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\), when \(t_{\mathrm{r}}\) equals \(0{,}1\,\tau\), \(\tau\) and \(10\,\tau\). The same strain gives, if we reach it in a tenth of the relaxation time, \(1{,}77\) times as much stress (\(1{,}95\)) as if we reach it in ten times the relaxation time (\(1{,}10\)). At \(t_{\mathrm{r}} = \tau\) the formula gives \(1 + 1\cdot(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-1}) = 1{,}6321\), which is a point on the curve. The modulus of a polymer is therefore undetermined without the stated loading rate.

20.5.7 What follows

A strain history that is not a step demands weights. For a material whose relaxation modulus is a sum of exponential terms the hereditary integral (20.21) is exact (theorem 20.30), not only an approximation by steps. The memory of the material is in \(N\) internal variables (lemma 20.31). What the integral gives for an oscillating strain is shown in section 20.6: it takes \(\varepsilon(s) = \varepsilon_0\cos\Omega s\) and computes the phase of the stress against the strain. Sources of the section: CM §9.3.1 (PDF pp. 436-439), BOWER §3.6.2 (PDF pp. 136-137) and §3.6.4 (PDF p. 139). The paths of the proofs (verification and uniqueness) are from theorem 9.79, the numbers are in outlines/ch-dusenje/num-05.out.

20.6 Complex modulus and loss factor of a material

In section 20.3 we wrote the stiffness for steady vibration as \(k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\) with a constant loss factor \(\gamma\), but that was not a model in time: one root of the characteristic polynomial had a positive real part, so the solution grew in time (lemma 20.18). In sections 20.4 and 20.5 we looked at a material with memory, in which the stress follows from the whole past history of the deformation. Now we join the two routes. What does such a material do when we stretch and compress it steadily with frequency \(\Omega\), as a vibrating structure does? How much energy does it lose in one period, and what does that depend on? Do we really get the constant \(\gamma\) of section 20.3 from its model, and on what band of frequencies does it hold (figure 20.17)?

The model is this. We watch a point of the material in a uniaxial stress state: the stress \(\sigma(t)\) and the strain \(\varepsilon(t)\) are numbers, tied together by the relaxation modulus \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\) of definition 20.20. The material is linearly viscoelastic (definition 20.19), and its relaxation modulus is a Prony series (definition 20.28),

\[E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t) = E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N} E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} , \qquad E_\infty \ge 0 ,\ E_{\mathrm{j}} > 0 ,\ \tau_{\mathrm{j}} > 0 , \tag{20.23}\]

with finitely many terms. Each term is the relaxation of one branch made of a spring \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\) and a dashpot \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) in series (a Maxwell element, definition 20.22), and \(E_\infty\) is a spring that does not give way. The sum \(E_0 = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(0) = E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the initial modulus. The standard linear solid of section 20.4 is the case \(N = 1\) with \(E_\infty > 0\). The symbol \(\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) here is a relaxation time, as in section 20.4, and has nothing to do with shear stress. We impose the strain from \(t = 0\) on, \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0\cos\Omega t\) for \(t \ge 0\) and \(\varepsilon(t) = 0\) before, with real \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(\Omega > 0\). At \(t = 0\) there is a jump \(\varepsilon_0\), for which the hereditary integral has its own term (theorem 20.30). We will draw the response as a loop of stress against strain (figure 20.15).

We will write the answer with one complex number. The expression for the stress will have two parts: a vibration with frequency \(\Omega\) that does not end, and terms that die out with \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\). The first gets a name (its loop is shown in figure 20.15).

Definition 20.32 Complex modulus (kompleksni modul)

Let a material under the strain \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0\cos\Omega t = \mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) (the loop is shown in figure 20.15), after the transient terms that tend to zero have died out, give the stress

\[\sigma(t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(\hat E(\Omega)\,\varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big) \tag{20.24}\]

with a complex number \(\hat E(\Omega)\) that does not depend on \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(t\). The number \(\hat E(\Omega) = E_{\mathrm{shr}}(\Omega) + \mathrm{i}\,E_{\mathrm{izg}}(\Omega)\) is the complex modulus (kompleksni modul) at frequency \(\Omega\), its real part \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) is the storage modulus (shranjevalni modul), its imaginary part \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) is the loss modulus (izgubni modul), and the quotient

\[\gamma(\Omega) = \frac{E_{\mathrm{izg}}(\Omega)}{E_{\mathrm{shr}}(\Omega)} \qquad (E_{\mathrm{shr}} > 0) \tag{20.25}\]

is the loss factor of the material (faktor izgub materiala). If for \(\varepsilon_0 > 0\) we write the stress as \(\sigma(t) = \sigma_0\cos(\Omega t + \delta)\) with amplitude \(\sigma_0 > 0\) and a phase shift \(\delta\) by which the stress leads the strain, then \(\hat E = (\sigma_0/\varepsilon_0)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\delta}\), so \(\gamma = \tan\delta\).

Explanation

The names have a reason. The modulus is "complex" because it is a number with a real and an imaginary part. The part in phase with the strain, \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\), acts like a spring: the loss in a period does not contain it (lemma 20.34). The part that leads the strain by a quarter of a period, \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\), loses energy. The hat over \(E\) separates the modulus from \(E^*\) of chapter 11, which is the plane-strain modulus, and the primes of the sources (\(E'\), \(E''\)) mean a derivative, so we do not use them. Compare with \(k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\) of section 20.3: there \(\gamma\) is constant, here it is a function of frequency, as the lower curve of figure 20.16 shows.

Source: GR equations (3.32) and (3.33) (PDF p. 181) write \(E_{\mathrm{hysteretic}} = E' + \mathrm{i}E''\) and \(E'(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\) with "storage modulus", "loss modulus" and "loss factor" \(E''/E'\). BOWER section 3.6.1.2 (PDF p. 134) introduces the same for the shear modulus, \(G^* = \tau_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\delta}/2\varepsilon_0 = G' + \mathrm{i}G''\) (the factor 2 comes from the tensor shear strain, \(G = \tau/2\varepsilon\) on PDF p. 132). The same page prints \(G' = \tau_0\cos\delta/\varepsilon_0\) and \(G'' = \tau_0\sin\delta/\varepsilon_0\) without the factor 2. This is a misprint, since the real and imaginary parts of \(G^*\) are \(\tau_0\cos\delta/2\varepsilon_0\) and \(\tau_0\sin\delta/2\varepsilon_0\). Here is the uniaxial form, and the symbols \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) are the book's choice.

Does the number of the definition exist, and how large is it? For a Prony series we compute it from the hereditary integral of section 20.5, and we draw the result in figure 20.16.

Theorem 20.33 Complex modulus of a Prony series (kompleksni modul Pronyjeve vrste)

Let a material have the relaxation modulus (20.23) and let \(\varepsilon(t) = \varepsilon_0\cos\Omega t\) for \(t \ge 0\) and \(0\) before, \(\varepsilon_0, \Omega > 0\). Then for \(t > 0\)

\[\sigma(t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(\hat E(\Omega)\,\varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big) + \varepsilon_0\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N}\frac{E_{\mathrm{j}}}{1 + \Omega^2\tau_{\mathrm{j}}^2}\,\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} , \tag{20.26}\]

where

\[\hat E(\Omega) = E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N} E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\frac{\mathrm{i}\,\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{1 + \mathrm{i}\,\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} . \tag{20.27}\]

So the material has the complex modulus (20.27) (curves: figure 20.16), and

\[E_{\mathrm{shr}} = E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N} E_{\mathrm{j}}\frac{\Omega^2\tau_{\mathrm{j}}^2}{1 + \Omega^2\tau_{\mathrm{j}}^2} , \qquad E_{\mathrm{izg}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N} E_{\mathrm{j}}\frac{\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{1 + \Omega^2\tau_{\mathrm{j}}^2} . \tag{20.28}\]
Idea

We write the hereditary integral of section 20.5 for the complex strain \(\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), because the exponential function integrates as in the real case. Each term of the series gives two parts: a vibration with frequency \(\Omega\) and a remainder \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\). We take the real part at the end, and we see the loop it traces in figure 20.15.

Proof

We must show the form (20.26). We write the stress with the hereditary integral, insert the series and integrate each term with the fundamental theorem.

  1. For \(t \ge 0\) we have \(\varepsilon(t) = \mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) and \(\varepsilon(0+) = \varepsilon_0\). The derivative of the complex exponential function is \((\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega s})' = \mathrm{i}\Omega\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega s}\) (theorem 9.29, item 3), so \(\dot\varepsilon(s) = \mathrm{Re}(\mathrm{i}\Omega\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega s}) = -\Omega\varepsilon_0\sin\Omega s\) (definition 9.28). By theorem 20.30
    \[\sigma(t) = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon_0 + \int_0^t E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\,\dot\varepsilon(s)\,\mathrm{d}s .\]
  2. The function \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}\) is real, and the integral of a complex function is the integral of its real part plus \(\mathrm{i}\) times the integral of its imaginary part, so \(\sigma = \mathrm{Re}\,Z\) for
    \[Z(t) = E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t)\,\varepsilon_0 + \int_0^t E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t - s)\,\mathrm{i}\Omega\varepsilon_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega s}\,\mathrm{d}s .\]
  3. After inserting the series (20.23) we have \(Z = Z_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Z_{\mathrm{j}}\). The term with \(E_\infty\) is \(Z_\infty = E_\infty\varepsilon_0\big(1 + \int_0^t\mathrm{i}\Omega\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega s}\,\mathrm{d}s\big)\). By the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.40) and step 1 the integral is \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} - 1\), so \(Z_\infty = E_\infty\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\).
  4. For term \(j\) we have \(Z_{\mathrm{j}} = E_{\mathrm{j}}\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} + E_{\mathrm{j}}\mathrm{i}\Omega\varepsilon_0\,I_{\mathrm{j}}\) with \(I_{\mathrm{j}} = \int_0^t\mathrm{e}^{-(t-s)/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega s}\,\mathrm{d}s\). Let \(\lambda = 1/\tau_{\mathrm{j}} + \mathrm{i}\Omega \ne 0\). By theorem 9.29, item 1, the integrand is \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}\), and the antiderivative is \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda s}/\lambda\) by item 3. The fundamental theorem gives \(I_{\mathrm{j}} = (\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} - \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}})/\lambda\), since \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t} = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), and \(1/\lambda = \tau_{\mathrm{j}}/(1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}})\).
  5. Therefore
    \[Z_{\mathrm{j}} = E_{\mathrm{j}}\varepsilon_0\Big[\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} + \frac{\mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\big(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} - \mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\big)\Big] = E_{\mathrm{j}}\varepsilon_0\Big[\frac{\mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} + \frac{1}{1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\Big] ,\]
    because \(1 - \dfrac{\mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}} = \dfrac{1}{1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\).
  6. The sum is \(Z = \hat E\,\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} + \varepsilon_0\sum_{\mathrm{j}} E_{\mathrm{j}}\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}/(1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}})\) with \(\hat E\) from (20.27). Since \(1/(1 + \mathrm{i}y) = (1 - \mathrm{i}y)/(1 + y^2)\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\) is real, the real part of the second term equals the term in (20.26).
  7. For the split of \(\hat E\) we use \(\mathrm{i}y/(1 + \mathrm{i}y) = \mathrm{i}y(1 - \mathrm{i}y)/(1 + y^2) = (y^2 + \mathrm{i}y)/(1 + y^2)\) with \(y = \Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\).
