This gives (20.28). The transient terms are \(\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}\) and tend to zero, and the number \(\hat E\) does not depend on \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(t\), so definition 20.32 holds.
Explanation

The remainder is not small at once. After the time \(5\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) we have \(\mathrm{e}^{-5} = 0{,}0067\), so below \(0{,}7\ \%\) of the original value of term \(j\), and the "steady" state makes sense only from there on. The core of the theorem is that all terms of the forced part, \(E_\infty\) and \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/(1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}})\), are multipliers of the same \(\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\). The jump at \(t = 0\) affects only the remainder: at \(t = 0\) we get \(\sigma(0+) = \mathrm{Re}\hat E\varepsilon_0 + \varepsilon_0\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}/(1 + \Omega^2\tau_{\mathrm{j}}^2) = \varepsilon_0(E_\infty + \sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}) = E_0\varepsilon_0\), as it must be for a jump of strain (initial modulus \(E_0\)). The loop of the steady part is shown in figure 20.15.

Source: The theorem is proved from the hereditary integral for Prony series, which theorem 20.30 provides. BOWER section 3.6.1.2 (PDF p. 134) only states the complex modulus. The proof is not from the source.

We checked the computation in step 5 numerically too: for a standard linear solid with \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\) and \(\Omega\tau = 1\) the hereditary integral, computed by the trapezoidal sum on \(40\,000\) pieces, gives at \(t/\tau = 0{,}5\), \(2\) and \(7\) the values \(1{,}379926\), \(-1{,}011201\) and \(0{,}802816\) in units of \(E_\infty\varepsilon_0\), and formula (20.26) gives the same to six digits.

What do \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) mean in terms of energy? In section 20.1 we defined the loss factor by the energy lost in a period (definition 20.3). Now we check that \(\gamma\) of (20.25) is the same quantity.

Lemma 20.34 Loss per period and the loss factor of the material (izguba v periodi in faktor izgub materiala)

Let \(\sigma(t) = \mathrm{Re}(\hat E\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) with \(\hat E = E_{\mathrm{shr}} + \mathrm{i}E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) and \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0\cos\Omega t\), \(T_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi/\Omega\) (loop: figure 20.15). The work of the stress per unit volume in one period (definition 3.42), that is the energy that turns into heat in one period per unit volume, is

\[w_{\mathrm{izg}} = \int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}\sigma\,\dot\varepsilon\,\mathrm{d}t = \pi\,E_{\mathrm{izg}}\,\varepsilon_0^2 . \tag{20.29}\]

With the stored energy \(U = \tfrac12E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon_0^2\) (the energy of an elastic material with modulus \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) at the largest strain, like \(\tfrac12kX^2\) in definition 20.3) we have \(w_{\mathrm{izg}}/(2\pi U) = \gamma\).

Proof

We must show (20.29) with integrals of sine and cosine over a period.

  1. From \(\hat E\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} = (E_{\mathrm{shr}} + \mathrm{i}E_{\mathrm{izg}})(\cos\Omega t + \mathrm{i}\sin\Omega t)\) the real part is \(\sigma = \varepsilon_0(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\cos\Omega t - E_{\mathrm{izg}}\sin\Omega t)\). The derivative of the strain is \(\dot\varepsilon = -\Omega\varepsilon_0\sin\Omega t\) (theorem 8.12).
  2. The product is \(\sigma\dot\varepsilon = -\Omega\varepsilon_0^2\big(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\sin\Omega t\cos\Omega t - E_{\mathrm{izg}}\sin^2\Omega t\big)\). By lemma 9.60 (item 3 with \(a = 0\)) the integral of the first term is zero, by item 2 we have \(\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{p}}}\sin^2\Omega t\,\mathrm{d}t = T_{\mathrm{p}}/2\).
  3. Therefore \(w_{\mathrm{izg}} = \Omega\varepsilon_0^2E_{\mathrm{izg}}T_{\mathrm{p}}/2 = \pi E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0^2\), because \(\Omega T_{\mathrm{p}} = 2\pi\). The quotient with \(2\pi U = \pi E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon_0^2\) is \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}/E_{\mathrm{shr}}\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The form \(\gamma = W/(2\pi U)\) is definition 20.3. CK (PDF p. 127) reads the loss of viscous damping per period, \(\pi c\Omega U^2\), as the area of the ellipse of force against displacement, and introduces \(\gamma\) in (4.79) (PDF p. 129).

The loss is therefore proportional to \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\), not to the whole of \(\hat E\): the complex number carries two roles, storage and loss, and each has its own part. This split can be seen in figure 20.15.

We build the figure as at a board. Horizontally we draw the \(\varepsilon\) axis and vertically the \(\sigma\) axis. If the material were elastic with modulus \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\), the point \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\) would move along the line through the origin with slope \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\), since then \(\sigma = E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon\). The strain oscillates between \(-\varepsilon_0\) and \(\varepsilon_0\), which we mark with the distance \(\varepsilon_0\) and the vertical dashed lines where the line reaches the extreme positions. For our material the stress \(\sigma = \varepsilon_0(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\cos\Omega t - E_{\mathrm{izg}}\sin\Omega t)\) is not only \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon\): the added term \(-E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0\sin\Omega t = E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0\cos(\Omega t + \pi/2)\) leads the strain by a quarter of a period, since it reaches its largest value a quarter of a period before the strain does. So the point does not run along the line but along a loop. Since \(\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1\) (lemma 8.10, item 1), we have

\[\Big(\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_0}\Big)^2 + \Big(\frac{\sigma - E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon}{E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0}\Big)^2 = 1 . \tag{20.30}\]

In the coordinates \(\varepsilon\) and \(\sigma - E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon\) this is an ellipse with semi-axes \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0\). In the plane \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\) adding \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon\) tilts it so that it lies along the line. At \(\varepsilon = 0\) we have \(\sigma = \pm E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0\): these are the orange points. Each lies \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0 = 0{,}5\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0\) from the line, so there the loop is \(2E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0 = E_\infty\varepsilon_0\) wide. The point travels clockwise, opposite to figure 9.27. That figure shows the force \(f_{\mathrm{D}} = -c\,\dot q\) with which the dashpot acts on the mass, while here we have the stress with which the surroundings pull on the material. By the law of action and reaction the two have opposite signs: the part of the stress that loses energy is \(-E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0\sin\Omega t = (E_{\mathrm{izg}}/\Omega)\,\dot\varepsilon\), proportional to \(+\dot\varepsilon\) and not to \(-\dot q\). The opposite sign mirrors the loop across the horizontal axis and reverses the direction of travel. The area of this ellipse is \(\pi\cdot\varepsilon_0\cdot E_{\mathrm{izg}}\varepsilon_0 = 1{,}5708\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0^2\) (the map \((\varepsilon, \sigma) \mapsto (\varepsilon, \sigma - E_{\mathrm{shr}}\varepsilon)\), which tilts the ellipse, has determinant \(1\) and does not change the area) and it equals the loss (20.29): both routes give the same number. The stored energy is \(U = 0{,}75\,E_\infty\varepsilon_0^2\) and \(\gamma = 1{,}5708/(2\pi\cdot 0{,}75) = 0{,}3333\).

Why does the loop have a width at all? We look at the branch of the standard linear solid, its Maxwell element with \(E_1 = E_0 - E_\infty\). It has a spring \(E_1\) and a dashpot \(E_1\tau\) in series. By step 5 of the proof the stress of the branch has the amplitude \(E_1\varepsilon_0\,\Omega\tau/\sqrt{1 + \Omega^2\tau^2}\), and the dashpot stretches with a rate whose amplitude is (the stress of the branch divided by its coefficient \(E_1\tau\)) \(\Omega\varepsilon_0/\sqrt{1 + \Omega^2\tau^2}\). The power of the dashpot is force times velocity (definition 8.54), so the dashpot loses much energy only when both are large at once. At \(\Omega\tau = 0{,}1\) the stress of the branch is \(0{,}0995\,E_1\varepsilon_0\) and the rate of the dashpot is \(0{,}995\,\Omega\varepsilon_0\): the dashpot moves with almost the whole rate of the strain, but with almost no force, since the branch has time to give way. At \(\Omega\tau = 10\) the stress of the branch is \(0{,}995\,E_1\varepsilon_0\) and the rate only \(0{,}0995\,\Omega\varepsilon_0\): the force hardly moves the dashpot, so the spring takes almost all the stretch of the branch. In the middle, at \(\Omega\tau = 1\), both are \(0{,}7071\) of their size, and the loss is largest.

Example 20.35 Complex modulus of the standard solid (kompleksni modul standardnega trdnika)

For a standard linear solid with \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\) (a model, not a substance, as in section 20.4, curves in figure 20.16) we have \(N = 1\), \(E_1 = E_0 - E_\infty = E_\infty\) and \(x = \Omega\tau\). From equations (20.28) we get \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}/E_\infty = 1 + x^2/(1 + x^2)\), \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}/E_\infty = x/(1 + x^2)\) and \(\gamma = x/(1 + 2x^2)\). For three frequencies:

\(\Omega\tau\) \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}/E_\infty\) \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}/E_\infty\) \(\gamma\)
\(0{,}1\) \(1{,}0099\) \(0{,}0990\) \(0{,}0980\)
\(1\) \(1{,}5000\) \(0{,}5000\) \(0{,}3333\)
\(10\) \(1{,}9901\) \(0{,}0990\) \(0{,}0498\)

Source: The computation is in num-06.py, SymPy and NumPy. The model is the book's choice.

Slowly (\(\Omega\tau = 0{,}1\)) the material behaves almost like an elastic material with modulus \(E_\infty \approx E_{\mathrm{shr}}\), quickly (\(\Omega\tau = 10\)) again like an elastic material, but with a stiffer modulus \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} \to E_0 = 2E_\infty\). Between the two, \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) climbs from \(E_\infty\) to \(E_0\), as the \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) curve of the next figure shows, and the \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) curve has a hump in it.

We read the figure from top to bottom. The axes are on a logarithmic scale, because the frequencies differ by decades. The upper curve \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) starts at \(1\) and ends at \(2\), in units of \(E_\infty\). Below it is \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\), which is close to zero at both ends. At the bottom is the loss factor \(\gamma\), the quotient of the two, with a peak between the decades, and the three points of the table are marked on it. This quotient is just what the model of section 20.3 needs. Where is the peak and how high is it?

Corollary 20.36 Peak of the loss factor of the standard solid (vrh faktorja izgub standardnega trdnika)

Let a material have the relaxation modulus \(E_{\mathrm{rel}}(t) = E_\infty + (E_0 - E_\infty)\mathrm{e}^{-t/\tau}\) with \(E_0 > E_\infty > 0\) and \(x = \Omega\tau\) (curves: figure 20.16). Then:

  1. \(\gamma(\Omega) = \dfrac{E_0 - E_\infty}{E_\infty/x + E_0x}\) (lower curve).
  2. \(\gamma(\Omega) \le \gamma_{\max} = \dfrac{E_0 - E_\infty}{2\sqrt{E_0E_\infty}}\), with equality exactly at \(x = \sqrt{E_\infty/E_0}\) (peak). With the retardation time \(\tau_\varepsilon = \tau E_0/E_\infty\) of theorem 20.27 this is \(\Omega = 1/\sqrt{\tau\,\tau_\varepsilon}\).
  3. \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}(\Omega) \le (E_0 - E_\infty)/2\), with equality exactly at \(x = 1\) (upper curve).
Proof

We must show three items: the first by computation from theorem 20.33, the second and third by the inequality of the square of a difference.

  1. With \(N = 1\) and \(E_1 = E_0 - E_\infty\) we have by equations (20.28) \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} = E_\infty + E_1x^2/(1 + x^2) = (E_\infty + E_0x^2)/(1 + x^2)\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} = E_1x/(1 + x^2)\). The quotient is \(\gamma = E_1x/(E_\infty + E_0x^2)\), which after dividing by \(x\) gives item 1.
  2. The square of a difference is nonnegative: \(\big(\sqrt{E_0x} - \sqrt{E_\infty/x}\big)^2 \ge 0\), so \(E_0x + E_\infty/x \ge 2\sqrt{E_0E_\infty}\), and equality holds exactly when \(E_0x = E_\infty/x\), that is \(x^2 = E_\infty/E_0\). The denominator of item 1 is thus at least \(2\sqrt{E_0E_\infty}\), which gives the inequality.
  3. At \(x = \sqrt{E_\infty/E_0}\) we have \(\Omega = (1/\tau)\sqrt{E_\infty/E_0}\) and \(\tau\tau_\varepsilon = \tau^2E_0/E_\infty\), so \(1/\sqrt{\tau\tau_\varepsilon} = \Omega\).
  4. From \((1 - x)^2 \ge 0\) we have \(1 + x^2 \ge 2x\), so \(x/(1 + x^2) \le 1/2\) with equality at \(x = 1\). We multiply by \(E_1\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The peak at \(x = 1/\sqrt2\) and the value \(0{,}35355\) for \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\) are confirmed by SymPy (num-06.py).

For \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\) the peak is at \(\Omega\tau = 0{,}7071\) with the value \(\gamma_{\max} = 1/(2\sqrt2) = 0{,}35355\) (figure 20.16). Here is also a case that almost succeeds: the peak of the loss modulus is at \(\Omega\tau = 1\) (item 3) with the value \(0{,}5\,E_\infty\), and there \(\gamma = 0{,}3333\), less than \(0{,}35355\). The peaks differ because the storage modulus in the denominator of the quotient between them grows, from \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} = 1{,}3333\,E_\infty\) at \(\Omega\tau = 0{,}7071\) to \(1{,}5\,E_\infty\) at \(\Omega\tau = 1\), and the quotient decreases although the numerator still grows a little.

The position of the peak has an explanation in the two times of the standard linear solid. The frequency \(1/\tau\) tells how fast the stress relaxes at constant strain, the frequency \(1/\tau_\varepsilon\) how fast the strain settles at constant stress (section 20.4). For \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\) we have \(1/\tau_\varepsilon = 0{,}5/\tau\), and the peak at \(0{,}7071/\tau\) is their geometric mean, since \(\sqrt{1\cdot 0{,}5} = 0{,}7071\).

The standard linear solid therefore has a peak, and above it and below it the losses fall. The Kelvin-Voigt element, which in section 20.4 is the second simple model, is different. Its law is \(\sigma = E\varepsilon + \eta\dot\varepsilon\) with \(\eta = E\tau\) (definition 20.24, where \(\tau = \eta/E\) is called the retardation time \(\tau_\varepsilon\)), without memory, so there are no transient terms and we get the complex modulus directly.

Lemma 20.37 Complex modulus of the Kelvin-Voigt element (kompleksni modul Kelvin-Voigtovega člena)

Let \(\varepsilon(t) = \mathrm{Re}(\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) and \(\sigma = E\varepsilon + E\tau\dot\varepsilon\) with \(E, \tau > 0\) (comparison with the standard linear solid: figure 20.16). Then for every \(t\)

\[\sigma(t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(E(1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau)\,\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big) , \tag{20.31}\]

so \(\hat E = E(1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau)\), \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} = E\), \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} = E\Omega\tau\) and \(\gamma = \Omega\tau\).

Proof

We must show only the derivative of the strain.

  1. By theorem 9.29 (item 3) we have \(\dot\varepsilon = \mathrm{Re}(\mathrm{i}\Omega\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\).
  2. Since the real part is linear, \(\sigma = \mathrm{Re}\big((E + E\tau\,\mathrm{i}\Omega)\varepsilon_0\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big)\). This is (20.31). From \(E + \mathrm{i}\,E\Omega\tau\) we read \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} = E\), \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} = E\Omega\tau\) and \(\gamma = \Omega\tau\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The law of the element is in definition 20.24.

The loss factor \(\gamma = \Omega\tau\) grows with \(\Omega\) without bound, because the loss modulus \(E\Omega\tau\) grows while the storage modulus \(E\) stays. A comparison with the standard linear solid from example 20.35 shows the difference: at \(\Omega\tau = 0{,}1\) the Kelvin-Voigt \(\gamma\) is \(0{,}1\) (standard linear solid \(0{,}0980\)), at \(1\) it is \(1\) (against \(0{,}3333\)), at \(10\) it is \(10\) (against \(0{,}0498\)). The Kelvin-Voigt element does not stiffen under fast stretching, but stays at the same modulus \(E\) and the dashpot holds it back more and more: the curve \(\gamma = \Omega\tau\), which is not in figure 20.16, would exceed the peak of the standard linear solid already at \(\Omega\tau = 0{,}3536\) and at \(\Omega\tau = 1\) would be three times as high as the curve of the standard linear solid (\(1\) against \(0{,}3333\)).

We can check the same on a dashpot that we know. For cantilever \(A\) (section 9.6) the dashpot \(c = 35{,}4175\) N s/m is parallel to the spring \(k = 62\,720\) N/m, which is a Kelvin-Voigt element with \(\tau = c/k = 5{,}647\cdot 10^{-4}\) s. At \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 35{,}4175\) 1/s we get \(\gamma = \Omega\tau = 0{,}0200\), and by lemma 20.4 we have \(\gamma = 2\zeta r = 2\cdot 0{,}01\cdot 1 = 0{,}0200\). The same number from two directions. At \(\Omega\tau = 0{,}02\), close to the left edge of figure 20.16, the Kelvin-Voigt element and the standard linear solid have almost the same \(\gamma\) (each \(0{,}0200\)), since there \(\gamma = x/(1 + 2x^2) \approx x\). A Kelvin-Voigt material with the same \(\tau\) in all elements also gives damping proportional to stiffness, \(\mathbf{C} = a_1\mathbf{K}\) of definition 10.45: the coefficient \(a_1\) is the time \(\tau\), and the loss factor \(\gamma = a_1\Omega\) grows with \(\Omega\), as the lemma says.

Does any Prony material have a constant \(\gamma\), as section 20.3 assumes (figure 20.17)? The answer is no, on the whole frequency axis.

Lemma 20.38 A Prony series has no constant loss factor (Pronyjeva vrsta nima stalnega faktorja izgub)

Let a material have the relaxation modulus (20.23) (curves: figure 20.17) with finite \(N \ge 1\), \(E_{\mathrm{j}}, \tau_{\mathrm{j}} > 0\), \(\tau_{\min} = \min_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\tau_{\max} = \max_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). Then:

  1. If \(E_\infty > 0\), then \(\gamma(\Omega) \le \Omega\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/E_\infty\) for every \(\Omega > 0\), and for \(\Omega \ge 1/\tau_{\min}\) we have \(\gamma(\Omega) \le \dfrac{\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}}{\Omega\,(E_\infty + \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}})}\). So \(\gamma \to 0\) as \(\Omega \to 0\) and as \(\Omega \to \infty\), as figure 20.17 shows left and right of the band.
  2. If \(E_\infty = 0\) (a liquid), then for \(0 < \Omega \le 1/\tau_{\max}\) we have \(\gamma(\Omega) \ge 1/(2\Omega\tau_{\max})\), so \(\gamma \to \infty\) as \(\Omega \to 0\).

In neither case is \(\gamma\) constant on \((0, \infty)\) (figure 20.17).

Idea

For each term, \(x/(1 + x^2)\) is at most \(x\) and at most \(1/x\), which is small for small and for large \(x\) respectively. So the loss modulus is small at both ends of the frequency axis, while the storage modulus stays at least \(E_\infty\). The result is seen at the edges of figure 20.17.

Proof

We must show the estimates from theorem 20.33 (equations (20.28)) and the conclusion that \(\gamma\) is not constant. Let \(x_{\mathrm{j}} = \Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\).

  1. Since \(1 + x^2 \ge 1\) and \(1 + x^2 \ge x^2\), we have \(x/(1 + x^2) \le x\) and \(x/(1 + x^2) \le 1/x\). Therefore \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} \le \Omega\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} \le (1/\Omega)\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}/\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  2. For \(E_\infty > 0\) we have \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} \ge E_\infty\), so \(\gamma \le \Omega\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}/E_\infty\).
  3. For \(\Omega \ge 1/\tau_{\min}\) every \(x_{\mathrm{j}} \ge 1\), so \(x_{\mathrm{j}}^2/(1 + x_{\mathrm{j}}^2) \ge \tfrac12\) and \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} \ge E_\infty + \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\). With the estimate of step 1 the second inequality of item 1 follows.
  4. For \(E_\infty = 0\) and \(\Omega \le 1/\tau_{\max}\) every \(x_{\mathrm{j}} \le 1\), so \(1 + x_{\mathrm{j}}^2 \le 2\) and \(x_{\mathrm{j}}/(1 + x_{\mathrm{j}}^2) \ge x_{\mathrm{j}}/2\). Therefore \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} \ge \tfrac12\Omega\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). At the same time \(x_{\mathrm{j}}^2/(1 + x_{\mathrm{j}}^2) \le x_{\mathrm{j}}^2 = \Omega^2\tau_{\mathrm{j}}^2 \le \Omega^2\tau_{\max}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\), so \(E_{\mathrm{shr}} \le \Omega^2\tau_{\max}\sum_{\mathrm{j}}E_{\mathrm{j}}\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\). The quotient is at least \(1/(2\Omega\tau_{\max})\).
  5. Since \(N \ge 1\) and \(E_{\mathrm{j}}, \tau_{\mathrm{j}} > 0\), both \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) are positive for every \(\Omega > 0\), so \(\gamma(\Omega) > 0\). A constant \(\gamma = c\) would have \(c > 0\), but by item 1 \(\gamma \to 0\) and by item 2 \(\gamma \to \infty\). Therefore in neither case is \(\gamma\) constant.

Source: The proof is not from a source.

The lemma says (figure 20.17) that the constant \(\gamma\) of section 20.3 is not a property of any Prony material on the whole frequency axis: at slow motion the material (since it has the firm spring \(E_\infty\)) is almost elastic, at fast motion just as much, and a liquid has more and more loss at slow motion. But it is possible to approximate a constant \(\gamma\) on a band of frequencies. We take \(N\) terms with times \(\tau_{\mathrm{j}}\) spread evenly on a logarithmic scale from \(1\) to \(0{,}01\) (for \(N = 1\) only \(\tau_1 = 0{,}1\), time in an arbitrary unit, \(\Omega\) in its inverse), \(E_\infty = 1\), and look for weights \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\) such that \(\gamma = 0{,}1\) on the band \(1 \le \Omega \le 100\). The condition \(E_{\mathrm{izg}} = 0{,}1\,E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) is by equations (20.28) linear in \(E_{\mathrm{j}}\),

\[\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N}E_{\mathrm{j}}\,\frac{x_{\mathrm{j}} - 0{,}1\,x_{\mathrm{j}}^2}{1 + x_{\mathrm{j}}^2} = 0{,}1\,E_\infty , \qquad x_{\mathrm{j}} = \Omega\tau_{\mathrm{j}} ,\]

which we require at 400 points spread evenly on a logarithmic scale and solve by the method of least squares.

In the figure there are the axes, \(\Omega\) horizontally and \(\gamma\) vertically, and the band with the target \(\gamma = 0{,}1\). The curve for \(N = 1\), so the standard linear solid, has a peak of \(0{,}1345\) in the band and \(0{,}0233\) at its edge, that is \(+35\ \%\) and \(-77\ \%\) relative to the target. Three terms follow the target in the band between \(0{,}0952\) and \(0{,}1047\), that is \(-4{,}8\ \%\) and \(+4{,}7\ \%\), and five terms between \(0{,}0952\) and \(0{,}1018\), \(-4{,}8\ \%\) and \(+1{,}8\ \%\). All weights are positive (for \(N = 3\): \(E_{\mathrm{j}}/E_\infty = 0{,}1847\), \(0{,}1792\) and \(0{,}2574\), for \(N = 5\) at least \(0{,}0552\)), so this is a real material (lemma 20.38 has the condition \(E_{\mathrm{j}} > 0\)). Outside the band all three curves fall, as the lemma requires: for \(N = 3\) we have \(\gamma(0{,}1) = 0{,}0203\) and \(\gamma(1000) = 0{,}0170\), that is a fifth and a sixth of the target. The bounds of the lemma hold: at \(\Omega = 0{,}01\) the upper bound of item 1 is \(0{,}00205\) and \(\gamma = 0{,}00205\) (the bound is almost reached, because all \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) are small), at \(\Omega = 10^4\) the bound is \(0{,}00211\) and \(\gamma = 0{,}00171\).

The band is therefore an approximation and not an equality, and its price has two sides. The first is the storage modulus: for \(N = 3\) we have \(E_0/E_\infty = 1{,}621\) and \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) is not constant on the band, but grows from \(1{,}094\,E_\infty\) to \(1{,}491\,E_\infty\), so by \(36\ \%\). The model \(k(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\) of section 20.3 has both constant, which is the second idealization that the band brings with it. The other side is a gain: the stress of a Prony material at time \(t\) depends, by the hereditary integral of section 20.5, only on the strain at times \(s \le t\), so it does not have the problem that hysteretic damping had in time (lemma 20.18). A constant \(\gamma\) therefore makes sense as a description of the frequency response on the band in which the structure moves, and not as a law of the substance.

In section 20.7 we will insert \(\hat E(\Omega)\), that is \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) on the band, into the stiffness matrices of elements. There \(\gamma\) will no longer be the number of one substance, but a property of each element.

20.7 Damping in the finite element model

Chapter 10 took the damping matrix \(\mat C\) as given: Rayleigh damping (definition 10.45) or modal damping (definition 10.47), where we choose the ratios of the modes. With finite elements a second question arises: can we assemble \(\mat C\) from elements, as we assembled the stiffness matrix \(\mat K\) (theorem 7.13) and the mass matrix \(\mat M\) (section 10.7.3)? The sources are cautious. CK (PDF p. 321) says that the damping matrix could in principle be derived by finite element procedures, but the material properties are not known well enough and most of the damping comes from joints and non-structural parts, so the damping is usually determined for the whole system. BATHE (PDF p. 813) says that the matrix \(\mat C\) cannot as a rule be assembled from element matrices as the mass and stiffness matrices are, and that it is introduced to capture approximately the total loss of energy.

Still, we know two mechanisms that can be written for one element: a material that resists the rate of strain (the Kelvin-Voigt term, section 20.4), and a dashpot that is attached along the body to a resting surroundings, such as air or oil (section 20.1). There are three questions. What matrix does each of them give for one element? When is the assembled matrix Rayleigh damping, that is classical, and what happens if it is not? And what do we do with damping that we know only for harmonic motion, hysteretic (section 20.3) and frequency-dependent material (section 20.6)? We are guided by frame A from section 10.1: two floors with mass \(m = 500\) kg, stiffness of each storey \(k = 501\,760\) N/m, natural frequencies \(\omega_1 = 19{,}578\) and \(\omega_2 = 51{,}257\) 1/s, and the modal matrix \(\mat\Phi\) from section 10.3.4 (in kg\(^{-1/2}\)).

20.7.1 Damping matrix of one element

Take a bar element with two nodes and length \(h\) (definition 7.1), with constant \(EA\) and \(\rho A\), and a beam element (section 12.1). In both the field on the element is \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) (for the beam \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\)), where the nodal displacements \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}(t)\) are functions of time and the shape functions are functions of position. How would we get the damping force on the nodes from this?

We draw the element as a line between two nodes that move by \(d_1\) and \(d_2\). On the nodes the surroundings act with the forces \(F_1\) and \(F_2\). They start at the nodes and point outward, because they stretch the element if we pull (lemma 7.9). The first mechanism is the material of the element. For the Kelvin-Voigt element (definition 20.24) the stress is the sum of two parts, \(\sigma = E\varepsilon + \eta\dot\varepsilon = E\,(\varepsilon + \tau_\varepsilon\dot\varepsilon)\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the strain, \(\eta\) the viscosity and \(\tau_\varepsilon = \eta/E\) the retardation time (čas zakasnitve) in seconds. The first part is the spring, as in chapter 7, the second is the dashpot in parallel with it, because both deform by the same strain and their stresses add. The second mechanism is the external dashpot. We draw it below the bar and attach it to the resting surroundings, because such a dashpot (air, oil, definition 9.1) acts on every piece of the bar with the force \(-c_{\mathrm{z}}\,\dot u_{\mathrm{h}}\) per unit length. The constant \(c_{\mathrm{z}}\) has the unit N s/m\(^2\).

Why the matrices of both mechanisms are so simple is told by the next lemma. For the beam the same conclusions hold, because we only replace the energy of stretching by the energy of curvature.

Lemma 20.39 Damping matrix of an element (matrika dušenja elementa)

Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be a finite element of a bar (definition 7.1) or of a beam (definition 12.3) with stiffness matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) (lemma 7.5, lemma 12.4) and mass matrix \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) (lemma 10.31, lemma 12.43) and with constant \(EA\) and \(\rho A\) (for the beam \(EI\) and \(\rho A\)). Let \(\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\) be the row of shape functions (for the beam \(\mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\)), \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) the field on the element and \(\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) the column of nodal velocities. Then:

  1. If the material is Kelvin-Voigt, \(\sigma = E\,(\varepsilon + \tau_\varepsilon\dot\varepsilon)\) with constant \(\tau_\varepsilon > 0\), the virtual work of the viscous part of the stress at a virtual displacement \(\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) equals \(-\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) with
    \[\mat c_{\mathrm{e}} = \tau_\varepsilon\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} . \tag{20.32}\]
  2. If an external dashpot with force \(-c_{\mathrm{z}}\,\dot u_{\mathrm{h}}\) per unit length acts on the element, the virtual work of this force equals \(-\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) with
    \[\mat c_{\mathrm{e}} = c_{\mathrm{z}}\int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}}\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{c_{\mathrm{z}}}{\rho A}\,\mat m_{\mathrm{e}} . \tag{20.33}\]
  3. Both matrices \(\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\) are symmetric and positive semidefinite (definition 7.15), for \(\tau_\varepsilon > 0\) and \(c_{\mathrm{z}} > 0\) the matrix \(\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\) of point 2 is even positive definite, and the matrix of point 1 has the same kernel as \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\).
Proof

We must show that in each case the virtual work of the viscous force is a bilinear form in \(\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) with the stated matrix. For the bar the quadratic form of the stiffness is \(\vek d^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d = \int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}} EA\,(u_{\mathrm{h}}')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) for every column \(\vek d\) (lemma 7.5, \(u_{\mathrm{h}}' = (d_2 - d_1)/h\) is constant), for the beam \(\int EI\,(v_{\mathrm{h}}'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) (lemma 12.4, step 2 of the proof of lemma 12.5).

  1. The strain of the field is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{h}} = u_{\mathrm{h}}'\) (for the beam the strain of the fibre at distance \(y\) from the axis is \(\varepsilon = -y\,v_{\mathrm{h}}''\), and with \(I = \int y^2\,\mathrm{d}A\) the moment of the section is \(EI\,(v_{\mathrm{h}}'' + \tau_\varepsilon\dot v_{\mathrm{h}}'')\), and the bending energy is \(\int EI\,(v_{\mathrm{h}}'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) instead of \(\int EA\,(u_{\mathrm{h}}')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\)). The shape functions do not depend on time, so \(\dot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{h}} = \dot u_{\mathrm{h}}' = \mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}'\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\). The viscous part of the stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{v}} = E\tau_\varepsilon\dot\varepsilon_{\mathrm{h}}\).
  2. The virtual work of the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{v}}\) at the virtual field \(\delta u_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) is \(-\int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}} A\,\sigma_{\mathrm{v}}\,\delta u_{\mathrm{h}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = -\tau_\varepsilon\int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}} EA\,\dot u_{\mathrm{h}}'\,\delta u_{\mathrm{h}}'\,\mathrm{d}x\). The sign is minus, because the stress acts on the element against the stretching.
  3. The integral \(\int EA\,u'w'\,\mathrm{d}x\) is a symmetric bilinear form of the fields \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{h}}\), and its quadratic form is \(\vek d^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d\) (introduction of the proof). A symmetric bilinear form is determined by its quadratic form (polarization identity, \(4B(a, b) = Q(a + b) - Q(a - b)\)), so the integral equals \(\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\). We insert it in step 2 and get point 1.
  4. The force \(-c_{\mathrm{z}}\,\dot u_{\mathrm{h}}\) per unit length does at \(\delta u_{\mathrm{h}}\) the work \(-\int c_{\mathrm{z}}\,\dot u_{\mathrm{h}}\,\delta u_{\mathrm{h}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). Since \(\dot u_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\delta u_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), the work is \(-\delta\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\big(c_{\mathrm{z}}\int\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mathrm{d}x\big)\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  5. By steps 1 to 3 of the proof of lemma 10.31 (for the beam of lemma 12.43) we have \(\int\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\rho A\,\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\), so \(c_{\mathrm{z}}\int\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mathrm{d}x = (c_{\mathrm{z}}/\rho A)\,\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\). This is point 2.
  6. The matrices are multiples of \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) with positive factors. By lemma 7.6 (for the beam 12.5) \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is symmetric and \(\vek d^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d \ge 0\), by lemma 10.31 (12.43) \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) is positive definite. Since \(\tau_\varepsilon > 0\), we have \(\tau_\varepsilon\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d = \vek 0\) exactly when \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d = \vek 0\), so \(\tau_\varepsilon\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) have the same kernel.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. COOK (PDF p. 402) says that viscous damping is supplied by a surrounding gas or liquid or by viscous dashpots added to the structure, and CK (PDF p. 321) says that the damping matrix could be derived by the procedures for stiffness and mass. BATHE (PDF p. 813) does not as a rule assemble damping matrices from elements. The lemma shows when it is possible.

The lemma showed that for both mechanisms we can use the matrices that we already know for the damping of an element: the dashpot in the material takes the form of the stiffness, the external dashpot the form of the mass. This is the promise from section 12.11. Two idealizations must be named. The material responds to strain by the Kelvin-Voigt law, which does not hold for polymers, which section 20.4 describes with several terms, and the external dashpot is linear and the same everywhere. The matrix of the external dashpot does not depend on the stiffness, only on the mass of the element, so it is diagonal if we lump the mass of the element in the nodes (section 10.7.2).

20.7.2 The assembled matrix and when it is classical

We assemble the elements as we assembled the stiffness. For motion, by virtual work, the element matrix \(\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\) is equivalent to the matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) for displacements, so the assembly is the same.

Theorem 20.40 Assembled damping matrix (sestavljena matrika dušenja)

Let the structure have \(n_{\mathrm{u}}\) unknowns and \(n_{\mathrm{e}}\) elements with the connection table and selection matrices \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) (definitions 7.10 and 7.11). Let element \(e\) have by lemma 20.39 the matrix \(\mat c_{\mathrm{e}} = \tau_{\varepsilon \mathrm{e}}\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} + (c_{\mathrm{z},\mathrm{e}}/\rho_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}})\,\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) with \(\tau_{\varepsilon \mathrm{e}} \ge 0\) and \(c_{\mathrm{z},\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\). Then:

  1. The damping matrix of the structure is \(\mat C = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\), symmetric and positive semidefinite (definition 7.15).
  2. If all elements have the same \(\tau_{\varepsilon \mathrm{e}} = \tau_\varepsilon\) and \(c_{\mathrm{z},\mathrm{e}} = a_0\,\rho_{\mathrm{e}} A_{\mathrm{e}}\) with the same \(a_0 \ge 0\), then \(\mat C = a_0\,\mat M + \tau_\varepsilon\,\mat K\), Rayleigh damping (definition 10.45) with \(a_1 = \tau_\varepsilon\). For positive definite \(\mat K\) it is classical and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = a_0/(2\omega_{\mathrm{r}}) + \tau_\varepsilon\,\omega_{\mathrm{r}}/2\) (lemma 10.46).
Proof

We must show that the damping forces of the elements add up like stiffness forces, and that the matrix in the second point splits into \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\).

  1. The force that the damping of the element exerts on the unknown \(I\) is by lemma 20.39 row \(i\) of the matrix \(-\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\,\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}}\), where \(g_{\mathrm{ei}} = I\). The selection matrix \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the same as for displacements, \(\dot{\vek d}_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\,\dot{\vek d}\) (lemma 7.12), so by the first point of theorem 7.13 (which uses only selection matrices and linearity) the total force is \(-\mat C\,\dot{\vek d}\) with the matrix \(\mat C = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\).
  2. Every \(\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\) is symmetric and \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat c_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\) (point 3 of lemma 20.39), so by corollary 7.14 the symmetry and positive semidefiniteness of the matrix \(\mat C\) follow.
  3. For equal \(\tau_\varepsilon\) and \(a_0\) we have \(\mat c_{\mathrm{e}} = \tau_\varepsilon\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} + a_0\,\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) in every element, so \(\mat C = \tau_\varepsilon\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}} + a_0\sum_{\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}} = \tau_\varepsilon\,\mat K + a_0\,\mat M\) by theorem 7.13 and section 10.7.3. What remains is the same statement as in lemma 10.46.

Source: COOK (PDF p. 403-404) and CK (10.76) (PDF p. 321) give Rayleigh damping as a linear combination of \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\), without a link to elements. The link with dashpots in the material and beside the body is ours, the proof is not from the sources.

Rayleigh damping now has a physical meaning: \(a_1\mat K\) is the viscosity of the material, which is the same everywhere, and \(a_0\mat M\) are dashpots that tie every mass to the resting surroundings, with the same constant \(a_0\) per unit mass. This is why CK (PDF p. 321) remarks at the formula for \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\) (CK (10.78)) that the mass term falls with frequency and the stiffness term grows, but does not say why. Now we know: the mass part is an external dashpot, which is stronger at low frequency, and the stiffness part is the material, whose viscous stress grows with the rate of deformation.

We test on frame A. We draw the frame, two floors with mass \(m\) above the ground, each on two columns. In the left frame the lower storey has the dashpot \(\tau_\varepsilon k\), parallel to its two columns, and the upper storey has one too. We choose \(\tau_\varepsilon = 2{,}8235\) ms, so that the dashpot of the lower storey, \(\tau_\varepsilon k = 1416{,}70\) N s/m, is the same as in section 10.9.3. We will need this for the middle frame. The matrix is \(\mat C = \tau_\varepsilon\,\mat K\) and by theorem 20.40 it is classical with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = \tau_\varepsilon\omega_{\mathrm{r}}/2 = 0{,}02764\) and \(0{,}07236\). The matrix \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat C\,\mat\Phi\) is diagonal, \(\mathrm{diag}(1{,}0823,\ 7{,}4179)\) 1/s, as it must be (\(2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\), SymPy and NumPy in outlines/ch-dusenje/num-07.py). The higher mode is damped \(2{,}618\) times more, \(0{,}07236/0{,}02764 = \omega_2/\omega_1\), because the viscous stress is proportional to the rate of strain, and for the same amplitude this is proportional to the frequency.

In the right frame we tie each floor to the resting wall with the dashpot \(a_0 m\) and get \(\mat C = a_0\mat M\). For \(a_0 = 0{,}56668\) 1/s, the Rayleigh constant of frame A from section 10.9, we have \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = a_0/(2\omega_{\mathrm{r}}) = 0{,}01447\) and \(0{,}00553\): the higher mode is damped less, exactly the opposite of the material. If we add the two mechanisms with \(\tau_\varepsilon = a_1 = 5{,}6469\cdot10^{-4}\) s, we get the Rayleigh damping of section 10.9 with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0{,}01447 + 0{,}00553 = 0{,}0200\) and \(0{,}00553 + 0{,}01447 = 0{,}0200\) for both modes. The Rayleigh damping of frame A is thus assembled from two mechanisms that we know from physics.

Now the hypothesis that the theorem demands: the same \(\tau_\varepsilon\) in all elements. Take the middle frame of figure 20.19, in which only the lower storey is viscous and the upper has no dashpot. Then \(\mat C = \tau_\varepsilon\,\mat K_1\) with \(\mat K_1 = k\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) (the lower storey is between the ground and floor 1, so it has only one unknown). This is the dashpot \(c_{\mathrm{d}} = \tau_\varepsilon k = 1416{,}70\) N s/m under floor 1, so the frame of section 10.9.3. The computation confirms \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat C\,\mat\Phi = \begin{pmatrix}0{,}7831 & 1{,}2671\\ 1{,}2671 & 2{,}0503\end{pmatrix}\) 1/s. The diagonal gives the ratios \(0{,}0200\) and \(0{,}0200\), and the off-diagonal term is \(1{,}2671 = \sqrt{0{,}7831\cdot 2{,}0503}\): the modes are coupled to the largest possible extent, the matrix is the product of a column and a row, \(c_{\mathrm{d}}\,\vek b\vek b^\T\) with \(\vek b = (\varphi_{11}, \varphi_{12})^\T\). The true roots are \(-0{,}39177\pm19{,}58141\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(-1{,}02493\pm51{,}2281\,\mathrm{i}\) 1/s with ratios \(0{,}0200\) and \(0{,}0200\). The classical replacement with the same diagonal is therefore good here (section 10.9.3 computed the difference of amplitudes \(-0{,}029\,\%\) at \(\omega_1\) and \(-1{,}5\,\%\) at \(\omega_2\)), but the shape of the motion is different, since the ratio of the floors is complex, \(u_2/u_1 = 1{,}61696 + 0{,}04000\,\mathrm{i}\).

This example has two lessons. The first: the same viscosity of the material in every storey gives classical damping, viscosity in a single storey does not (middle frame). The condition of the theorem is therefore no decoration. The second: the difference between the true roots and the classical replacement is small for light damping, but the shape of the motion changes. The general theory of such systems (first-order form and complex modes) is in section 20.8.

The condition \(\tau_{\varepsilon \mathrm{e}} \ge 0\) and \(c_{\mathrm{z},\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\) of the theorem also has its meaning. If the damping matrix is not built from physics but from two prescribed ratios, the constant \(a_0\) can get a negative value. BATHE (PDF p. 814, example 9.9) prescribes \(\zeta_1 = 0{,}02\) at \(\omega_1 = 2\) and \(\zeta_2 = 0{,}10\) at \(\omega_2 = 3\) and gets \(a_0 = -0{,}336\) and \(a_1 = 0{,}104\) (the same by the formula of lemma 10.46). The matrix \(\mat C = a_0\mat M + a_1\mat K\) is no longer positive semidefinite: a mode with \(\omega < \sqrt{-a_0/a_1} = 1{,}797\) 1/s has by lemma 10.46 \(\zeta = a_0/(2\omega) + a_1\omega/2 < 0\), for example \(-0{,}034\) at \(\omega = 1{,}5\) 1/s, and its amplitude would grow in oscillation. For the two prescribed modes this does not show, for others it does. Such a \(\mat C\) belongs to no physical dashpot, because it would need a negative \(c_{\mathrm{z}}\).

20.7.3 Rigid-body motion and damping

Does the mechanism \(a_0\mat M\) have a further consequence that the formula for \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\) hides? In the formula there is \(a_0/(2\omega_{\mathrm{r}})\), which grows beyond all bounds as \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} \to 0\). For a structure that is not fixed (aircraft, vehicle, railway cars) \(\mat K\) has a zero eigenvalue with a rigid mode (theorem 10.23), and lemma 10.46 demands a positive definite \(\mat K\). What happens to the rigid mode?

Take the two cars of section 10.5, without friction on the rails, connected by a buffer. We use the damping \(a_0\mat M\), which ties each car to the resting surroundings. On each car there acts then the force \(F_{\mathrm{i}} = -a_0 m_{\mathrm{i}}\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\), which starts at the centre of mass and points against the velocity (lemma 9.2). The buffer acts on the cars with equal and opposite forces (Newton's third law), so in adding the equations of motion it drops out: \(m_1\ddot q_1 + m_2\ddot q_2 = -a_0\,(m_1\dot q_1 + m_2\dot q_2)\). The momentum \(P = m_1\dot q_1 + m_2\dot q_2\) satisfies \(\dot P = -a_0 P\). If the cars move together at \(10\) m/s, then \(P = 5{,}0\cdot10^5\) kg m/s and after the time \(\ln 2/a_0 = 1{,}223\) s it is one half. The graph shows the ratio \(v/v_0\) against the time \(t\), which we put on the axes. One half is the point on the curve \(\mathrm{e}^{-a_0 t}\) at the height \(1/2\) (one half), after \(1\) s there is still \(0{,}5674\) of the initial velocity. The velocity never falls exactly to zero, and the distance travelled by the cars approaches \(v_0/a_0 = 17{,}65\) m with time (\(16{,}6\) m after \(5\) s). On a level track without friction the cars would travel forever, so this is not a property of the cars but a defect of the model.

Lemma 20.41 Damping of rigid-body motion (dušenje togega gibanja)

Let \(\vek s \ne \vek 0\) be a column with \(\mat K\vek s = \vek 0\) (rigid mode, definition 10.22) of a structure with positive definite mass matrix \(\mat M\), and let there be no external forces. Then for the motion \(\vek q = \vek s\,w(t)\):

  1. For \(\mat C = a_0\mat M + a_1\mat K\) we have \(\ddot w + a_0\,\dot w = 0\), so \(\dot w(t) = \dot w(0)\,\mathrm{e}^{-a_0 t}\), and for \(a_0 > 0\) the distance \(w(t) - w(0)\) approaches \(\dot w(0)/a_0\) as \(t \to \infty\).
  2. If \(\mat C\vek s = \vek 0\), for example for dashpots between two points of the structure and for \(\mat C = a_1\mat K\), then \(\ddot w = 0\): the rigid motion is not damped.
Proof

We must show that the equation of motion for such a \(\vek q\) turns into an equation for \(w\), and solve it.

  1. The equation of motion \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek 0\) (theorem 10.2) gives for \(\vek q = \vek s\,w\) the equation \(\mat M\vek s\,\ddot w + \mat C\vek s\,\dot w + \mat K\vek s\,w = \vek 0\). The last term is zero.
  2. For \(\mat C = a_0\mat M + a_1\mat K\) we have \(\mat C\vek s = a_0\mat M\vek s\), so we multiply the equation from the left by \(\vek s^\T\) and divide by the positive \(\vek s^\T\mat M\vek s\): \(\ddot w + a_0\,\dot w = 0\).
  3. For the velocity \(v = \dot w\) this is a first-order equation \(\dot v = -a_0\,v\) and by lemma 9.34 we have \(v(t) = v(0)\,\mathrm{e}^{-a_0 t}\), that is \(\dot w(t) = \dot w(0)\,\mathrm{e}^{-a_0 t}\). The motion \(w(t) = w(0) + \dot w(0)\,(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-a_0 t})/a_0\) approaches \(w(0) + \dot w(0)/a_0\) as \(t \to \infty\).
  4. For \(\mat C\vek s = \vek 0\) the second term of step 1 drops out, \(\mat M\vek s\,\ddot w = \vek 0\) remains and \(\ddot w = 0\). A dashpot between the points \(A\) and \(B\) gives by lemma 9.2 a force proportional to \(\dot\ell\), that is to the rate of the distance, and the distance does not change in a rigid motion.

Source: CK (PDF p. 334) says that for a damped system with rigid modes special procedures are needed, examples with dashpots between bodies are on PDF p. 338-339. COOK (PDF p. 404) says that proportional damping can be imagined as immersing the structure in a non-physical fluid whose viscosity becomes infinite for rigid motion (\(\omega = 0\)), which corresponds to \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = a_0/(2\omega_{\mathrm{r}})\to\infty\). The proof and the numbers are ours (outlines/ch-dusenje/num-07.py).

The lemma showed two things. For \(a_0 > 0\) the model \(a_0\mat M\) damps rigid motion, which a real system does not have. This is the defect of an external dashpot on a resting wall, which physically does not exist if the structure floats freely. With dashpots between parts of the structure and with \(a_1\mat K\) rigid motion cannot be damped. So for free structures we must take \(a_0 = 0\) or dashpots between the parts. For the cars with \(a_1\mat K\) and \(a_1 = 5{,}6469\cdot10^{-4}\) s the roots are \(-0{,}0471\pm12{,}9099\,\mathrm{i}\) and a double zero: the elastic mode is damped (\(\zeta = a_1\omega/2 = 0{,}00365\)), and the rigid one has a double root zero, so \(\vek q = \vek s\,(c_1 + c_2 t)\) (theorem 10.23).

20.7.4 Hysteretic damping in elements

So far we had two viscous mechanisms in the time domain. Hysteretic damping (definition 20.12) is written only for harmonic motion, where the stiffness \(k\) is replaced by \(k\,(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\) and \(\gamma\) is the loss factor (definition 20.3). How do we build it into a structure with several elements? Each element can have its own material and its own \(\gamma_{\mathrm{e}}\). The matrix that we get is called complex, because its real part is the stiffness, which stores energy (storage), and its imaginary part is the loss of energy in a cycle (section 20.1), as with the complex stiffness \(k\,(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\).

Definition 20.42 Complex stiffness matrix (kompleksna togostna matrika)

Let the structure have elements with stiffness matrices \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) (theorem 7.13) and loss factors \(\gamma_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 0\) (definition 20.3). The complex stiffness matrix (kompleksna togostna matrika) of the structure is the complex \(n_{\mathrm{u}} \times n_{\mathrm{u}}\) matrix

\[\hat{\mat K} = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma_{\mathrm{e}})\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat K' + \mathrm{i}\,\mat K'' , \qquad \mat K' = \mat K , \quad \mat K'' = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\gamma_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}} . \tag{20.34}\]

The matrices \(\mat K'\) and \(\mat K''\) are real, symmetric and positive semidefinite (corollary 7.14). The equation of motion for the harmonic force \(\vek Q = \mathrm{Re}(\vek Q_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) is

\[\big(-\Omega^2\mat M + \mat K' + \mathrm{i}\,\mat K''\big)\,\vek x = \vek Q_0 , \tag{20.35}\]

where \(\vek x\) is the column of complex amplitudes, \(\vek q = \mathrm{Re}(\vek x\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) (as in equation (10.63)).

Source: GR (3.31)-(3.33) (PDF p. 180-181), where \(\mat K'\) and \(\mat K''\) are called the "storage" and "loss" matrix. The symbols \(\mat K'\) and \(\mat K''\) are from GR, where the prime does not mean a derivative. For the moduli of a material we use \(E_{\mathrm{shr}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{izg}}\) (section 20.6), because the prime in this book means a derivative.

The matrix \(\hat{\mat K}\) is complex and symmetric, not Hermitian. Equation (20.35) has the same form as equation (10.63), with \(\mathrm{i}\,\mat K''\) in place of \(\mathrm{i}\Omega\,\mat C\): at the frequency \(\Omega\) viscous damping with \(\mat C = \mat K''/\Omega\) equals the hysteretic one for this \(\Omega\) (section 20.2). So the question from section 10.9.1 appears again: when is it decoupled?

Lemma 20.43 One material: hysteretic damping has real modes (en material: histerezno dušenje ima realne načine)

Let \(\mat K\) be positive definite, \(\mat\Phi\) the modal matrix of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) (definition 10.15) and \(\mat K'' = \gamma\,\mat K\) with the same \(\gamma \ge 0\) in all elements. Then:

  1. The eigenproblem \(\big(\mat K' + \mathrm{i}\mat K''\big)\vek u = \lambda\,\mat M\vek u\) has exactly the eigenvalues \(\hat\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = (1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\,\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) with real eigencolumns \(\vek u = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) (the modes of the undamped structure), and \(\mathrm{Im}\,\hat\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/\mathrm{Re}\,\hat\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \gamma\) for every mode.
  2. For \(\vek x = \mat\Phi\hat{\boldsymbol\eta}\) (definition 10.19) equation (20.35) splits into \(n\) equations \(\big((1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\,\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2 - \Omega^2\big)\,\hat\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek Q_0\), so every mode oscillates as the hysteretic oscillator of section 20.3 with the same loss factor \(\gamma\).
Proof

We must show that the modal matrix decouples the equation and that there are no other eigenvalues.

  1. By lemma 10.16 \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat M\mat\Phi = \mat I\) and \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat K\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2)\). The matrix \(\mat\Phi\) is real, so \(\mat\Phi^\T\hat{\mat K}\,\mat\Phi = (1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\,\mathrm{diag}(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2)\).
  2. We multiply equation (20.35) with \(\vek x = \mat\Phi\hat{\boldsymbol\eta}\) from the left by \(\mat\Phi^\T\) and by step 1 get \(\big((1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\,\mathrm{diag}(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2) - \Omega^2\mat I\big)\hat{\boldsymbol\eta} = \mat\Phi^\T\vek Q_0\). This is point 2, since the matrix is diagonal.
  3. From \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) it follows that \((1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\,\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = (1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), so \((\hat\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}, \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}})\) is an eigenpair.
  4. For an arbitrary number \(\mu\) we have \(\det(\hat{\mat K} - \mu\mat M) = (1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma)^n\det\big(\mat K - \tfrac{\mu}{1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma}\mat M\big)\) (definition 2.50, we factor \(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma\) out of every row). This is zero exactly at \(\mu/(1 + \mathrm{i}\gamma) = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), so the only eigenvalues are \(\hat\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) and there are no others.

Source: GR (3.39) (PDF p. 182) gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}} = \gamma/2\) for \(\mat K'' = \gamma\mat K'\) ("the damping remains proportional"). The proof is ours.

The lemma showed that one material with one loss factor does not change the shapes of the modes, which stay real, and that every mode loses the same share of energy. At resonance the ratio is by theorem 20.14 \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = \gamma/2\). How far does this hold when the materials are not the same? The example is frame A with \(\gamma = 0{,}04\).

On the horizontal axis we put the number \(r\) of the mode, on the vertical one its loss factor \(\gamma_{\mathrm{r}}\). The first pair of bars is the frame with the same \(\gamma = 0{,}04\) in both storeys: the eigenvalues are \(383{,}311 + 15{,}332\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(2627{,}249 + 105{,}090\,\mathrm{i}\) and the ratios of the imaginary and real part are by point 1 of the lemma \(0{,}04\) and \(0{,}04\) (blue bars). The second pair is the frame in which \(\gamma = 0{,}04\) is only in the lower storey, where there is for example a rubber bearing (the upper storey has \(\gamma = 0\)). Then \(\mat K'' = 0{,}04\,\mat K_1 \ne \gamma\mat K\) and the eigenvalues are \(383{,}454 + 11{,}093\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(2627{,}106 + 29{,}047\,\mathrm{i}\) with the ratios \(0{,}02893\) and \(0{,}01106\), so different from \(\gamma\) and from each other. The reason is the distribution of strain energy. In the first mode the strains of the storeys are in the ratio \(1 : 0{,}618\), so the lower storey holds \(1/(1 + 0{,}618^2) = 72{,}4\,\%\) of the energy and \(0{,}04\cdot 0{,}724 = 0{,}0290\). In the second the ratio is \(1 : 1{,}618\) and the lower storey holds \(1/(1 + 1{,}618^2) = 27{,}6\,\%\) of the energy and \(0{,}04\cdot0{,}276 = 0{,}0111\). The eigencolumns are no longer real, \(u_2/u_1 = 1{,}61789 + 0{,}02895\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(-0{,}61789 + 0{,}01105\,\mathrm{i}\), a complex ratio as in section 10.9.3. The lemma does not hold, because its condition \(\mat K'' = \gamma\mat K\) is missing.

GR (PDF p. 181-182) proposes an estimate: if the damping is light and the natural frequencies are well separated, we take only the diagonal terms of the matrix \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat K''\,\mat\Phi\), and every mode gets the loss factor

\[\gamma_{\mathrm{r}} \approx \frac{\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K''\,\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}} , \qquad \zeta_{\mathrm{r}} \approx \frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{r}}}{2} . \tag{20.36}\]

For frame A the estimate gives \(0{,}02894\) and \(0{,}01106\) (grey ticks). For the first mode this is \(0{,}05\,\%\) above the true value \(0{,}028930\), for the second \(0{,}01\,\%\) below the true value \(0{,}011057\), which does not show to four digits. The damping is light here: \(\mat K''\) is at most \(4\,\%\) of the matrix \(\mat K\), and the error of the estimate is of the order of the square of this ratio, \(0{,}04^2 = 0{,}16\,\%\), as with the coupling of modes in section 10.9.3, and the measured one is \(0{,}05\,\%\). This is an estimate, not a theorem: a complete treatment requires the eigenproblem of a complex symmetric matrix, which section 20.8 does for viscous damping, and for hysteretic damping GR only states it. A warning: in GR the equations (3.35), (3.37) and (3.38) have \(\mat K'\) printed and not \(\mat K''\) (PDF p. 181-182). This is a misprint, since for \(\mat K'' = \gamma\mat K'\) equation (3.38) would give \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}} = 1/2\), while equation (3.39) says \(\gamma/2\). Correct is equation (20.36) with the matrix \(\mat K''\).

20.7.5 Material that depends on frequency

The loss factor of a real material is not constant (section 20.6): for the standard linear solid with \(\gamma(\Omega)\) from theorem 20.33 it is small at small and at large \(\Omega\tau\). A finite element with a material that has the complex modulus \(\hat E(\Omega)\) (definition 20.32) gets the stiffness matrix \(\big(\hat E(\Omega)/E\big)\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\), if \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is computed with the modulus \(E\). This is our step, not a result from a source: GR (3.32) (PDF p. 181) has \(E'\) and \(E''\) as constants, and we replace them by functions of frequency. No source in the book builds frequency-dependent viscoelastic damping into element matrices (outlines/ch-dusenje/outline.md, O4). The matrix of the structure is therefore \(\hat{\mat K}(\Omega) = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\big(\hat E_{\mathrm{e}}(\Omega)/E_{\mathrm{e}}\big)\,\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\).

We test on frame A, which in both storeys is made of the same standard linear solid with \(E_0/E_\infty = 2\) (section 20.4, a chosen model, not a material), and the stiffness \(k\) is computed with \(E_\infty\). The complex modulus is then \(\hat E/E_\infty = 1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau/(1 + \mathrm{i}\Omega\tau) =: c(\Omega)\) (at \(\Omega\tau = 1\) it is \(1{,}5 + 0{,}5\,\mathrm{i}\), as in section 20.6), and \(\hat{\mat K} = c(\Omega)\,\mat K\). The same conclusion as in lemma 20.43 holds for the complex scalar \(c\): the modes are real, every mode has the equation \(\big(c(\Omega)\,\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2 - \Omega^2\big)\hat\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek Q_0\). The amplitude is largest approximately where \(\Omega^2 = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\,\mathrm{Re}\,c(\Omega)\), since \(c\) changes slowly with frequency. Take \(\tau = 10/\omega_1 = 0{,}5108\) s. For the first mode we get resonance at \(\Omega = 27{,}65\) 1/s (\(\Omega\tau = 14{,}1\)) and for the second at \(72{,}48\) 1/s (\(\Omega\tau = 37{,}0\)), loss factors \(\gamma = 0{,}0353\) and \(0{,}0135\), so \(\zeta \approx 0{,}0177\) and \(0{,}0068\). Two lessons. First: the resonance of the first mode moved up by the factor \(1{,}412 = \sqrt{1{,}995}\) (of the second by \(1{,}414 = \sqrt{1{,}999}\)), because at large \(\Omega\tau\) the material is already almost at its instantaneous modulus \(E_0 = 2E_\infty\) (\(\mathrm{Re}\,c = 1{,}995\) and \(1{,}999\)). The frame is therefore almost twice as stiff, and its natural frequencies are almost \(\sqrt 2\) times higher. Second: the two modes do not have the same loss factor, because \(\gamma(\Omega)\) is a function of frequency. A model with a single \(\gamma\) would prescribe the same value. The damping is light at both resonances (\(\gamma < 0{,}04\)), so the estimate \(\zeta \approx \gamma/2\) is reasonable, but it holds only for oscillation near each resonance.

20.7.6 What we have obtained

In finite elements the damping matrix has a precisely determined origin when we know it: the material (Kelvin-Voigt) gives \(\tau_\varepsilon\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\), the external dashpot \((c_{\mathrm{z}}/\rho A)\,\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) (lemma 20.39), and the assembly is the same as for stiffness (theorem 20.40). With the same constants in all elements this is Rayleigh damping and classical. Its constant \(a_0\) gets the meaning of dashpots that tie each mass to the resting wall, and \(a_1\) the meaning of the viscosity of the material. With different constants it is not classical, which we saw on frame A. In the frequency domain: one material with one loss factor gives real modes with the same \(\gamma\) (lemma 20.43), several materials do not, and we estimate their factors by equation (20.36). In a free structure the dashpots \(a_0\mat M\) on the resting wall damp the rigid motion, which the real system does not have, while dashpots between parts of the structure and \(a_1\mat K\) do not damp it (lemma 20.41). We reach the first-order form and the complex modes, which treat all non-classical cases, in section 20.8.

20.8 First-order form and complex modes

For frame A (figure 20.22) we put a single dashpot under floor \(1\) in section 10.9.3 and saw that the modes are no longer uncoupled: the matrix \(\mat\Phi^{\T}\mat C\mat\Phi\) is not diagonal, theorem 10.49 demands a diagonal one, and we obtained the roots \(-0{,}39177 \pm 19{,}58141\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(-1{,}02493 \pm 51{,}2281\,\mathrm{i}\) 1/s with a complex ratio between the floors. There we computed them with NumPy from the "first-order form", which we only named, and promised that this section tells it to the end. Now we must answer three questions. What is the first-order form and why is it equivalent to the equation of motion? What remains of the modes when the matrix \(\mat C\) is not classical? And does it still hold that every motion is a sum of modes that we compute one by one?

The idea is short. For a system with one degree of freedom we solved in chapter 9 the equation of second order by breaking it into a chain of equations of first order (theorem 9.36). Here we do the same with a vector: we take the velocities for additional unknowns. We get \(2n\) equations of first order, written with two matrices. The matrix in front of the derivative, however, is no longer positive definite, so the spectral theorem of section 10.3 does not apply to it and we will prove orthogonality and expansion once more. (figure 20.22)

Model and assumptions. A system with \(n\) coordinates \(\vek q(t)\) has the equation of motion \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek Q(t)\) (theorem 10.2). The matrices \(\mat M\), \(\mat K\) and \(\mat C\) are real and symmetric, \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) are positive definite (definition 6.27) and \(\mat C\) is positive semidefinite (definition 7.15), as with several viscous dashpots (lemma 9.2). The force \(\vek Q\) is continuous. So the system cannot move as a whole without deforming (rigid-body modes are not treated, definition 10.22). The running example is frame A with one dashpot: masses \(m = 500\) kg, stiffness of one storey \(k = 501\,760\) N/m and a dashpot \(c_{\mathrm{d}} = 1416{,}70\) N s/m under floor \(1\) (section 10.9.3). (figure 20.22)

Let us draw the frame as we will need it. First the ground, which stays at rest. On it we put the columns, two in each storey. The columns of one storey together act as a spring of stiffness \(k\), because the force they give is proportional to the difference of the displacements of their ends. On top of the columns we lay the floors, each of mass \(m\). The displacements of the floors are measured from the rest position, so we mark them by the distances \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) between the dashed and the solid position. Under floor \(1\) we fix the dashpot with coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{d}}\), which connects only floor \(1\) to the ground, floor \(2\) does not feel it. Hence \(\mat C = c_{\mathrm{d}}\,\mathrm{diag}(1, 0)\), as in equation (10.61).

On the right is floor \(1\) as a free body. Newton's law for it is the same as in section 10.1, except that a third force is added: the dashpot pulls back with \(c_{\mathrm{d}}\dot q_1\) (orange arrow below), the lower columns pull back with \(k q_1\) (blue arrow upper left) and the upper ones forward with \(k(q_2 - q_1)\) (blue arrow right). All three pull, so they start at the edge of the body.

20.8.1 First-order form

What should we take for unknowns so that the equation is of first order? For one degree of freedom the initial conditions \(q(0)\) and \(\dot q(0)\) determined the solution (theorem 9.36, order \(2\)). Also with \(n\) coordinates we need \(2n\) numbers, positions and velocities, for the future to be determined. We call these numbers the state (stanje), because they contain everything we must know about the system at this moment to be able to compute its further course. (figure 20.22)

Definition 20.44 State and first-order form (stanje in zapis prvega reda)

Let \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek Q(t)\) be the equation of motion of a system with \(n\) coordinates with the assumptions above. The column with \(2n\) elements

\[\vek z(t) = \begin{pmatrix} \vek q(t) \\ \dot{\vek q}(t) \end{pmatrix} \tag{20.37}\]

is the state, the matrices with \(2n\) rows and columns

\[\mat A = \begin{pmatrix} \mat C & \mat M \\ \mat M & \mat 0 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat B = \begin{pmatrix} \mat K & \mat 0 \\ \mat 0 & -\mat M \end{pmatrix} \tag{20.38}\]

are the state matrices (the blocks are \(n \times n\)), and the equation

\[\mat A\,\dot{\vek z} + \mat B\,\vek z = \vek F(t) , \qquad \vek F = \begin{pmatrix} \vek Q \\ \vek 0 \end{pmatrix} \tag{20.39}\]

is the first-order form.

Source: CK (10.91) to (10.95) (PDF p. 325-326), the same form. GR (3.65) to (3.68) (PDF p. 192-193) have the same equation with the names \(\mat A\) and \(\mat B\) exchanged: their \(\mat A\) is our \(\mat B\) and conversely, and the form \(\mat A\vek r + \mat B\dot{\vek r} = \vek s\). GR writes that the form is not unique, and that the chosen one is symmetric (PDF p. 193).

The name "first order" is because the highest derivative in equation (20.39) is the first: only \(\dot{\vek z}\) appears. (figure 20.22)

Does equation (20.39) really say the same as the equation of motion? This is not self-evident. The lower row has no right-hand side, so it must express that the lower part of the state really is the velocity of the upper. (figure 20.22)

Lemma 20.45 Equivalence of the two forms (enakovrednost zapisov)

Let the assumptions of definition 20.44 hold.

  1. A differentiable function \(\vek z = (\vek x, \vek y)\) with values in \(\mathbb R^{2n}\) solves equation (20.39) exactly when \(\vek y = \dot{\vek x}\) and \(\vek x\) is a solution of \(\mat M\ddot{\vek x} + \mat C\dot{\vek x} + \mat K\vek x = \vek Q\). Then \(\vek z = (\vek x, \dot{\vek x})\).
  2. For a complex number \(s\) and a column \(\vek w = (\vek w_1, \vek w_2)\) with \(2n\) complex elements, \((s\mat A + \mat B)\vek w = \vek 0\) holds exactly when \(\vek w_2 = s\vek w_1\) and \((s^2\mat M + s\mat C + \mat K)\vek w_1 = \vek 0\).
  3. The matrices \(\mat A\) and \(\mat B\) are symmetric, \(\mat A\) is invertible, and neither of them is positive semidefinite.
Proof

We must show that both rows agree with the equation of motion and with the relation between velocity and position, and that the block with zeros does not spoil the properties of the matrices.

  1. The first row of equation (20.39) is \(\mat C\dot{\vek x} + \mat M\dot{\vek y} + \mat K\vek x = \vek Q\), the second is \(\mat M\dot{\vek x} - \mat M\vek y = \vek 0\).
  2. The matrix \(\mat M\) is positive definite, hence invertible: \(\mat M\vek v = \vek 0\) gives \(\vek v^{\T}\mat M\vek v = 0\), so \(\vek v = \vek 0\). The second row therefore gives \(\vek y = \dot{\vek x}\), and then \(\dot{\vek y} = \ddot{\vek x}\), so that the first row becomes the equation of motion. Conversely, if \(\vek y = \dot{\vek x}\) and the equation of motion hold, both rows are satisfied. This proves point 1.
  3. Point 2 follows in the same way, with \(s\) in place of the derivative: the second row \(s\mat M\vek w_1 - \mat M\vek w_2 = \vek 0\) gives \(\vek w_2 = s\vek w_1\), and the first row \(s\mat C\vek w_1 + s\mat M\vek w_2 + \mat K\vek w_1\) becomes \((s^2\mat M + s\mat C + \mat K)\vek w_1\).
  4. Symmetry: transposing a block matrix transposes every block and exchanges the off-diagonal blocks, and \(\mat C\), \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) are symmetric, \(\mat M\) stands at both places.
  5. Invertibility of \(\mat A\): \(\mat A(\vek x, \vek y) = \vek 0\) means in the second row \(\mat M\vek x = \vek 0\), so \(\vek x = \vek 0\), and then in the first row \(\mat M\vek y = \vek 0\), so \(\vek y = \vek 0\). A square matrix with only the zero kernel is invertible (as in lemma 2.53, there for \(3 \times 3\)).
  6. For every \(\vek u \ne \vek 0\) and number \(\varepsilon > 0\), with \(\vek z_\pm = (\vek u, \pm\varepsilon\vek u)\) the quadratic form is \(\vek z_\pm^{\T}\mat A\vek z_\pm = \vek u^{\T}\mat C\vek u \pm 2\varepsilon\,\vek u^{\T}\mat M\vek u\). For large enough \(\varepsilon\) it has a positive value for \(\vek z_+\) and a negative one for \(\vek z_-\), because \(\vek u^{\T}\mat M\vek u > 0\). So \(\mat A\) is neither positive nor negative semidefinite. For \(\mat B\) we take \(\vek z = (\vek 0, \vek v)\) with the value \(-\vek v^{\T}\mat M\vek v < 0\), so \(\mat B\) is not positive semidefinite (the value at \((\vek u, \vek 0)\) is \(\vek u^{\T}\mat K\vek u > 0\), so it is not negative semidefinite either).

Source: CK (10.94) to (10.95) (PDF p. 326): the same form and a remark that the matrices are symmetric. Points 2, 5 and 6 are not from the source.

For frame A (figure 20.22) the matrices are

\[\mat A = \begin{pmatrix} 1416{,}70 & 0 & 500 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 500 \\ 500 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 500 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat B = \begin{pmatrix} 1\,003\,520 & -501\,760 & 0 & 0 \\ -501\,760 & 501\,760 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -500 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -500 \end{pmatrix} \tag{20.40}\]

and \(\det\mat A = 6{,}25 \cdot 10^{10} = (\det\mat M)^2\). For \(\vek u = (1, 0)\) and \(\varepsilon = 10^3\) we get \(\vek z_+^{\T}\mat A\vek z_+ = 1{,}0014 \cdot 10^6\) and \(\vek z_-^{\T}\mat A\vek z_- = -9{,}9858 \cdot 10^5\). So the matrix \(\mat A\) cannot be used as a mass matrix in the eigenproblem of chapter 10: that needed positive definiteness for orthogonality (theorem 10.13).

20.8.2 Complex modes and their roots

For one degree of freedom we looked for the solution in the form \(\mathrm{e}^{st}\) (theorem 9.29). Let us try the same with the state: \(\vek z = \vek w\,\mathrm{e}^{st}\) in the homogeneous equation \(\mat A\dot{\vek z} + \mat B\vek z = \vek 0\) gives \((s\mat A + \mat B)\vek w\,\mathrm{e}^{st} = \vek 0\). Before we know \(s\), we know the form of \(\vek w\): by point 2 of lemma 20.45, \(\vek w = (\vek u, s\vek u)\) and \(\vek u\) solves equation (10.62) of section 10.9.3. (figure 20.23)

Definition 20.46 Eigenpair of the first-order form and complex mode (lastni par zapisa prvega reda in kompleksni način)

A complex number \(s\) and a nonzero column \(\vek w \in \mathbb C^{2n}\) are an eigenpair of the first-order form if \((s\mat A + \mat B)\vek w = \vek 0\). By point 2 of lemma 20.45, then \(\vek w = (\vek u, s\vek u)\) with \(\vek u \ne \vek 0\) and \((s^2\mat M + s\mat C + \mat K)\vek u = \vek 0\). The motion \(\vek q(t) = \mathrm{Re}\,(\vek u\,\mathrm{e}^{st})\) is a complex mode of the system. For \(s = -\alpha + \mathrm{i}\omega\) with \(\omega > 0\), \(\omega\) is the damped angular frequency and \(\zeta = \alpha/|s|\) the damping ratio of the mode, as in definition 9.5.

Source: CK (10.96) to (10.98) (PDF p. 326): \(\vek z = \boldsymbol\theta\,\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\) and "complex modes" (PDF p. 327), (10.111) and (10.112) (PDF p. 328): frequency and ratio from the real and imaginary part. GR (3.69) and (3.70) (PDF p. 193-194).

The name comes from the numbers in \(\vek u\). For an undamped or classically damped system \(\vek u\) can be chosen real, and all parts of the structure reach their extreme position at the same time. If \(\vek u\) cannot be chosen real, each of its elements has its own modulus and its own argument, that is its own amplitude and its own phase, and the parts move with shifted phases. For frame A, \(u_2/u_1 = 1{,}61696 + 0{,}04000\,\mathrm{i}\), which is a phase of \(1{,}417^\circ\) (section 10.9.3). (figure 20.23)

What can we say about the numbers \(s\) before we compute them? For one degree of freedom the roots were \(-\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} \pm \mathrm{i}\,\omega_{\mathrm{d}}\) (theorem 9.43), lying in the left half-plane and meeting on the real axis at \(\zeta = 1\). Is there again no root with \(\mathrm{Re}\,s > 0\) (decay instead of growth)? (figure 20.23)

Lemma 20.47 The eigenvalues lie in the left half-plane in conjugate pairs (koreni so v levi polravnini in v konjugiranih parih)

Let the assumptions of definition 20.44 hold.

  1. If \((s, \vek w)\) is an eigenpair, then \((\bar s, \bar{\vek w})\) is also an eigenpair. The eigenvalues are therefore real or in pairs \(s\), \(\bar s\).
  2. For every eigenpair with \(\vek w = (\vek u, s\vek u)\) let \(m_{\mathrm{u}} = \bar{\vek u}^{\T}\mat M\vek u\), \(c_{\mathrm{u}} = \bar{\vek u}^{\T}\mat C\vek u\) and \(k_{\mathrm{u}} = \bar{\vek u}^{\T}\mat K\vek u\). These numbers are real, \(m_{\mathrm{u}} > 0\), \(k_{\mathrm{u}} > 0\), \(c_{\mathrm{u}} \ge 0\), and \(s\) is a root of the equation \(m_{\mathrm{u}} s^2 + c_{\mathrm{u}} s + k_{\mathrm{u}} = 0\).
  3. If \(c_{\mathrm{u}}^2 < 4 m_{\mathrm{u}} k_{\mathrm{u}}\), then \(s\) is non-real and \(\mathrm{Re}\,s = -c_{\mathrm{u}}/(2 m_{\mathrm{u}}) \le 0\). If \(c_{\mathrm{u}}^2 \ge 4 m_{\mathrm{u}} k_{\mathrm{u}}\), then \(s\) is real and negative. Hence \(\mathrm{Re}\,s \le 0\) for all eigenvalues, and \(\mathrm{Re}\,s = 0\) only for \(c_{\mathrm{u}} = 0\).
Proof

We must show that the reality of the numbers and the sign of the coefficients follow from symmetry and definiteness, and what remains is a quadratic equation with real coefficients.

  1. The matrices \(\mat A\) and \(\mat B\) are real (lemma 20.45, point 3). Conjugating the equation \((s\mat A + \mat B)\vek w = \vek 0\) gives \((\bar s\mat A + \mat B)\bar{\vek w} = \vek 0\) and \(\bar{\vek w} \ne \vek 0\). This proves point 1.
  2. Multiply the equation \((s^2\mat M + s\mat C + \mat K)\vek u = \vek 0\) (lemma 20.45, point 2) from the left by \(\bar{\vek u}^{\T}\). We get \(m_{\mathrm{u}} s^2 + c_{\mathrm{u}} s + k_{\mathrm{u}} = 0\).
  3. Let \(\mat S\) be a real symmetric matrix and \(\vek u = \vek a + \mathrm{i}\vek b\) with real columns. Then \(\bar{\vek u}^{\T}\mat S\vek u = \vek a^{\T}\mat S\vek a + \vek b^{\T}\mat S\vek b + \mathrm{i}(\vek a^{\T}\mat S\vek b - \vek b^{\T}\mat S\vek a)\), and the bracket is zero, because \(\vek a^{\T}\mat S\vek b\) is a scalar equal to its transpose \(\vek b^{\T}\mat S\vek a\). So \(m_{\mathrm{u}}\), \(c_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(k_{\mathrm{u}}\) are real, \(m_{\mathrm{u}}\) and \(k_{\mathrm{u}}\) positive because \(\vek a\) or \(\vek b\) is nonzero, \(c_{\mathrm{u}} \ge 0\).
  4. If \(c_{\mathrm{u}}^2 < 4m_{\mathrm{u}}k_{\mathrm{u}}\), the roots of the quadratic equation are \((-c_{\mathrm{u}} \pm \mathrm{i}\sqrt{4m_{\mathrm{u}}k_{\mathrm{u}} - c_{\mathrm{u}}^2})/(2m_{\mathrm{u}})\), the real part is \(-c_{\mathrm{u}}/(2m_{\mathrm{u}})\). If \(c_{\mathrm{u}}^2 \ge 4m_{\mathrm{u}}k_{\mathrm{u}}\), the roots are real with product \(k_{\mathrm{u}}/m_{\mathrm{u}} > 0\) and sum \(-c_{\mathrm{u}}/m_{\mathrm{u}} \le 0\). Equal signs with a positive product and a non-positive sum mean that both are negative (a sum of zero would mean \(c_{\mathrm{u}} = 0\) and a negative discriminant).

Source: CK, PDF p. 327: real or conjugate pairs and the conjugate vector. GR, PDF p. 194: "conjugate eigensolutions", and PDF p. 195-196: multiplying by the conjugate vector gives a quadratic equation with real coefficients and \(\alpha_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) for positive definite \(\mat C\). The proof with a positive semidefinite \(\mat C\) is not from the source.

Let us inspect the lemma on figure 20.23. We draw the complex plane, horizontally the real part \(\mathrm{Re}\,s\) and vertically \(\mathrm{Im}\,s\), and shade the left half-plane, where by point 3 of the lemma all roots fall. The roots of frame A are \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) and their conjugates, which point 1 of the lemma places mirror-wise across the real axis. Both pairs are shown as a dashed vertical segment between \(s\) and \(\bar s\), which the axis bisects. The roots are very close to the vertical axis, because the damping ratios are \(0{,}02\). That is why the real axis in the figure is stretched.

For mode \(1\), \(m_{\mathrm{u}} = 1808{,}08\) kg, \(c_{\mathrm{u}} = 1416{,}70\) N s/m, \(k_{\mathrm{u}} = 693\,552{,}6\) N/m, so \(c_{\mathrm{u}}^2 - 4m_{\mathrm{u}}k_{\mathrm{u}} = -5{,}014 \cdot 10^9 < 0\) and \(\mathrm{Re}\,s = -1416{,}70/(2 \cdot 1808{,}08) = -0{,}39177\) 1/s, as the NumPy roots give. For mode \(2\), \(m_{\mathrm{u}} = 691{,}12\) kg and \(\mathrm{Re}\,s = -1{,}02493\) 1/s. The difference between them is not in the dashpot, which is the same, but in how much mass moves: in the first mode both floors move in the same direction, \(m_{\mathrm{u}}\) is larger and the damping per unit mass smaller. (figure 20.23)

On the right are the axes and on them the semicircle of roots of cantilever A (chapter 9, theorem 9.43) for growing \(\zeta\). It starts at \(\pm\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) (\(\zeta = 0\), no damping, \(\mathrm{Re}\,s = 0\) by point 3 of the lemma with \(c_{\mathrm{u}} = 0\)), for every \(\zeta < 1\) it lies on the circle of radius \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) (because \(|s|^2 = (\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}})^2 + \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2(1 - \zeta^2) = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\)) and at \(\zeta = 1\) the two ends meet in the double root \(-\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). For \(\zeta > 1\) two real roots \(-\omega_{\mathrm{n}}(\zeta \pm \sqrt{\zeta^2 - 1})\) leave it, negative by point 3 of the lemma. We will need the double root at the end of this section as a near miss.

A near miss for the lemma is a dashpot with a negative coefficient, so that \(\mat C\) is not positive semidefinite. For frame A with \(-c_{\mathrm{d}}\) instead of \(c_{\mathrm{d}}\) the roots are \(+0{,}39177 \pm 19{,}58141\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(+1{,}02493 \pm 51{,}2281\,\mathrm{i}\) 1/s. The real parts are positive, because \(c_{\mathrm{u}} = -1416{,}70 < 0\) and \(\mathrm{Re}\,s = -c_{\mathrm{u}}/(2m_{\mathrm{u}}) > 0\): the amplitude of mode \(1\) doubles every \(\ln 2/0{,}39177 = 1{,}77\) s and does not decay, as it decays with the dashpot \(c_{\mathrm{d}}\) to \(1/\mathrm{e}\) every \(2{,}55\) s. Point 3 of the lemma therefore needs \(c_{\mathrm{u}} \ge 0\), that is a positive semidefinite \(\mat C\). (figure 20.23)

20.8.3 Orthogonality of complex modes

The goal is to expand every motion in complex modes, as we did in real ones (theorem 10.49). For real modes the key was orthogonality with respect to \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) (theorem 10.13). What about here? Let us try the same idea as there: multiply the eigen-equations of two modes by the other mode and subtract.

Theorem 20.48 Orthogonality of complex modes (pravokotnost kompleksnih načinov)

Let the assumptions of definition 20.44 hold and let \((s_{\mathrm{i}}, \vek w_{\mathrm{i}})\) and \((s_{\mathrm{j}}, \vek w_{\mathrm{j}})\) be eigenpairs of the first-order form with \(s_{\mathrm{i}} \ne s_{\mathrm{j}}\). Then

\[\vek w_{\mathrm{j}}^{\T}\mat A\,\vek w_{\mathrm{i}} = 0 , \qquad \vek w_{\mathrm{j}}^{\T}\mat B\,\vek w_{\mathrm{i}} = 0 , \tag{20.41}\]

where \(\vek w_{\mathrm{j}}^{\T}\) is the transposed column without conjugation. For every eigenpair with \(a = \vek w^{\T}\mat A\vek w\) and \(b = \vek w^{\T}\mat B\vek w\) we have \(s\,a + b = 0\).

Proof

We must show that in the difference of the two eigen-equations, each multiplied by the other column, the term with \(\mat B\) cancels and only the term with the factor \(s_{\mathrm{i}} - s_{\mathrm{j}}\) remains.

  1. Multiplying the equation \((s_{\mathrm{i}}\mat A + \mat B)\vek w_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek 0\) from the left by \(\vek w_{\mathrm{j}}^{\T}\): \(s_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek w_{\mathrm{j}}^{\T}\mat A\vek w_{\mathrm{i}} + \vek w_{\mathrm{j}}^{\T}\mat B\vek w_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\).
  2.
